title: Ephemeral container fails to be created for Static Pod
body:
### What happened?

I created an ephemeral container for a Static Pod using the `kubectl debug` command. The command succeed.

```console
❯ kubectl debug --image=busybox --share-processes=true --target=kube-apiserver -n kube-system kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane -- sleep infinity
Targeting container "kube-apiserver". If you don't see processes from this container it may be because the container runtime doesn't support this feature.
Defaulting debug container name to debugger-vgkn4.
```



The API server accepted the ephemeral container:
```console
❯ kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane --output=jsonpath='{.spec.ephemeralContainers}'
[{"command":["sleep","infinity"],"image":"busybox","imagePullPolicy":"Always","name":"debugger-vgkn4","resources":{},"targetContainerName":"kube-apiserver","terminationMessagePath":"/dev/termination-log","terminationMessagePolicy":"File"}]
```

However, the container is not created.

Its status is also not available:

```console
❯ kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane --output=jsonpath='{.status.ephemeralContainerStatuses}'

```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these:

(a) the API server rejects the request to create an ephemeral container for a Static Pod
(b) kubelet creates the ephemeral container, and update the Static Pod's status sub-resource

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Using a recent version of [docker engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/), [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/)  v0.17 or newer, and [kubectl](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/#kubectl) v1.25.0 or newer, create a cluster and create an ephemeral container running `sleep infinity`. Since the ephemeral container is not running, the output of `grep` is 0. 

```
kind create cluster
kubectl debug --image=busybox --share-processes=true --target=kube-apiserver -n kube-system

title: Set v1beta3 as the storage version for flowconrol in 1.27
body:
### What happened?

- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/112306 adds new version `v1beta3` for `flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io` in 1.26. 
- For 1.26, we are setting the storage version to `v1beta2` because vN-1 understands that level.  
- In 1.27, we should change the storage version from `v1beta2` to `v1beta3`.

title: An option to disable Preferred Inter-pod affinity of existing pods
body:
### What would you like to be added?

An option in the scheduler's ComponentConfig to ignore calculating preferences of exiting pods' affinity rules for the general case, and consider them only if the incoming pod has inter pod affinities.  In most cases this is sufficient because pods set inter-pod affinity against each other.

In the past we optimized this case by tracking only pods with inter-pod affinity, but to achieve the next level of scheduling throughput, optionally disabling this feature will be useful.

Specifically, I am suggesting that [PreScore](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3e26e104bdf9d0dc3c4046d6350b93557c67f3f4/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/interpodaffinity/scoring.go#L126) exits early if this option is enabled and the pod has no inter-pod affinities.

### Why is this needed?

To optimize for higher scheduling throughput.

/sig scheduling

/cc @Huang-Wei @alculquicondor

title: kubectl logs -f should wait when in state PodInitializing
body:
It's a minor gripe, but when I'm trying to find out why my pod fails, I tend to "kubectl logs -f [podname]".  A common problem is that it's still initializing and kubectl tells me to go away.

Given that I specified '-f', I'd rather it just hang out in that state and then start piping logs when it's ready, versus me having to manually poll for when it's out of that state.

title: Move `coscheduling` plugin from scheduler-plugins to kubernetes/kubernetes
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add `coscheduling` plugin from https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/scheduler-plugins/tree/master/pkg/coscheduling to the default `kube-scheduler`.

### Why is this needed?

1. `coscheduling` plugin is one the [motivations for the scheduling framework](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-scheduling/624-scheduling-framework/README.md#coscheduling). Number of features in the `kube-scheduler` (e.g. pods waiting in the Permit extension point or https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/103383) were added to support `coscheduling`. It would be easier to develop `kube-scheduler` and its scheduling framework if this plugin was part of kubernetes.

2. `coscheduling` is highly anticipated feature and supporting it by default would be great for adoption.

3. Working with `scheduler-plugins` repository is painful:
  - `scheduler-plugins` does not get patches when default `kube-scheduler` does
  - `scheduler-plugins` is sometimes few releases behind main Kubernetes
  - It is harder to build, deploy (e.g. additional controller has to be deployed) and maintain custom `kube-scheduler`.

---

I know it is not trivial to do it, but I think it is worth discussing it.

---

/sig scheduling

title: Pods need to pre-declare service links iff they want the environment variables created
body:
Forked from #1107 and #386.

Now seems like a good time to decide whether we want to require/encourage/allow pods to declare services they depend upon. Internally, we've often wished we had such a mechanism. 

Not only would pre-declaration reduce accidental/lazy coupling, but it would also improve scalability by reducing the number of iptables rules that must be created. Pre-declaration would also be compatible with Docker's approach to links. If we supported service aliasing in these declarations, that would facilitate dependency injection for tests and a wide variety of deployment adaptation scenarios, which seems like a compelling alternative to custom environment variables, command-line flags, dynamic configuration services, and so on.

However, it at least needs possible to opt out of static declaration and/or enforcement of service dependencies, such as in the case that dependent services are registered dynamically -- think of a proxy, load balancer, web browser, monitoring service, or naming/discovery service running in a container. 

We'd also definitely need to support more flavors of services (cardinal services, headless services, master election, sharding, ...) in order for most clients to be able to utilize the pre-declaration mechanism.

Something else to consider is how to address dependencies pulled in by client libraries, though perhaps it's not unreasonable to require client libraries to be transparent regarding which services they access.

/cc @thockin @smarterclayton

title: Reconciliation strategy of port/IP allocation collisions is flawed
body:
/kind bug

**What happened**:
If you see an event like this on a service:
```
Events:
  Type     Reason                Age   From                             Message
  ----     ------                ----  ----                             -------
  Warning  PortAlreadyAllocated  4s    portallocator-repair-controller  Port 32457 was assigned to multiple services; please recreate service
```

You will attempt to rectify the situation by deleting and recreating the service in hopes it'll be assigned a non-conflicting port. However, on service deletion, ports are blindly released from the allocator without regard to it being allocated by another service.

Therefore, until the repair controller runs (every three minutes), it's possible to create a service and be allocated the same nodeport. This is reproducible by manually specifying the nodeport on the service at recreation. 

cc @bowei @MrHohn

title: Proposal: Add status.data in `Job/CronJob` to pass job output
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently, the status section in `Job/CronJob` workload contains fields `succeeded/active/failed`, etc.
But usually we need the job to pass the output data, to let us do more logic rely on the result data.

So propose to add `status.data` in `Job/CronJob` to pass the job output, the data field type could be a string, then it can support more complex json string.

Demo:
```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
...
status:
  completionTime: "2022-11-04T15:38:37Z"
  startTime: "2022-11-04T15:37:14Z"
  succeeded: 1
  data: '{"repo":"my-repo","imageTag":"v1.4.4-24.g5e8cc5be"}' // output data
```

### Why is this needed?

Usually, we run a job A, then run a controller or a script which need the job output data to do more logic.
But currently the `Job/CronJob` status does not support data output, so propose to add `status.data` to achieve it.

title: windows cpu maximum incorrect with more than one processor group
body:
### What happened?

When submitting a windows pod using resource limits on a node with more than one processor group, the specified `CpuMaximum` count is incorrect due to the usage of `runtime.NumCPU()` which does not take processor groups into account.

For example:
- node with 96 cores
- cpu limit 94
- `runtime.NumCPU()` returns `48`

This results in a CPU maximum of 10000 since the range is from [1, 10000]:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_windows.go#L82..L91

```go
	limit := int64(94 * 1000)
	numCPU := 48
	fmt.Println(((10000 * limit) / int64(numCPU) / 1000))

// Output:
// 19583
```

Our initial goal for this was to limit a process to not use all available CPU and therefore render the node uncontrollable. 

### What did you expect to happen?

A CPU maximum of `9791` instead of `10000` for that specific case. For the calculation, it should use the CPU count for all available processor groups instead of just the current one. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Launch a node with a lot of CPUs, for example [a Azure Standard_D96a_v4](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/dav4-dasv4-series) and schedule the following pod on it:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: debug-windows
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
  - args:
    - ping /t 127.0.0.1
    command:
    - cmd
    - /c
    image: mcr.microsoft.com/windows/nanoserver:1809
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    name: main
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "94"
        memory: 300Gi
      requests:
        cpu: "90"
        memory: 200Gi
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/os: windows
```

Then SSH into the node and inspect the running container using `crictl.exe inspect <id>`. The `cpu_maximum` value will be set to 10000. 

### Anything else we need to know?

[tklauser/numcpus](https://github.com/tklause

title: Add the new kernel scheduler load balance algorithm to ipvs-scheduler option on kube-proxy ipvs-mode
body:
The ipvs mode `ipvs-scheduler` limit the scheduler algorithm to :
```
              rr - Round Robin: distributes jobs equally amongst the available real servers.

              wrr - Weighted Round Robin: assigns jobs to real servers  proportionally  to  there
              real  servers'  weight.  Servers with higher weights receive new jobs first and get
              more jobs than servers with lower weights. Servers with equal weights get an  equal
              distribution of new jobs.

              lc - Least-Connection: assigns more jobs to real servers with fewer active jobs.

              wlc  -  Weighted Least-Connection: assigns more jobs to servers with fewer jobs and
              relative to the real servers' weight (Ci/Wi). This is the default.

              lblc - Locality-Based Least-Connection: assigns  jobs  destined  for  the  same  IP
              address to the same server if the server is not overloaded and available; otherwise
              assign jobs to servers with fewer jobs, and keep it for future assignment.

              lblcr - Locality-Based Least-Connection with Replication: assigns jobs destined for
              the  same  IP  address  to  the  least-connection node in the server set for the IP
              address. If all the node in the server set are over loaded, it picks up a node with
              fewer  jobs  in  the  cluster  and  adds it in the sever set for the target. If the
              server set has not been modified for the specified time, the most  loaded  node  is
              removed from the server set, in order to avoid high degree of replication.

              dh  -  Destination Hashing: assigns jobs to servers through looking up a statically
              assigned hash table by their destination IP addresses.

              sh - Source Hashing: assigns jobs  to  servers  through  looking  up  a  statically
              assigned  hash  table  by their source IP addresse

title: kube-apiserver using unregistered and unusual label
body:
### What happened?

The code at
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/86f3fa94f1b75da275a8040e4155840a7b473dc1/pkg/controlplane/instance.go#L126 specifies a ~annotation~ label that API servers set on Leases (each API server registers its own lease).

https://k8s.io/docs/concepts/architecture/leases/#api-server-identity is likely to document this once v1.26 is released; the alpha for API server identity didn't get documented.

Here's the problems:
- as a project, we use `kubernetes.io` as the domain for labels and annotations - see https://k8s.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/
  - there are a couple of exceptions in https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/audit-annotations/, FWIW
- if we document and register this `k8s.io/component` label, people may well confuse it with https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/#app-kubernetes-io-component and use the wrong thing

### What did you expect to happen?

I guess ideally we'd have proposed and then been able to review docs for this when it went alpha, and in that alternative history the discrepancy would have been much more obvious, and it could have been fixed earlier.

I think we should fix it so that we follow the convention of nearly every other annotation used in Kubernetes code.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Look at the source code. Any text editor would work.

title: client-go's InClusterConfig does not implement documented API discovery heuristics
body:
### What happened?

client-go uses `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` to discover the API service address:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/67bde9a1023d1805e33d698b28aa6fad991dfb39/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/config.go#L507-L541 

This at odds with the documentation at https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/access-api-from-pod/#directly-accessing-the-rest-api which states:

> While running in a Pod, the Kubernetes apiserver is accessible via a Service named `kubernetes` in the `default` namespace. Therefore, Pods can use the `kubernetes.default.svc` hostname to query the API server. Official client libraries do this automatically.

client-go does **not** do this. Though, it includes a TODO:

```go
		// TODO: switch to using cluster DNS.
		Host:            "https://" + net.JoinHostPort(host, port),
```

Ambiguity around the documented client discovery policy causes problems for client libraries; and cloud providers continue to promulgate the (now undocumented) legacy env configuration, e.g. https://github.com/Azure/AKS/issues/3183.

Would you accept a PR to remove the environment based in-cluster configuration in favor of always using `kubernetes.default.svc`?

### What did you expect to happen?

client-go should use `kubernetes.default.svc` and it should not honor the `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` environment variable.

OR the client docs should be updated with the proper heuristics.

title: Each time a pod exits, kubelet cpu usage increases with cgroups v2
body:
### What happened?

When a pod exits, there is some problem in the cgroup cleanup. The containerd cgroup within the kubelet cgroup does not get deleted, and then the kubelet keeps trying to delete the kubelet cgroup, which fails because of the child cgroup. The kubelet continues to try to delete the cgroup every 1 second or so. As pods start and stop, the number of cgroups in this state grows, and the kubelet process itself gradually consumes more and more cpu, until it gets to 100% of available.

Here are snippets of the /var/log/syslog for a single example. title: [Winkernel Proxier] Implement support for internal traffic policy in windows kube proxy
body:
### What would you like to be added?

- These are changes as per KEPS: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-network/2086-service-internal-traffic-policy
- When a InternalTrafficPolicy is set to Local, consider only local endpoints for creating cluster ip load balancer.
- When both InternalTrafficPolicy and ExternalTrafficPolicy is set to Local, ignore creating remote endpoints.

### Why is this needed?

- With these changes, kube proxy will take constant time always for load balancer creation.
- Implementing InternalTrafficPolicy feature will optimize the load balancer recreation during rolling updates.
- This will also minimize the leaking of traffic through stale deleting endpoints during rolling update.

title: Change in semantics for the device plugin registration process
body:
### What happened?

The following refactoring of the kubelet's devicemanager was done as part of the 1.25 release: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/db88676c20629354d8eeb4b7014ae7884481ffca

As part of this, a change in semantics was (unintentionally) introduced which is breaking at least one 3rd party plugin. The logic required to go back to the old semantics is fairly straight forward. However, it's not obvious that we should actually go back to the old semantics because (at least in my opinion) the new semantics are actually more correct.

Previously, the kubelet's devicemanager would do the following upon receiving a plugin registration request:
1. Register the plugin
2. Launch a go-routine to connect to the gRPC service being served by the plugin (with a timeout of 10s)
3. Return

This gave the plugin the opportunity to first register itself with the kubelet and then (within a 10s time window) start its gRPC server.

The new semantics are similar, except that no go-routine is launched to connect to the gRPC service. The connection is attempted synchronously. This means that the plugin must now start serving its gRPC server *before* registering itself with the kubelet. Otherwise the registration call will fail.

As mentioned before, this change was not necessarily intentional, but it's also not clear if it should be reverted. It brings the device plugin's custom registration process more in line with the kubelet's standard registration process and the order is actually a bit more intuitive. Why bother registering if you aren't able to start serving your API?

The first plugin to report this problem was the KubeVirt plugin and a discussion of the issue can be found here:
https://groups.google.com/g/kubevirt-dev/c/HE2lVvsLd3Y

The question now is -- should we revert the kubelet code to the old semantics to avoid breaking plugins that rely on this (somewhat awkward) ordering. Or do we leave the new semantics in place and send out a

body:
Today you need multiple encryption providers to communicate to the API server if data stored in etcd is stale (i.e. the KMS v1beta1 API has no way to communicate staleness). title: Allow scaling up to meet PDB constraints
body:
**What would you like to be added**:

Currently if you have a PDB spec like `minAvailable: 1`, and a HPA defining minReplicas=1 and maxReplicas=N, you may end up in a scenario where disruptions get "stuck" if the HPA has scaled to 1. At any point an increase in load could cause the HPA to scale up to 2+, allowing the PDB to be satisfied, which leads to a weird scenario where a disruption can only occur if there is high load.

Ideally, the PDB would be able to trigger the HPA to scale up to meet constraints. For example, if I have 1 replica and a disruption is triggered, scale up a new replica first, then terminate the old one. Given an HPA is in place, I have already clearly specified I am OK with my pod being scaled up, so this shouldn't have negative impact on stateful workloads.

Some more context: https://github.com/istio/istio/issues/12602

title: Node lifecycle controller takes too long to mark pods NotReady
body:
### What happened?

We run a cluster spread across 3 sites/availability zones, and when an entire site becomes unreachable at once we observe that the node lifecycle controller takes too long to mark all the pods NotReady.

Example logs:
```
I0713 16:03:36.538269       1 node_lifecycle_controller.go:1092] node ... hasn't been updated for 20.062703613s.
…
I0713 16:04:48.014322       1 node_lifecycle_controller.go:1092] node ... hasn't been updated for 1m27.527087635s.
```

We set `--node-monitor-grace-period=20s`, and the first node is processed right at the 20s mark. But it takes over a minute until it processes the last node.

I believe this is because the main loop in monitorNodeHealth processes each node serially.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17bf864c1fc20e4badc9a6e0659c5190310462e1/pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/node_lifecycle_controller.go#L796
And processing each node requires setting the ready status of each of its pods to false, serially.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17bf864c1fc20e4badc9a6e0659c5190310462e1/pkg/controller/util/node/controller_utils.go#L119

With enough nodes and pods, this time quickly adds up and leaves unreachable pods in endpoints for too long.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the node lifecycle controller to mark pods on unreachable nodes NotReady soon after the nodes exceeded the node monitor grace period.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We observe this with a cluster of ~150 nodes spread evenly across 3 sites, so ~50 nodes become unreachable at once when we drop a site.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is somewhat similar to #110341, but at a different stage. We tested with 1.25.2 as well (it contains the fix for #110341) and observed the same behavior.

title: RoleBindings deleted by namespace finalizer before other objects using those permissions finish stopping/finalizing
body:
### What happened?

When you delete a Namespace, Kubernetes automatically deletes all the objects in that namespace. 

However, if you have a workload in that namespace (e.g. a custom resource) AND the workload has a finalizer AND the controller that manages that finalizer is granted permission by a RoleBinding in the same namespace, then when the Namespace is deleted, the workload object and the RoleBinding are deleted at roughly the same time. So the finalizer controller may (often) deadlock, unable to use the permissions that have been revoked and unable to remove the finalizer on the workload object. This then also blocks the namespace finalizer and namespace deletion.

The only way to recover fromt his situation is the manually remove the finalizer on the workload object. But removing finalizers manually is often unsafe and can cause memory leaks or worse. Worse, namespace tenants won't be able to delete the finalizer either, because their RoleBindings will have been deleted too; a cluster admin would have to do it.

### What did you expect to happen?

title: Higher kube-apiserver memory usage k8s 1.20.15 vs 1.21.14
body:
### What happened?

After upgrading k8s cluster from 1.20.15 to 1.21.14, we noticed significantly higher memory usage from kube-apiserver pods.

Below are the graphs that show clearly the difference in memory consumption before and after. The spike in the middle is when the control-plane nodes were being rolled to 1.21.

This is a plot of `container_memory_working_set_bytes`.
On 1.20.15 for leader was 5.7Gi, other pods 3Gi.
On 1.21.14 for leader is 9.6Gi, other pods 5.5Gi.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/89029096/182935427-c1ca78d5-76f3-47c7-85c6-27f9a696f2cb.png)

However, if instead `process_resident_memory_bytes` was plotted, memory usage actually decreased.
On 1.20.15 it was 9.6Gi, on 1.21.14 it is 5.1Gi.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/89029096/182935628-5cc9a94b-4cf5-4c61-9983-f07f09b3f38e.png)

From my understanding the difference is that `container_memory_working_set_bytes` includes active cache, but the numbers still doesn't quite make sense.
Using `node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes` the control-plane nodes have 5Gi less memory available on 1.21.14, meaning the new 1.21.14 control-plane is using much more memory.

I looked at the k8s 1.21 changelogs and did not find any entries for increased memory usage.
The cluster is quite large at ~100 nodes, with 3 control-plane nodes.

**Questions:**
Is `container_memory_working_set_bytes` an appropriate measure of kube-apiserver memory consumption?
If so, is there an explanation for increased memory usage for kube-apiserver going from 1.20.15 to 1.21.14?

### What did you expect to happen?

No significant change in kube-apiserver memory usage.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Compare `container_memory_working_set_bytes` of kube-apiserver between k8s 1.20 vs 1.21

_No response_

title: Kubelet cannot finish terminating a pod that uses a PVC with `volumeMode: Block` if the underlying block device is accidentally disconnected from the node
body:
### What happened?

A pod uses a PVC with `volumeMode: Block`. The block volume is backed by a block device on the node (which is created by some CSI storage providers).  If the underlying block device corresponding to the volume is accidentally disconnected from the node (due to network, hardware problem, etc...), the user cannot delete the pod. The pod would be stuck in terminating forever since Kubelet refuses to unmount the block volume. This prevents the user from cleaning up the pod and spinning up a new replacement pod thus leading to a long service degradation. For example, if the pod is part of a statefulset, the replacement pod cannot come up due to the old pod being stuck terminating. 




### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should be able to finish terminating a pod when the corresponding block device is already removed from the node.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install a CSI storage provider that supports `volumeMode: Block`. For example, [Longhorn](https://github.com/longhorn/longhorn)
2. Deloy a statefulset that has volumeClaimTemplates with `volumeMode: Block`. For example:
    <details close>
    <summary>click to open yaml manifest</summary>

    ```
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Service
    metadata:
      name: test-bv
      labels:
        app: test-bv
    spec:
      ports:
      - port: 80
        name: test-bv
      selector:
        app: test-bv
      type: NodePort
    ---
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: StatefulSet
    metadata:
      name: test-bv
      namespace: default
    spec:
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app: test-bv
      serviceName: "test-bv"
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            app: test-bv
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Always
          terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 10

          - name: test-bv

title: Default `.spec.replicas` value for HorizontalPodAutoscaler
body:
When applying a HorizontalPodAutoscaler on a resource which has a missing `.spec.replicas` value (which may be the default state for any given custom resource), it fails with something like:
```
Internal error occurred: the spec replicas field ".spec.replicas" does not exist
```
The immediate workaround is to set `.spec.replicas` to 1 but I wonder if we could instead interpret the missing field with the default value of 1 or instead looking at `.status.replicas` which may hold the correct value.

Ref https://github.com/apache/camel-k/issues/3132

title: HPA: scaling replica count directly based on a metric
body:
### What would you like to be added?

HPA policy where simpler algorithm is used: desiredReplicas = factor * currentMetricValue.

I'd like this to be supported at least for app/custom metrics.

### Why is this needed?

Current scaling algorithm: desiredReplicas = ceil[currentReplicas * ( currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue )]

Has several issues:
* It's harder to understand (one can easily find several k8s bugs about its impact)
* It does not allow handling properly situations when there's a significant delay between deployment count change, and (custom) metric value change. In such situations it causes:
  * very excessive deployment counts on scale up (which is natural result of delay with currentReplicas*currentMetricValue relation),
  * massive amount of flapping (metric drops fast after the delay due to excessive deployment count, and the resulting sharp deployment count drop causes then immediately drastic metric increase)

One could avoid this by telling HPA to act slower than the delay, but when that delay can be significant, HPA can then be too slow to be useful.

These issues could be avoided by HPA supporting additional "desiredReplication = factor * currentMetricValue"  algorithm/policy.

Use-case example:
* Custom metric on service request queue (e.g. number of queued items not yet being processed)
* HPA that scales replica count for backends that serve these requests, based on that custom metric
* Requests taking tens of seconds to complete (= delay impacting custom metric change)
* Desired scaling response time being in single-digit seconds

title: Pod Security Standards vs Service Mesh
body:
### What happened?

Pod Security Standards (https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/) went beta at v1.23. Pod Security Standards are direct ascendant of Pod Security Policies which were deprecated in v1.21 and removed in v1.25.

Pod Security Standards  definies three policies: Privileged, Baseline and Restricted. Enforcing Baseline or Restricted policy, would limit allowed capabilities that Pod can use. The problem is that when enforced both policies disallows for NET_ADMIN capability which is required i.e. to run sidecar of Service Mesh like ISTIO (https://istio.io/latest/docs/ops/deployment/requirements/#pod-requirements)

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect that in a Namespace that enforces one of Pod Sscurity Standards policy can exist ISTIO-aware Pods. I'm aware that NET_ADMIN is very powerfull capability, but without it we can't have both of these.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create Namespace which enforces Baseline or Restricted policy and allows auto-injecting ISTIO sidecar.
2. Check if Istio sidecar will start.

### Anything else we need to know?

I think there is a need for:
- another Pod Security Standards lighter than Baseline dedidated to Service Meshes
- mechanism for defining custom PSS policies
- PSS annotation(s) that add extensions/exclusions to enforced policy
-

title: Deletecollection failing after 34 seconds
body:
### What happened?

In a cluster with large enough numbers of objects, it seems to be impossible to clean them up with `deletecollection`.  Because the deletecollection is failing while listing the objects from etcd.  The failure happens after exactly 34 seconds, due to the 34-second max timeout introduced in PR #96901 (cc @tkashem for insight on that PR).



### What did you expect to happen?

The deletecollection should be able to run for longer, and succeed.

I recognise that there are still risks of the API server using too much RAM, if deleting a very large collection due to issue #90743.  But, until _that_ issue is fixed, it seems like allowing `deletecollection` to run for longer might be a good idea.  As far as I can tell, the 34 second timeout does not apply to normal LIST calls, so on that basis I feel it should not apply to the giant unchunked LIST call that happens inside `deletecollection`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a few hundred thousand objects of some particular type.  (Argo workflowtaskresults happen to be the type I'm looking at while I write this)
2. Call deletecollection. (Optionally passing some kind of fieldSelector, but I don't think that's essential)
3. Observe that a 504 failure code is logged in kube-audit logs, and that a log entry similar to this is logged by the API Server `"List etcd3" key:<some key>,...,limit:0 ... (total time: 34000ms)`  (In practice, the total time may be a little over 34000 ms).
4. As far as I can tell, the delete collection really has failed at this point.  I notice that PR #96901 says that, in general, "The go-routine can keep running, while the timeout logic will return a timeout to the client" but I don't _think_ that's what's happening here.  I think that, because the 34 sec timeout is used in the context of the etcd call, the etcd list call really does fail, and so the code never proceeds to actually deleting anything.

title: Generic ephemeral volume e2e tests may fail in a multizone cluster
body:
Let's assume this scenario:

- linux node, zone A, tainted
- windows node, zone B, untainted

In a multizone cluster, while trying to run the generic ephemeral volume tests in Windows nodes it might be possible that a volume that's supposed to be for a Windows node is created in the zone for the Linux node instead. 

The generic ephemeral storage tests use [different patterns](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/889e60ab33/test/e2e/storage/testsuites/ephemeral.go#L59):

- [Testpattern: Generic Ephemeral-volume (default fs) (late-binding)] ephemeral
- [Testpattern: Generic Ephemeral-volume (default fs) (immediate)] ephemeral
- [Testpattern: Generic Ephemeral-volume (block volmode) (late-binding)] ephemeral

This issue is happening because we're using the immediate testpattern which is not compatible with a multizone cluster.

/kind failing-test
/sig storage

title: DeleteCollection API fails if request body is non-empty
body:
### What happened?

In v1.25.0, invoking the DeleteCollection API with a non-empty request body fails with HTTP 500 - the error message is `no kind "DeleteOptions" is registered for version "meta.k8s.io/v1" in scheme "pkg/api/legacyscheme/scheme.go:30"`

All DeleteCollection APIs are specced (in the OpenAPI spec, eg `deleteCoreV1CollectionNamespacedPod` for the repro below) to take a `DeleteOptions` in the request body, and the simplest such value is `{}`. I maintain the Rust API client library, and my library's generated code always sets the request body to `{}` when all the delete options are default (the serialized form of a `DeleteOptions` with no set fields), which is how I noticed this bug.

### What did you expect to happen?

This works with v1.24 and earlier.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

(This repro uses `curl` for full control of the request headers and body.)

1. Create kind cluster of v1.25.0

1. Create client-cert.pem containing the private key and cert extracted from kubectl config. (curl's `--cert` expects PEM-encoded private key followed by PEM-encoded cert in the file.)

    ```sh
    (kubectl config view -o json --raw | jq '.users[0].user["client-certificate-data"]' -r | base64 -d; kubectl config view -o json --raw | jq '.users[0].user["client-key-data"]' -r | base64 -d) >client-cert.pem
    ```

1. Try to delete all pods with label `foo=bar`

    ```sh
    $ base="$(kubectl config view -o json --raw | jq '.clusters[0].cluster.server' -r)"

    $ curl -kD - -XDELETE --cert client-cert.pem -H 'content-type:application/json' -H 'content-length:2' --data-raw '{}' "${base}/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods?labelSelector=foo%3Dbar"

    HTTP/2 500 
    audit-id: b3c6ed2c-1e53-48a7-8a7c-324706c86ae3
    cache-control: no-cache, private

title: Remove getting PrevKv for apiserver for most kind of objects
body:
Details: 
For etcd, whether it is native etcd or other customized version of etcd, if K8s apiserver wants to obtain PrevKv, etcd needs to do a Range operation for every event.
Range for native etcd is operated on local boltdb, it takes time in less than 1s, on the order of ms. But the aggregation of all range operations can take seconds.

Given the below code in etcd3/watcher.go where apiserver is taking all objects of a kind (e.g, Pod, Node, ConfigMap, etc), oldObj is not needed. So in this case, etcd's operation for getting PrevKv can be removed. 

```
// transform transforms an event into a result for user if not filtered.
func (wc *watchChan) transform(e *event) (res *watch.Event) {
	curObj, oldObj, err := wc.prepareObjs(e)
......
	switch {
	case e.isDeleted:
......
	case e.isCreated:
......
	case e.isProgressNotify:
......
	default:
		if wc.acceptAll() {
			res = &watch.Event{
				Type:       watch.Modified,
				Object:     curObj,
			}
			return res
		}
......
}
```

If this is a valid change, I'd like to submit the proposal and change of code, and love to hear your suggesitons, thanks
/sig api-machinery
/sig scalability
cc @wojtek-t

title: Why are all pods on this node restarted?
body:
### What happened?

First of all, this problem has been going on for a long time. I have analyzed some conclusions, but still can't find the root cause.
For a while, we had a collective restart of pods on many kubernetes nodes that powered by containerd as the runtime.
We didn't know why, so we took the nodes offline and started looking for the reason.
After a period of analysis, we found that:

#### Missing configuration

The original runtime of these nodes is docker. We follow the method of this [blog](https://www.jetstack.io/blog/cri-migration/) to change the runtime from docker to containerd. BUT, we FORGOT to configure this:

```
[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runc]
  ...
  [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runc.options]
    SystemdCgroup = true
```

to use the systemd cgroup driver in `/etc/containerd/config.toml` with runc.  After I added this config, **everything was fine**.

#### Wrong cgroup path

Therefore, we found that the cgroup path of the container is NOT the same as the normal node, they are like this:

```
$ cat /proc/80595/cgroup

title: client-go: set the default of the 'host' label to an empty string for client metrics
body:
### What happened?

the default value of the `host`  label is `none` for all client metrics, see

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1f02f43ec6910cbcd46222b16a2f3965458e5e45/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request.go#L792-L795

in a query, we want the user to use `{host!=""}` rather than `{host!="none"}`.
in reality, the `RESTClient.base` may never be empty, so the label is never set to `none` in a real cluster?

title: Kube-proxy facing locking timeout in large clusters during load test with services enabled
body:
Follows from discussion in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/48052

We noticed this while performing load test on 4000 node clusters with services enabled. The iptables restore step in the proxier fails with:
```
E0625 09:03:14.873338       5 proxier.go:1574] Failed to execute iptables-restore: failed to acquire old iptables lock: timed out waiting for the condition
```

And the reason quite likely is because of "huge" size of iptables (tens of MBs) as we run 30 pods per node and each pod is part of exactly one service
=> 30 * 4000 = 120k service endpoints (and these updates happen on all 4000 nodes)

cc @kubernetes/sig-network-misc @kubernetes/sig-scalability-misc @danwinship @wojtek-t

title: service.alpha.kubernetes.io/tolerate-unready-endpoints misuses the Endpoints API object
body:
**BUG REPORT**: The [addEndpointSubset method](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/endpoint/endpoints_controller.go#L509-L528) of the endpoints controller is currently adding EndpointSubsets with Address that are unready base on the `service.alpha.kubernetes.io/tolerate-unready-endpoints` annotation. 

At a minimum those addresses need to be added as EndpointSubsets with UnreadyAddresses, and the decision on whether to add them should be made, based on the annotation or its equivalent field, in the default DNS implementation's [handleEndpointUpdate](https://github.com/kubernetes/dns/blob/master/pkg/dns/dns.go#L320-L381) and [generateRecordsforHeadlessService](https://github.com/kubernetes/dns/blob/master/pkg/dns/dns.go#L480-L520) methods.

We might also consider simply always creating SRV records without respect to readiness. That is, the DNS implementation could disregard readiness for the endpoints associated with a headless services when creating SRV records and only worry about readiness when creating A records. However, if we consider this approach, we might want to give careful thought to what we might break.

Before proceeding with the implementation of either, I'd like to get feedback (and maybe participation) from SIG Network. Particularly as some clusters may not use the kube-dns add-on. I'd like to fix this in the 1.8 - 1.9 time frame if possible.

 /kind bug

title: GCE EnsureLoadBalancer() for static IPs should error if the IP is not static
body:
Seen by inspection, potentially a cause for a user-reported symptom.

Setup:
1. Create a Service, type=LoadBalancer
2. A public IP is assigned
3. Copy that public IP to the Service's locadBalancerIP field

The assumption is that this guarantees your Service will use that IP.  That's true, but it was true without step 3.  If you now delete this Service and create a new one with that loadBalancerIP, it will fail because that IP is not a GCE static address, and was released with your Service.

We should instead throw an error if you do step 3, but have not manually promoted that IP to a static IP through GCE.  This will force users to acknowledge that *they* own that IP, not kubernetes.

This behavior, combined with the fact that we log-and-forget failures to release the IP can result in public addresses being "promoted" to static and left there, without the user having done that action == a leak.

title: Service controller removes unschedulable nodes from LB pools
body:
This is not obviously correct.  It's subtle - a cordon is usually part of a draining operation, so it kind of makes sense to remove things from it.  The service controller removes cordoned nodes from LB pools, but the pods themselves seem to remain in service endpoint lists.  But in the case of an OnlyLocal service, the pods on a cordoned node are cut off.

The GCE L7 LB controller seems to do the same.

For better or worse, we use that Unschedulable flag for a few things. Perhaps we could disentangle it from the "is master" logic (which I think is a taint now?) and change this.

example use case: A customer creates a new node pool and cordons the old one, to move workload.  This would kill traffic to any OnlyLocal Services.

We need a way to know which machines to count as LB targets (gateways)

We need a way to know when a machine is actually going away, so we can remove it from LB pools gracefully.

I don't have bandwidth to drive this right now, but perhaps we need something like graceful deletion or finalizers for nodes?  Or maybe we need a taint that is specific to "do not use for network gatewaying", so reboot operators could be cleaner wrt LBs...  @philips maybe interesting to your reboot operator.

title: kube-dns should support custom tolerations
body:
/kind feature

(note: we're not using the latest Kubernetes version yet, but I couldn't find any changes related to this in the latest updates, so please close this if I simply updating will fix this for us)

Currently, when you edit a kube-dns deployment, some changes are persisted (f.e. adding a `nodeAffinity` config block), while others are reverted (f.e. adding a second toleration to the already existing `CriticalAddonsOnly` toleration).

The last example is problematic for us (running on GKE).

We have two node pools:

- a regular node pool with a taint applied to the nodes to only allow pods to run on them that we manually approve
- a preemptible node pool without any taints

We want `kube-dns` (and any other critical pods) to run on the regular nodes for better uptime (see also: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/41125), so we update its deployment with the following blocks:

```yaml
affinity:
  nodeAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: type
          operator: In
          values:
          - regular
```

```yaml
tolerations:
- key: CriticalAddonsOnly # this one is already present by default
  operator: Exists
- key: dedicated # we add this one to allow scheduling on the tainted regular nodes
  operator: Equal
  value: regular
  effect: NoSchedule
```

After saving this change, for a brief moment, the pods are scheduled as expected, but moments after, the change is reverted, and specifically the added toleration is removed, the nodeAffinity is still there however.

Can we make toleration changes persistent and not be reverted by the API itself?

title: Service Status should include information similar to workload controller status
body:
The workload controllers now report replicas, ready replicas, and available replicas. It would be useful for Service.Status to contain similar information. The information could be easily aggregated from Endpoints. We can't implement available replicas until/unless minReadySeconds moves into Pod/Kubelet, but we could report total and ready replicas. That would make it easier to detect common issues such as mismatched selector and labels and determining when one can expect a service to be reachable.

I thought there was an issue about this, but only found ones relating to cloudprovider LB status.

/kind feature
/sig network

cc @kubernetes/sig-network-feature-requests @kubernetes/sig-apps-feature-requests

title: NetworkPolicy: consider defining empty `from` as "none"
body:
Covered in #51351 comments.

What we SHOULD HAVE DONE, perhaps, is define an empty NetworkPolicyPeer (no podSelector or namespaceSelector or ipBlock) as "none". Perhaps we should do that now, and update docs to say:

Default-deny ingress:

```
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: foobar
spec:
  policyTypes: [ "Ingress" ]
  ingress:
  - from: [{}]
```

Default-deny egress:

```
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: foobar
spec:
  policyTypes: [ "Egress" ]
  egress:
  - to: [{}]
```

Default-deny everything:

```
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: foobar
spec:
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress" ]
  ingress:
  - from: [{}]
  egress:
  - to: [{}]
```

Why?

1) future rollbacks where a `from` field was newly added will default to fail-closed rather than undefined

2) If we normalize and document this syntax, we have an opportunity in v2 to get rid of the `policyTypes` field and the weird "ingress:[] means deny-all, but ingress:{from:[]} means allow all" semantics.

title: Allow type LoadBalancer for Headless service for specialized proxiers
body:
## Feature requested

Allow type LoadBalancer for Headless service for specialized proxiers. A service of type LoadBalancer with clusterIP None is rejected with:

```
# kubectl create -f /etc/kubernetes/svc-headless-lb/svc.yaml 
The Service "alpine" is invalid: spec.clusterIPs[0]: Invalid value: "None": may not be set to 'None' for LoadBalancer services
```
Even if the [service.kubernetes.io/service-proxy-name](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/#servicekubernetesioservice-proxy-name) label is used.

<details><summary>manifest</summary>

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: alpine
  labels:
    service.kubernetes.io/service-proxy-name: kpng-example
spec:
  ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack
  selector:
    app: alpine
  type: LoadBalancer
  clusterIP: None
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false
  ports:
  - port: 5001
    name: nc
```

</details>

This is just a check, not that anything fails if the combination is allowed.

I want that check removed for specialized proxiers.

## Why?

A specialized proxier using the [service.kubernetes.io/service-proxy-name](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/#servicekubernetesioservice-proxy-name) label may handle external traffic, while it can't handle internal traffic to the `ClusterIP`. For such a service the combination `type:LoadBalancer` and `clusterIP:None` makes perfect sense. Otherwise one must document something like:

> Even though the clusterIP is defined with valid endpoints, **you can't use it** since the specialized proxier don't care about clusterIP.

Access to the service via DNS addresses which (provided for Headless services) is proably something the service _can_ handle, which make this feature _valuable_ and not just a cosmetic thing.

title: Pods on node with temporary unknown status never marked ready again
body:
# Summary

When a node (kubelet) is unable to heartbeat with the apiserver for a long time, the node-lifecycle controller sets the status of the node to "unknown" and immediately adds the following taint to the node 
```
  - effect: NoSchedule
    key: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable
    timeAdded: "2019-08-03T00:34:24Z"
```
And immediately marks all pods on the node as `NotReady`. This is done [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/node_lifecycle_controller.go#L796)

5 seconds later (this is the frequencey of the node lifecycle contrller's node health checking loop) the following taint is added

```
  - effect: NoExecute
    key: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable
    timeAdded: "2019-08-03T00:34:30Z"
```

Which evicts most pods from the node.
However, in some cases the node heartbeats *after* the first taint is added but *before* the second taint is added. In this case, pods don't get evicted from the node however *they stay not ready despite the fact that all containers on the pod are ready and the node the pods are running on is now healthy (Ready)*. This state never recovers without manual intervention, either by marking the pod ready manually, or deleting it if there is a controller that will bring it back.  

Expected is that if a pod is scheduled on a healthy node and all containers of the pod are ready, the pod should be marked as ready regardless of edge cases of lifecycle transition of the node.

# Repro

One way to repro this is to cause a node to fail to heartbeat for long enough that the node goes into unknown status, but not long enough that the no execute taint is added.
I did this by breaking comms with the apiserver with the kubelet using some iptables hacks:

./break-network.sh
```
#!/bin/bash

# ips the kubelet uses to talk to the apiserver
ips=""

for ip in $ips; do
    echo $ip
    iptables -I OUTPUT -d $ip -m conntrack --ctstate NEW,RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j DROP
d

title: MultiCIDRRangeAllocator requires node reboot to assign ranges
body:
### What happened?

When the `ClusterCIDR` is created *after* a node has booted, addresses are not defined;

```
> kubectl get cc -A
No resources found
> kubectl create -f kubernetes/clustercidr.yaml
clustercidr.networking.k8s.io/default created
> kubectl get cc -A
NAME      PERNODEHOSTBITS   IPV4          IPV6         AGE
default   8                 11.0.0.0/16   1100::/112   5s
> kubectl get node -o json vm-002 | jq .spec
{}
# (reboot node vm-002 ...)
> kubectl get node -o json vm-002 | jq .spec
{
  "podCIDR": "11.0.0.0/24",
  "podCIDRs": [
    "11.0.0.0/24",
    "1100::/120"
  ]
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Addresses shall be allocated for all nodes with empty `spec.podCIDRs` when a `ClusterCIDR` is created (*then* they become immutable).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Probably the easiest way is to check the controller:

* Create the controller with MultiCIDRRangeAllocator enabled and configured
* Create a `ClusterCIDR`
* Check the node.spec on the controller
* Reboot it
* Check again


### Anything else we need to know?

I can't see a clean way to start a cluster without this fixed. It the cni-plugin requires spec.podCIDRs to work the node will not become ready until it's rebooted.

As a work-around in my test env I can create a controller that is _not a node_ in the cluster (I think k3s and AWS does like this).

title: dynamic resource allocation: ensure PrepareResources called before CNI invoked
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Ensure that `PrepareResources()` is called against all DRA `kubelet` plugins for all containers before CNI is invoked.

This can be done by either moving this call earlier in the process of doing pod creation, or moving it into the `PodAdmission` loop (as is done by the existing device plugin framework).

Ideally, we would follow the pattern used by the existing device plugin. This would allow us to integrate seamlessly with the `TopologyManager`, for example, for DRA kubelet plugins that wished to do so.

However, there are unfortunate issues with this approach. The biggest one being that there is no retry loop for transient failures when calling out to external plugins. This means that if a transient failure does occur, the pod fails admission with an `UnexpectedAdmissionError` (even though it could have quickly recovered with a subsequent call out to the plugin, for example. Other resource managers, beyond DRA (especially the device plugin) could also benefit from improving the situation around transient failures, so this approach is worth exploring

The alternate approach, i.e. simply moving the `PrepareResources()` earlier in the process if pod creation is fairly straightforward, and a PR for doing so has already been created:
* https://github.com/pohly/kubernetes/pull/43

However, this doesn't allow us to integrate as nicely with the other resource managers, as moving it to the pod admission loop would.

We will need to consider what the right approach is as we start to work on this.

### Why is this needed?

This link summarizes the reasons behind needing this enhancement well:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/111023#discussion_r1005306039

Quoted from that review comment:
> The PrepareResources is called after the CNI is invoked. This is a problem for network devices that want to use DRA framework.
>
> In our case we have complex netdevice with several of other devices that we want to map

title: Auto-closing issues is harmful and causes friction
body:
Previously open issue : https://github.com/kubernetes/community/issues/5473
Twitter Discussion : https://twitter.com/BenTheElder/status/1407774856033181696

There's pros and cons to having a bot do this, let me try to enumerate current situation here:
- maintainers don't have to play bad cop
- keep set of open issues at a maintainable level
- bot commands are available to org members to `/reopen` reduces friction
- lifecycle labels help folks specify which issues not to touch
- we currently do not have dedicated team(s) that do issue triage well (except for some SIG like api-machinery that do this really well with twice a week triage session)
- initial issue labeling is still a problem, routing issues to the correct sig
- we have a new triage label which is not widely used yet across sigs

However there are numerous problems with the current situation:
- impression that project does not care about bugs
- folks open new issues for things that may be already present but closed
- too much traffic/noise from the bot activity
- issues where some follow up was requested/needed gets closed 

Options to do better?
- triage party 
- more hands on deck, train incoming folks to do issue triage and manage that as a subproject of some SIG
- stop the bot cold and let the SIGs adjust

What did i miss @BenTheElder ?

/sig contributor-experience

PS: It will be ironic if this issue gets auto-closed!

title: Make kubectl respect XDG base directory specification for caches
body:
### What would you like to be added?

`kubectl` under Linux keeps `cache` and `http-cache` directories under `~/.kube` by default.

Many Linux application have adopted )XDG base directory specification)[https://specifications.freedesktop.org/basedir-spec/basedir-spec-latest.html] that specifies, beside other directories, a location for cache files.

I propose to make `kubectl` respect XDG base directory specification for caches. Backward compatibility may be maintained by creating symlinks from `~/.kube` to the cache directory if necessary.

### Why is this needed?

XDG-specified cache directories are typically excluded from backups by default, thus adopting this specification will eliminate hundreds of megabytes of useless backup data per `kubectl` user.

title: The GCE cloudprovider's functions and assumptions should be documented
Identify, document and maybe remove kubelet dependencies
body:
Kubelet has a few dependencies, and we should be aware of them, document them so users know what's the minimum amount of other programs kubelet needs around it to execute successfully.

I'm testing this by compiling kubelet statically and running it in a `busybox` container with absolutely nothing. I've been surprised how well it runs after all.

I'm listing some, both hard and soft dependencies:
- `glibc`: hard dependency on the right libraries at runtime. We should get rid of this, as it's unnecessary: #26028
- `root` access: hard dependency and unavoidable. The kubelet has to have full control of the machine (`CAP_SYS_ADMIN` is one of the privs that are needed, at least when running in a container)
- `cgroups`
  - `cpu` and `memory`: required and used in the meantime
  - `cpuacct` and `cpuset`: required but not used (but @vishh said they will be used in the future)
- `journalctl`: _bug in cAdvisor_, should not be required
- `iptables`: Is required for the kubelet it seems: #26264, although now flannel isn't initialized when not used.
- `ethtool`: Required for `hairpin` [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/network/hairpin/hairpin.go#L72). I do not really understand what `hairpin` is required/used for... @thockin @bprashanth  
- `nsenter`: Used as `util/io/writer` when `--containerized`. Used by `--docker-exec-handler`, but not default. Used with `socat` for port forwarding within a pod.
- `mount`, `umount` and `findmnt`: Used in `NsenterWriter` in `util/io/writer`
- `socat`: Used for port forwarding within a pod. [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/dockertools/manager.go#L1056)
- `touch`: Used by `rkt` [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/rkt/rkt.go#L215)
- `docker` or `rkt` obviously
- `systemd`? Does `rkt` require a `systemd` host? @yifan-gu 
- Paths:
  - `/:ro` it must be able to read from the whole host
  - `/var/run/:rw` required for communicating with do

title: MinReadySeconds in statefulset does not work with parallel podManagementPolicy
body:
### What happened?

I've just noticed that [minReadySeconds](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/#minimum-ready-seconds) does not work in statefulset with [parallel podManagementPolicy](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/#parallel-pod-management).

I have a sts with `minReadySeconds: 10` and `podManagementPolicy: Parallel`. There is no `minReadySeconds` delay when statefulset is rolled out with `kubectl rollout restart`:
```
$ kubectl get pods
NAME    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
web-0   1/1     Running   0          2s
web-1   1/1     Running   0          4s
web-2   1/1     Running   0          5s
```

Is it bug or I'm missing something?

### What did you expect to happen?

`minReadySeconds` is honored when statefulset is rolled out even with parallel podManagementPolicy.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Deploy sts with `parallel` podManagementPolicy :
```
# File: /tmp/web.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  serviceName: "nginx"

title: Create ability to do zero downtime deployments when using externalTrafficPolicy: Local
body:
I am using externalTrafficPolicy set to Local for my a LoadBalancer service for an ingress controller on GKE.

Right now, when a pod gets terminated, it is immediately removed from the NodePort service, which stops traffic from routing to the pod (step 5 at https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod/#termination-of-pods). 

The problem is that the GCP Load Balancer doesn't update itself immediately, so it continues to send traffic to the NodePort even though Kubernetes has already removed the pod from the NodePort as part of the termination process. This results in timeouts and an inability to do zero downtime deployments when a node no longer has an active application residing on it when externalTrafficPolicy is set to Local.

I'd like to see an option where we can use Local, but allow for zero-downtime deployments. 

I'm wondering if there could be a configurable option to wait until a preStop hook has finished (or grace period hits) before removing the pod from the NodePort service? With something like this, we could make a preStop hook that can make health checks fail but have the pod continue to serve traffic normally. The preStop hook could then sleep for a certain amount of time while the load balancers gracefully stop sending traffic because the health checks start to fail. Once the preStop hook completes, then it removes the pod from the NodePort. This would allow for graceful draining of outgoing pods.

Or maybe the answer is a pre-PreStop hook that can run before termination officially begins?

In a multi-node setup, when one of nodes fails (has `NotReady` status) deployment (with 1 replica) will recreate pod on healthy node. title: Pods mounting wrong PV during CSI migration on Azure
body:
### What happened?

We tried to upgrade our cluster to use CSI on kubernetes v1.21.12. During the migration process we deploy the CSI components and start creating new nodes with the appropriate settings while draining and decommissioning old nodes.

During the transitioning phase where both CSI and non-CSI nodes exist in the cluster, we noticed that some of our workload that uses azuredisk PVCs were mounting the wrong Volumes. To be more precise, we noticed that certain pods were writing to the volume that belonged to another pod that was scheduled on the same node. Given that these are RWO volumes, this is a behaviour that should not happen.

This PVC "mangling" happens because we can manage to have 2 PVCs use the same LUN on an Azure VM. Before outlining the incident timeline, an important information is that our workload is a deployment that mounts a pre-provisioned PVC. The incident timeline is the following:

1) The pod (pod `A1`) referencing PVC `A` on the old node is set to terminating. Because it belongs to a deployment, a new pod (pod `A2`) referencing  the same PVC (`A`) is immediately scheduled in the new CSI-enabled node.
2) `volumeattachment` is created for the new node and azuredisk-csi tries to attach the volume. It gets a dangling volume error because `A1` is still in `Terminating` state. It then forcefully detaches the volume and attaches it to the new node in `LUN 0` all the while pod `A1` is still up. Pod `A2` is now running.
3) kube-controller-manager reconciles its desired-state-of-the world. Because the `A1` is scheduled in a non-CSI node, KCM uses the in-tree provider to reconcile the volume. It sees that `A1` exists still (even in `Terminating`) but because the  volume is not attached to the node, it forcefully detaches the volume from the CSI node and puts it back to the old one. `LUN 0` in the new node is now free.

title: Enforce ReadWriteOncePod PVC access mode during scheduling
body:
See [KEP-2485](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-storage/2485-read-write-once-pod-pv-access-mode) for more context.

#### What would you like to be added:

The `ReadWriteOncePod` PVC access mode guarantees only a single pod can access the provided PVC as a volume. This is enforced during volume mount (in kubelet), and should be additionally enforced during scheduling.

#### Why is this needed:

Because without it the scheduler will assign pods to nodes and they will fail to start (due to failed volume attachment / mount).

#### Implementation details:

- The `NodeInfo` type will be extended to store a mapping of PVC names to the number of pods on the node consuming that PVC
- The `VolumeRestrictions` scheduler plugin is extended to have a lister for PVC and for `NodeInfo`
- During PreFilter, the plugin enumerates each `NodeInfo` checking the reference count for each PVC in the pod to be scheduled
- If the pod to be scheduled's PVC is using the `ReadWriteOncePod` access mode and that PVC is found with a reference count > 0, mark the pod `UnschedulableAndUnresolvable` (alpha)
  - For beta, we will mark the pod `Unschedulable` and implement preemption logic

title: CSI migration race condition can cause unexpected detach and data loss
body:
### What happened?

After the cluster was updated to enable PD CSI Driver, there was a race condition where AD Controller (kube-controller-manager) started to [populate the desired state of world](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dc2898b20c6bd9602ae1c3b51333e2e4640ed249/pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/attach_detach_controller.go#L438-L447) BEFORE the PD CSI Driver was up, thus AD Controller gave us the error 

```
Error creating spec for volume "elasticsearch", pod "XXX"/"elasticsearch-0": error performing CSI migration checks and translation for PVC "dXX"/"elasticsearch-elasticsearch-0": in-tree plugin kubernetes.io/gce-pd is migrated on node gke-stage-XXXXX but driver pd.csi.storage.gke.io is not installed.
```

Then AD Controller triggered the disk detach because the disk/volume was not populated in the desired state of world.

Unfortunately the disk was in use during this detach and got corrupted.

### What did you expect to happen?

Since cluster upgrades can cause the controller manager and CSI drivers to start at different times, the AD controller needs to be more conservative when detaching

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

title: client-go: if an error occurs during request construction, URL() can return a useless result with no indication of an error
body:
### What happened?

When constructing a `rest.Request`, _e.g._ to stream I/O from a pod:

```
	req := k8s.CoreV1().RESTClient().Post().Resource("pods").Name(podName).Namespace(podNamespace).SubResource("exec")
	req.VersionedParams(&v1.PodExecOptions{
		Command: command,
		Stdin:   false,
		Stdout:  true,
		Stderr:  true,
		TTY:     true,
	}, scheme.ParameterCodec)
	exec, err := remotecommand.NewSPDYExecutor(config, "POST", req.URL())
```

if `req.err` ends up set, `req.URL()` will still return a result without indicating that something went wrong, resulting in a misleading error further down the line. (In my case, I wasn’t providing the correct scheme; the parameters therefore couldn’t be encoded, and the SPDY upgrade failed with an error saying that at least one of stdin, stdout or stderr had to be provided.)

### What did you expect to happen?

Other operations on `rest.Request` fails as appropriate if `req.err` is not `nil`; I would expect `URL()` to do so too. I realise that means a backwards-incompatible change.

Another solution could be to provide a `req.Error()` (same as on the response).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See above, with any scheme other than client-go’s.

title: kube-proxy IPVS mode configured with method SourceHash and Maglev should evenly distribute connections to all endpoints
body:
### What would you like to be added?

# Problem
The current support of the load distribution method `sh` and `mh` in kube-proxy ipvs mode only performs hashing of source IP address to select endpoints. As a result, all connections from a single client (i.e. from a particular source IP) are always forwarded to only one endpoint matching with the hash value of this source IP. If the client opens a vast majority of connections to the k8s cluster, it will result in traffic imbalance as only one endpoint located on one node handles the connections while the remaining endpoints/nodes are idle. 

Here is an example of the problem when using `mh` method for kube-proxy

- Deploy a service with 4 endpoints located on 4 nodes.

```console
~ # kubectl get pods -o wide
NAME                                READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE     IP         NODE     NOMINATED NODE   READINESS GATES
alpine-deployment-ffdbfd876-hzff4   1/1     Running   0          2m24s   11.0.2.2   node-002   <none>           <none>
alpine-deployment-ffdbfd876-vrw69   1/1     Running   0          2m24s   11.0.1.2   node-001   <none>           <none>
alpine-deployment-ffdbfd876-w4vh5   1/1     Running   0          2m24s   11.0.4.2   node-004   <none>           <none>
alpine-deployment-ffdbfd876-xgd59   1/1     Running   0          2m24s   11.0.3.2   node-003   <none>           <none>

~ # kubectl get services
NAME             TYPE           CLUSTER-IP    EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)          AGE
alpine-service   LoadBalancer   12.0.234.80   <pending>     7001:32000/TCP   3m56s
```

- Open 200 connections from a client to node IP of any node (e.g. telnet 192.168.1.1 32000). All connections receive replies from only one single endpoint.

title: Allow Resource Quotas to be scoped based on label selectors
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently Resource Quotas can be [scoped](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/#quota-scopes) based on whether a pod is terminating or not, best effort or not, its priority, and its CrossNamespacePodAffinity.

It should be possible to scope a Resource Quota to any objects which match a particular label selector. This would allow providing more fine grained control of Resource Quotas than is currently possible.

I would be willing to implement this if it is accepted.

### Why is this needed?

Currently Resource Quotas focus mainly on allocating resources fairly between teams sharing the same cluster. For this purpose having quotas which only apply to a particular set of labels is pointless, as the team could just edit the labels till the quota no longer applies.

However Resource Quotas have the potential to provide more fine grained control over individual workloads that might be running in the same namespace.

For example, we have a controller that will spin up a number of pods to handle a task. The number of pods scales linearly with the size of the task but we want to make sure that the task doesn't use more than its fair share of CPU resources, so that other workloads running in the same namespace don't suffer. Resource Quotas would be a great way to enable this, but currently don't have the fine grained control necessary for this.

If Resource Quotas could be scoped to pods matching a particular label selector, we could easily do this by giving all the pods created by the controller a particular label, and selecting that label in the Resource Quota.

title: Proposal: Extend NetworkPolicy to Layer 7
body:
/kind feature
/sig network

# Extend NetworkPolicy to Layer 7
## Objective
This proposal extend NetworkPolicy to include Layer 7 attributes at both ingress and egress to extend filtering on HTTP method, HTTP path, Kafka topic, etc.

## Motivation
The current NetworkPolicy allows to apply security policies based on L3
and L4 information (pod to pod connectivity, pod to IP, port filtering). Many applications running in Kubernetes pods use modern protocols such as gRPC or REST to expose APIs. Securing such pods on pod and port level only provides limited security as the entire API is exposed. This proposal provides users the capability to lock down pods on API call level.

## Goals
* Provide a L7/API aware security specification compatible with NetworkPolicy
* The goal is to provide enforcement for:
   * Traffic that is coming from a pod (egress)
   * Traffic that is going to a pod (ingress)
* Find a simple language to express the most common use cases in locking down on L7/API level

## Non-Goals
* This proposal does not intent to capture L7 routing intent and is not a replacement for Ingress
* It is not the goal to provide capability to filter on every possible L7 protocol field.

## Implementation details

### API changes
We introduce a new field `Rules` on the existing `NetworkPolicyPort` structure which will contain rules for traffic passing through that port.

```go
// NetworkPolicyPort describes a port to allow traffic on
type NetworkPolicyPort struct {
	// The protocol (TCP or UDP) which traffic must match. If not specified, this
	// field defaults to TCP.
	// +optional
	Protocol *v1.Protocol `json:"protocol,omitempty" protobuf:"bytes,1,opt,name=protocol,casttype=k8s.io/api/core/v1.Protocol"`

	// The port on the given protocol. This can either be a numerical or named port on
	// a pod. If this field is not provided, this matches all port names and numbers.
	// +optional
	Port *intstr.IntOrString `json:"port,omitempty" prot

default value: 3 * time.Minute

The relistthreshold needs to be greater than the relisting period + the relisting time, which can vary significantly. Set a conservative threshold to avoid flipping between healthy and unhealthy.

expect result: pvc-1 and pvc-2 should pending.

body:
### What happened?

For quite a while we have seen that some controllers/informers suddenly get out of sync with the state of the world, and keep `x` (different number every time).

After more investigation, we think we narrowed it down to the informer having a queue of events while a relist occur, and for some objects, we never see the `DELETED` event. This leads to a leak of some sort, and the informer is stuck in a bad state. The informers in question have resyncs disabled, so this only goes back to normal after a new relist. It should be noted that the queue at the point of the relist have been `1000`+ elements, so the controller are clearly in a state where they are lagging very far behind.

### What did you expect to happen?

Overall we expect that after a reflector relist, no objects should be stuck in a dangling state where they are added to the informer store, but never cleared; even when they are no longer present in k8s.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A rough timeline about what we think happens;
```
1. new Object is added O, agent gets CREATED event for it
2. watch is terminated, and the agent runs a new list, L
3. CREATE event for O is still on the queue to be processed.
4. informer replaces the old data in store with L, and O is not in L

title: Explore `go buildmode` to simplfy building custom scheduler binary
body:
## Background

Kube scheduler, along with other Kubernetes core components, provides extensions to build custom scheduling logic to fit different business needs. As of today, the scheduler provides 3 ways to achieve that:

1. scheduler framework (the most recommended)
2. scheduler extender
3. multiple schedulers

The 2nd and 3rd options don't apply to the subject of this issue, but let me mention a bit here how they basically work and their shortages: the extender communicates the interim scheduling results with an external extender webhook, which in turn imposes extra HTTP communication and marshall/unmarshall overhead, and hence cannot apply to large-scale cluster; while for secondary schedulers, they may compete with each other on the limited node resources and if there is a conflict, the latter scheduled Pod will fail by kubelet - which cause unpleasant UX, and even worse, the failed Pod's `.spec.nodeName` won't be auto cleared, and hence will stay on that particular node until resources get released.

With that said, the most recommended way to customize scheduling logic is to build scheduler plugins via the scheduler framework. It keeps 100% functionalities of the vanilla scheduler - both core capabilities and so-called in-tree plugins, and also empower you to build compatible scheduling plugins.

## Challenge of scheduler plugins

The scheduler plugins function well as it builds (`go build`) the custom plugins based on the vanilla scheduler. And to avoid the shortages mentioned in multiple schedulers above, we usually recommend users to replace the vanilla scheduler with the custom scheduler as the single and universal scheduler image.

However, these 2 operational tasks are non-trivial indeed, and hence may prevent developers from exercising the scheduler framework.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

A proper linter like something built on https://github.com/quasilyte/go-ruleguard may become a more reliable and capable linter for test guidelines.

- [ ] usage of `framework.ExpectError`
- [ ] avoid the [`Expect.Equal(someBoolean, ...) ` anti-pattern](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105678)
- [ ] [gomega annotations](https://onsi.github.io/gomega/#annotating-assertions) support printf-formatting and thus should not be passed the result of fmt.Sprintf

An [enhanced forbidigo](https://github.com/ashanbrown/forbidigo/pull/22) could detect:
- [ ] usage of `wait.Poll` and friends instead of [`gomega.Eventually`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113298)
- [ ] usage of gomega instead of the new [framework.Gomega](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113298) inside test/e2e/framework in functions that don't accept a stack offset

import-boss should  to
- [ ] that test/e2e/framework itself remains light-weight and doesn't import sub-packages


### Why is this needed?

The script uses grep to enforce certain code patterns. This is prone to false negatives. For example, it missed this until the code was changed to be all in one line

test/e2e_node/resource_collector.go:
```
                       gomega.Expect(e2epod.WaitForPodToDisappear(f.ClientSet, f.Namespace.Name, pod.ObjectMeta.Name, labels.Everything(),
