title: seccomp-default in kubelet to support custom profile.
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently, `seccomp-default` in kubelet supports only `true` OR `false`. Could we think about the possibility of expanding this to support something like `Localhost` so that the user can specify seccomp profile in another new flag to kubelet?

### Why is this needed?

If we want to enable seccomp in production clusters that have some real-life traffic, we were planning to enable RuntimeDefaultProfile with logging the exceptions instead of erroring out to analyze the audit logs.
With the current solution, there is no way to easily specify a custom profile (RuntimeDefault+logging in our case) for all workloads.
With the current situation, we might have to use something like [security profiles operator](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/security-profiles-operator) to achieve this. Which is not ideal. I am not sure if there is any other way to override the containerd RuntimeDefault profile.

Thanks!

title: Define ownership of controller/nodelifecycle
body:
/kind cleanup
/kind documentation

/sig scheduling
/sig node
/sig apps

The ownership of controller/nodelifecycle is unclear.

The [OWNERS file of pkg/controller/nodelifecycle](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/15894cfc85cab64df081bb753b8ccf32a243da68/pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/OWNERS) currently has some individual names and no labels, although it gets a sig/apps label from the parent pkg/controller OWNERS.

This controller has the following functionality:
- Add taints based on health of the node (from conditions)
- Evict Pods based on NoExecute taints.

The candidates for long term ownership are:
1. Scheduling: The ones who introduced it and overall maintain taints and tolerations.
2. Node: Because it's called "node lifecycle", although this could be a misnomer.
3. Apps: Due to implications to the lifecycle of applications and because they are the main shepherds of kcm.

I think it makes the most sense under scheduling, but wanted to gather all stakeholder's feedback.

title: Deleting pods that mount volumes from missing config-maps/secrets causes an abnormal deletion time.
body:
### What happened?

If you create a pod that mounts a volume from a secret or a config-map and then you delete that pod, it takes an abnormally long time to delete the pod.  



### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect a similar time for deletion from a successful case as an unsuccesful case.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

If you have the following yaml:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: config-map-mount
spec:
  containers:
    - name: test-container
      image: registry.k8s.io/busybox
      command: [ "sleep", "100" ]
      volumeMounts:
      - mountPath: /clusters-config
        name: clusters-config-volume
  volumes:
    - configMap:
        name: clusters-config-file
      name: clusters-config-volume
```
And you create it with no config-map and delete the pod it takes around 60-75 seconds to delete the pod.  

If you create that config-map/secret it only takes a few seconds to delete the pod.  

Secret example:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secret-example-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: secret-test-container
      image: busybox
      command: [ "/bin/sh", "-c", "cat /etc/secret-volume/*" ]
      volumeMounts: 
          - name: secret-volume
            mountPath: /etc/secret-volume 
            readOnly: true 
  volumes:
    - name: secret-volume
      secret:
        secretName: test-secret 
  restartPolicy: Never
```

body:
### What would you like to be added?

A field to the Job spec that allows setting a `queueName`.

### Why is this needed?

While in core k8s we don't have support for queues, and so nothing will act on it, `queueName` will help external queueing controllers to converse into a unified API for batch users.

title: Deployment should support both Failure Domains and Update Domains
body:
Feature Request: Deployments should support the concepts of Failure Domains and Update Domains as first class citizens and it should be easy to request those features in the Deployment Spec.

Currently Kubernetes Deployments can spread pods across failure zones using the annotations  `failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone` on a best effort basis.We can make that a hard requirements by using pod anti affinity which requires some expression. Making pods spread across failure domains on a best effort basis or as a hard requirement should be as simple as flipping a switch in Deployment. We shouldnt have to write a pod anti affinity rule to achieve this. 


Deployments while they support the concept of failure domains, do not have any such understanding of update domains. What that means is that an application can define what set of pods belong to which update domains and when doing a Rolling Update, only pods belonging to a single update domain are brought down at a time. This could potentially in the simplest case using the rack as a update domain, so Deployments spreads pods across racks and while updating only brings down pods per rack at a time. 

We should support both these feature in an easy to use way. 
Looking to see what others think in this area.
@kargakis @janetkuo @brendandburns @smarterclayton @thockin @nikhiljindal

title: A K8s POD using mmap(2) can cause oom-kills on the K8s node
body:
### What happened?

With a manifest that sets a memory limit for the container it is possible to allocate any size of "rss-file" memory and still run (not get evicted).

This have caused kernel oom-kills on the node. Fortunately, the process itself got oom-killed, but the kernel can pick any process on the node with a high oom score.



### What did you expect to happen?

The over-use of memory should be detected by K8s and the POD should be evicted.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Compile the example in https://docs.kernel.org/networking/packet_mmap.html and start it in a container as "packet_mmap eth0". Deploy with something like;

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: rssfile
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rssfile
  replicas: 4
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: rssfile
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: rssfile
        image: registry.nordix.org/cloud-native/rssfile:latest
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "50Mi"
          limits:
            memory: "50Mi"
        securityContext:
          privileged: true
#          capabilities:
#            add: ["NET_ADMIN", "NET_RAW"
```
Please note the memory limit. Check the _real_ memory usage with "grep Rss /proc/<pid>/status". It shows;
```
# grep Rss /proc/851/status 
RssAnon:               0 kB
RssFile:          263552 kB
RssShmem:              0 kB
```
The RssFile memory is real memory and exceeds the limit by 5x.

If replicas are increased the kernel-oom killer will eventually kick in.



### Anything else we need to know?

It seems "privileged: true" is required. At least I have not found any capabilities that allows mmap(2).

The ~256M rss-file memory is not visible with `kubectl top`:
```
# kubectl top pods
NAME                       CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)   
rssfile-77cc7d6dc5-2pq4w   0m

title: Consider PodDisruptionBudgets to allow zonal disruptions
body:
Some applications can tolerate multiple disruptions if the pods being disrupted are in the same Availability Zone. For instance, one of our applications have replicated data across AZ using a StatefulSet (+ topologySpreadConstraints) to make sure the data is available during an eventual AZ outage. Because of that, we can tolerate multiples pods being disrupted IF they are in the same AZ.

Is it possible to configure the PDB in a way that it continue to allow disruptions only if the pods being disrupted belongs to the same AZ?

I was thinking that we can extent the PDB to add a something like `disruptionBudgetKey` where we can set a node/pod label:

```
apiVersion: policy/v1beta1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: ingester-pdb
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      name: ingester
disruptionBudgetKey: "topology.kubernetes.io/zone"
podDisruptionBudget:
   maxUnavailable: 1
```

Thanks :D

title: Windows: Disappearing/missing windows loadbalancers for k8s services
body:
### What happened?

In our windows clusters, sometimes, we notice that the windows pod cannot access a clusterIP service. 

The instances we have seen this issue is when a windows pod tries to resolve a DNS name by trying to contact the DNS server clusterIP (i.e nslookup fails from inside a pod). When this happens, a `hnsdiag list loadbalancers` does not show the VIP for the kube-dns clusterIP. But kube-proxy logs indicate that this loadbalancer was created. So it likely got deleted at some point (or did not get created at all).  The DNS server inside the pod is correct. As an experiment, we reset DNS server (inside pod) to one of the kube-dns endpoint IP (directly pod IP) address and nslookup worked correctly. We set it back to DNS clusterIP and it started failing again.

Once we delete a kube-dns pod (running on a linux node) to let it get recreated, we see that a new event to windows kube-proxy will trigger the creation of loadbalancer again and things start working correctly.

We expect that the windows loadbalancers is in sync with kubernetes services.

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Handle pod CPU resize where caller requests CPU value of 1m
body:

When a pod is created with CPU request of 1m or 2m, they lead to a value of cpu.shares = 2 in both cases. This is due to kernel [clamping](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/27bc50fc90647bbf7b734c3fc306a5e61350da53/kernel/sched/fair.c#L3452) the value of cpu.shares to MIN_SHARES=2.

title: Standardization of the OOM kill communication between container runtime and kubelet
body:
Opening the issue to move the discussion here, based on the [message to CNCF Tag Runtime](https://lists.cncf.io/g/cncf-tag-runtime/topic/standardization_of_the_oom/94093173?p=,,,20,0,0,0::recentpostdate/sticky,,,20,2,0,94093173,previd%3D1664812590813586286,nextid%3D1637210209940337491&previd=1664812590813586286&nextid=1637210209940337491) and the group meeting discussion.

The motivation is from the KEP we are working on in Kubernetes: “Retriable and non-retriable Pod failures for Jobs“ (https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329). In particular, for Beta, we are going to add a Pod condition `ResourceExhausted` to the Pod status whenever a pod’s container is killed by the OOM killer.

Currently, the leading implementations of the CRI set the container’s `reason` field to `OOMKilled`:

Containerd (see: https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/23f66ece59654ea431700576b6020baffe1a4e49/pkg/cri/server/events.go#L344 and https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/36d0cfd0fddb3f2ca4301533a7e7dcf6853dc92c/pkg/cri/server/helpers.go#L62)

and CRI-O (see: https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/edf889bd277ae9a8aa699c354f12baaef3d9b71d/server/container_status.go#L88-L89).

However, there are two issues with the status quo:

1. The communication between container runtime and Kubelet is not standardized, leaving the reason field an unrestricted CamelCase string (see CRI API: https://github.com/kubernetes/cri-api/blob/3af67d6e7a5160e066444dac2a62e6218d67066b/pkg/apis/runtime/v1/api.proto#L1147).

2. There is no way to determine from within the Kubelet if the container was OOM killed due to exceeding its configured limits or due to the system running low on memory.

We suggest the following solutions (up for discussion):

For the first issue, we suggest extending the documentation of the CRI API field `reason`, to say that the reason field should be set to `OOMKilled` if the container is killed due to “OOM killer”. This way we would ens

title: client-go/kubectl rejects discovery API responses with charset encoding info
body:
We are using `client-go` (and `kubectl`) to interact with Kubernetes clusters behind a couple of proxy layers. One of these proxies completes the `Content-Type` headers to include character encoding details.

This was working fine until recently, when client-go/kubectl have started to fail when interacting with the discovery API. It seems that a recent change has made kubectl more restrictive of the content-type that it expects. I suspect that it is related to this commit: https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/commit/25d5761bfa0603c77cf5efefb14fd2e63a03a773

For example, this is an error from a kubectl command:
```
...
E0422 16:28:02.626222   86629 memcache.go:265] couldn't get current server API group list: Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
I0422 16:28:02.626258   86629 cached_discovery.go:120] skipped caching discovery info due to Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
I0422 16:28:02.626346   86629 shortcut.go:100] Error loading discovery information: Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...
```

We can of course try to fix it on our end, removing that charset information. However, it is a valid content-type and the way kubectl is handling the content-type there seems like it is relying on implementation details of kube-apiserver (that it does not add metadata to the content-type). I propose to fix this issue in `kubectl`, by properly parsing and handling the content-type.

title: Add CRI check to localhost healthz endpoint
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add a check for CRI service to localhost healthz endpoint in `kubelet` (i.e. localhost:10248/healthz and localhost:10248/healthz/cri). 

### Why is this needed?

CRI service is usually a separate process in the system (Containerd, for example). So it requires a health check to make sure the process is running healthily. Using command `ctr` or `crictl` is with extra overhead and slightly complex than simply using a `curl` if the CRI implementation doesn't already provide a http endpoint. Using the same method to health check both `kubelet` and CRI implementation (containerd) make things simpler.

title: Full Pod Disruption Budget support for Daemonsets
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Pod Disruption Budgets to have full support for Daemonsets. Currently only [minAvailable with integer values](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#arbitrary-controllers-and-selectors) is supported.

### Why is this needed?

Daemonsets are used for cluster level networking functions like Ingress and Kubernetes system components like kube-proxy. Pod Disruption Budget support allows proper signaling that it is not safe to restart all pods in the Daemonset simultaneously. With the current available implementation there are situations where tools like the [Vertical Pod Autoscaler](https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/tree/master/vertical-pod-autoscaler) will evict all pods at the same time in an undesirable way.

### Background

Similar to as seen by [Nginxinc](https://github.com/nginxinc/kubernetes-ingress/blob/master/deployments/daemon-set/nginx-ingress.yaml) we currently run our Nginx Ingress as a Daemonset. This is done for two reasons:

1. To work around an issue in GKE where it is not possible for nodes to reach an ingress running within the cluster unless the ingress pod is on their node (we run a Docker registry in GKE).
2. It allows us to naturally scale our ingress workload with the amount of nodes in the cluster. Without the workaround needed from 1 we would use a deployment with Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.

As a result of this we now use the [Vertical Pod Autoscaler](https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/tree/master/vertical-pod-autoscaler) to scale this Daemonset in our cluster based on usage metrics. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler uses the evict API to update pods which respects configured Pod Disruption Budgets.

Without a PDB configured the VPA will replace all pods at the same time resulting in a short period of downtime. If you attempt to configure a PDB of `maxUnavailable: 1` VPA is unable to evict pods because the calculated status is incorrect:

title: Infinite ImagePullBackOff CronJob results in resource leak
body:
**What happened**:
A CronJob without a ConcurrencyPolicy or history limit that uses an image that doesn't exist will slowly consume almost all cluster resources. In our cluster we started hitting the pod limit on all of our nodes, and began losing our ability to schedule new pods.

**What you expected to happen**:
Even without a ConcurrencyPolicy, CronJob should probably have the same behavior as most of the other pod schedulers. If I try to start a deployment with X replicas and I get ImagePullBackOff on one of the containers in a pod, the deployment won't keep trying to schedule more pods on different nodes until it consumes all cluster resources.

This is especially bad with CronJob, because unlike Deployment where an upper limit for horizontal scalability has to be set, CronJob with no history limit and ConcurrencyPolicy will slowly consume all resources on a cluster.

While this is up for debate, I would personally say when a scheduled Job has the ImagePullBackOff error, it shouldn't try to keep scheduling new pods. It should probably kill the pod trying to pull an image and make a new one, or wait for the pod to successfully pull the image.

Worst case scenario it will consume all cluster resources, best case scenario there is a thundering herd of CronJobs all rushing to completion when the image becomes available.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
```yml
apiVersion: batch/v1beta1
kind: CronJob
spec:
  schedule: "* * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: hello
            image: darrienglasser.com/busybox:does-not-exist
```

title: Emit events to PVC for attachdetach detach workflow
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The attachdetach controller currently emits on a pod when it encounters errors attaching a volume to a pod. This can be seen here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/reconciler/reconciler.go#L416

On detach, a pod is deleted, but a PVC still remains, that corresponds to a volume to be detached. It would be useful to emit events to the PVC when events or errors are encountered in the detach flow. Currently the controller does not emit any events to other objects that it operates on.

### Why is this needed?

Slow recursive fsgroup mounts (as detailed in #69699) can result in delays prior to detach. If a user force deletes a pod, the attachdetach controller can still get delayed, even after the pod is deleted in API server. Currently the user has no way of understanding the cause of these delays, unless they inspect their kubelet and control plane logs, which may not be readily accessible. Having metrics emitted about the stage in the attachdetach workflow emitted to a PVC would be helpful to diagnose these types of delays.

title: Support an optional topologyKeys *list* on PodTopologySpread to capture a unique subset of nodes
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Support for an _optional_ `topologyKeys` *<list>* on _PodTopologySpread_, whose values are ANDed, giving the ability to capture some unique subset of nodes.




### Why is this needed?

Consider the following (real) example we are facing attempting to use topology spread constraints on a cloud provider that has two intra-regional failure boundaries: zones and fault-domains e.g.

- 3 separate _availability zones_, which are data-centers in _different buildings_ (node key values: AZ-1, AZ-2, AZ-3)
- _each_ availability zone / building has 3 separate _fault domains_, which are separate server racks whose nodes can fail _together_ (node key values: FD-1, FD-2, FD-3) 

Therefore, we want to evenly spread pods across nodes in the different zones, and within each of those zone, evenly spread pods across the fault-domains of nodes _in that zone_.  We don't need (or want) the to balance pods across the fault-domains of different zones since they (1) are in a _separate_ building and (2) may unnecessarily exclude an otherwise available nodes in one zone based on the fault-domain in another zone. 

Now the difficulty: the provider happens to use the _same key values_ for fault domains in the various zones, even though, for example, nodes in **FD-1** in AZ-1 are not in the same failure boundary as nodes in **FD-1** in _AZ-2_ (they are separate racks in separate buildings). 

Without the ability to specify _multiple_ `topologyKeys` in the second fault-domain constraint below, pods (1) will be spread across availability zones (as expected), but also (2) spread across the fault-domains in _all_ zones, leading to nodes in one zone being excluded based on how many pods are in another zone that happen to have the same fault-domain key-value:

```yaml
...
topologySpreadConstraints:
- labelSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: critical-app
  maxSkew: 1
  topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
  whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedul

title: Allow for more flexible retry logic with Cloud Controller Manager
body:
<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->

**What would you like to be added**:
Currently, CCM uses exponential backoff when failing to process a service change. It would be great if this behavior—not only the minimum and maximum delay values—could be adjusted if needed.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8508875e4d400c1454561aa6d879860984bcdf59/pkg/controller/service/controller.go#L54-L58
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8508875e4d400c1454561aa6d879860984bcdf59/pkg/controller/service/controller.go#L150

**Why is this needed**:
It is possible to change the minimum and maximum delay values but in some cases that's not enough. Changing those values affects all kinds of service changes, and it would be great if it were possible to adjust that behavior in specific circumstances.

Take for example a new Load Balancer being created. We might want to reduce the max retry delay to just a few seconds long so it's ready within the cluster with minimal delay, but for other types of sync failures, keep the max retry delay set to 5 minutes as to not overload the API endpoint that is being polled.

/sig cloud-provider

/cc @timoreimann — Timo, could you please take a look and make sure this is in line with what we discussed?

title: Inconsistent Job state on DeadlineExceeded
body:
### What happened?

We have a maintenance task running in our clusters to delete obsolete jobs. The task uses a field selector to list completed jobs, `status.successful=1`, and then uses the `.status.completionTime` field to decide if the job should be deleted. This has been running fine for a long time, but suddenly the task started crashing in one of our clusters. After some initial investigation it turns out that this is caused by `.status.completionTime` being unset, even if the job appeared to have been completed successfully, based on `status.successful`/`status.succeeded`.

After removing irrelevant fields, the job may look like this:
````yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
spec:
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 220
  backoffLimit: 7
  completionMode: NonIndexed
  completions: 1
  parallelism: 1
status:
  conditions:
  - lastProbeTime: "2023-04-12T09:16:57Z"
    lastTransitionTime: "2023-04-12T09:16:57Z"
    message: Job was active longer than specified deadline
    reason: DeadlineExceeded
    status: "True"
    type: Failed
  ready: 0
  startTime: "2023-04-12T08:24:47Z"
  succeeded: 1
````
Which I find quite inconsistent. Has the job completed successfully or did it fail?

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect a consistent state based on the job pod status, and it seems like the correct state for these jobs is `Failed` - since the deadline exceeded before the pod containers were allowed to finish normally with exit code 0. So I would expect `.status.succeeded` to be unset (0) and `.status.failed` to be 1.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We have tried to reproduce this problem without success. I suspect the root cause to be the cluster job-controller being overwhelmed with work - caused by some unfortunate user cronjobs defined in a "playground" namespace. We got reports of long delays in job pod creation (over 1 hour) when this was going on. After some investigation, we decided to delete

title: kube-proxy: traffic to healthcheck host ports is dropped because of iptables rule order
body:
### What happened?

We are running self managed Kubernetes clusters on GCP and use Services of `type: LoadBalancer` with both public and private `EXTERNAL-IP`s to create load balancers for our clusters. Since upgrading kube-proxy to 1.26.3 (from 1.25.5) we saw that all healthchecks from GCP started to fail and traffic is now blindly load balanced across all nodes, which broke Services with
`externalTrafficPolicy` set to `Local`.
The issue seems to be introduced with this change: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460
Here, `KUBE-IPVS-IPS` ipset is introduced and is used in iptables on chain `KUBE-IPVS-FILTER` as:
```
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-LOAD-BALANCER dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-CLUSTER-IP dst,dst -j RETURN                                                                                                                                           
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-EXTERNAL-IP dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -m set --match-set KUBE-IPVS-IPS dst -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable 
```
`KUBE-IPVS-IPS` seems to include external IPs (as also noted here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117613 and here: https://github.com/k3s-io/k3s/issues/7183#issuecomment-1491205024) so the last rule above is dropping packets to external IPs that are not routed before reaching this point.
The next chain in iptables is `KUBE-NODE-PORT` and contains a single rule:
```
-A KUBE-NODE-PORT -m comment --comment "Kubernetes health check node port" -m set --match-set KUBE-HEALTH-CHECK-NODE-PORT dst -j ACCEPT
```
which seems specific to route packets arriving to health check ports

Workarounds to get health checks to work again from GCP are to either flush `KUBE-IPVS-IPS` ipset (temporary since kube-proxy will fight back) or move the ule to route packets to health check packets on top of `KUBE-IPVS-FILTER`:
```
sudo iptables

title: Add `--diff` flag to `kubectl get xxx -w -oyaml` to see the diff lines
body:
### What would you like to be added?

To add a `--diff` flag to `kubectl get xxx -w -oyaml` to see the diff lines, like this:
```
kubectl get xxx -w -oyaml | json --diff
```

With this `--diff` flag, we can see the diff lines more clearly, to facilitate resource watching.
Also see the https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3493.

### Why is this needed?

When we use `kubectl get xxx -w -oyaml | json` to watch a resource change, it is hard to spot the diff lines
between the watching stream output, so we need a `--diff` to just show the diff lines to make it easy.

When the regular pod is deleted it's status immediately transitions into `Terminating`, however when the static pod is deleted it stays in `Running` status until almost till the end just before it gets wiped out.

title: Unexpected Running state for DaemonSet Pods on NotReady worker nodes
body:
### What happened?

DaemonSet-created Pods remain in the Running state even when the worker node is in a NotReady state.

### What did you expect to happen?

A Pod is completely terminated.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

### Summary
- Deploy a DaemonSet
- Confirm that all pods are in the ```Running``` state
- Shut down one worker node
- Verify that the shut down worker node is in the ```NotReady``` state
- After 5 minutes (with tolerationSeconds=300), confirm that the pod on the shut down worker node remain in the ```Running``` state

<details>

### Reproduce

Deploy a DaemonSet.
```yaml:daemonset.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: nginx-ds
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx-ds
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx-ds
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.24.0

title: In-tree vSphere volumes are not detached after KCM restart
body:
### What happened?

I am enabling CSI migration on a vSphere cluster. A node was fully drained, all its Pods are deleted, but just before KCM detaches in-tree vSphere volume volumes from it, KCM restarts. A new KCM starts, sees attached volumes in `node.status.volumesAttached` that are not needed by any Pod on the node and calls vSphere in-tree volume plugin `Detach()`.

The in-tree vSphere volume plugin + cloud provider marks the volume as detached right away, without reaching to vCenter API. The volume remains attached forever.

I don't think it's related to CSI migration, IMO a regular node drain + KCM restart at the same time can cause the same issue.

title: `ResourceQuota` with "PriortyClass" as its scope is not calculated properly
body:
### What happened?

If a Pod is subjected to a `ResourceQuota` with "PriortyClass" as its scope, the quota's calculation is incorrect. See repo steps for more details.

### What did you expect to happen?

`ResourceQuota` with "PriortyClass" as its scope can be calculated at all times.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create a PriorityClass named "p1"
```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: p1
value: 100
```
- Create a quota with `PriorityClass` as its scope. ⚠️ Note: w/o specifying `PriorityClass`, this issue won't happen
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-p4
spec:
  hard:
    count/pods: "8"
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: 2000Gi
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 400Gi
  scopes:
  - PriorityClass <=== Notice this line
  scopeSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - operator: In
      scopeName: PriorityClass
      values:
      - p1
```
- Create a Job and wait for its completion.
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: countdown
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      name: countdown
    spec:
      priorityClassName: p1
      containers:
      - name: counter
        image: alpine
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: 2Gi
          requests:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: 2Gi
        command:
         - "sh"
         - "-c"
         - "for i in 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 ; do echo $i ; done"
      restartPolicy: Never
```

title: Monitoring gaps in apiserver extension mechanisms
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Following up from this discussion - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116420#issuecomment-1500602135

There are different components that fall in the critical path for the k8s API today (apiserver (core), authn/authz webhooks, mutating/validating/conversion webhooks, etcd, extension apiservers - maybe more I'm missing). While some of those do, bunch of them don't seem to have metrics tracking request/error counts and latency metrics. Here's what I found so far (will update as we learn more):

- [Authentication webhook](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad18954259eae3db51bac2274ed4ca7304b923c4/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters/authentication.go#L47)
  - [x] request/error counts ([xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad18954259eae3db51bac2274ed4ca7304b923c4/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters/metrics.go#L53))
  - [x] request latencies ([xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad18954259eae3db51bac2274ed4ca7304b923c4/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters/metrics.go#L62))
- [Authorization webhook](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad18954259eae3db51bac2274ed4ca7304b923c4/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters/authorization.go#L45)
  - [ ] request/error counts

title: attachable-volumes-aws-ebs Allocatable Field Does Not Account For ENIs
body:
### What happened?

The`attachable-volumes-aws-ebs` Allocatable field attached to EC2 nitro nodes (c5/m5s) on start up by default is set to 25. However, this limit does not account for dynamic ENI allocation/deallocation that CNIs like the [aws-cni](https://github.com/aws/amazon-vpc-cni-k8s) performs. This causes the scheduler to over schedule pods with EBS PVCs onto nodes that are already at their 28 ENI + EBS Volume attachment limits. Note that the scheduler only looks at the Allocatable field and counts the number of EBS Volumes it currently has and is about to attach ([see here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodevolumelimits/non_csi.go#L212-L275)).

### What did you expect to happen?

On allocation/deallocation of ENIs, Allocatable field should be dynamically updated, OR the EBSLimits plugin should account for ENIs in its calculations.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I am using an m5a.16xlarge instance which has max attachment limit of 28. With 3 ENIs, 1 root EBS volume, Allocatable reports 25 attachable EBS volumes. However, only 24 can be attached. The scheduler will try to schedule an additional PVC pod, but the volume will be stuck in attaching state.

title: kubelet sync node status more frequently when node not ready
body:
### What would you like to be added?

When kubelet  firstly startup and registrated, a CNI pod will be assigned to this node.  After the CNI pod finished initialization, the node should be `Ready` to run Pod.

Kubelet updates it status to apiserver periodically, as specified by --node-status-update-frequency. The default value is 10s. The latency will be 10s. It is not user-friendly for auto-scaling scenario.

If kubelet sync node status more frequently when node not ready, it can help to reduce the latency.


### Why is this needed?

Kubelet sync node status more frequently when node not ready, it will reduce the node `Ready` latency. Auto-scaling will benefit from it.

/sig node

title: kube-proxy v1.26 blocks host services
body:
### What happened?

We run some Kubernetes “single-node clusters” that combine the control-plane and the workload onto a single host besides some services installed directly on the operating system (SSH, BIND9). With the upgrade to v1.26, all local services become unreachable as soon as kube-proxy configures the network stack. This happens because kube-proxy adds the node’s IP address to the ipset `KUBE-IPVS-IPS`.

We configure the node IP address explicitly for `kubelet`:

```shell
KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS=--container-runtime-endpoint=unix:///run/cri-dockerd.sock --node-ip=10.169.8.6
```

Also, `kube-proxy` is configured to exclude the node IP address explicitly:

```yaml

    ipvs:
      excludeCIDRs:
      - 10.169.8.6/32
```

@liaralabs has collected more information in https://github.com/k3s-io/k3s/issues/7183#issuecomment-1491205024.

Overriding the `iptables` rules from `kube-proxy` with a higher-priority rules makes the services reachable again. Also, removing the node’s IP address from the `ipset` helps (until kube-proxy syncs the set again).

### What did you expect to happen?

kube-proxy should keep away from node-local services.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Setup a minimal one-node cluster with `kubeadm` and configure it for `ipvs`.
- Add a `Service` of type `LoadBalancer` with `externalIPs` configured.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: In daemonset controller, prioritize items in workqueue
body:
### What would you like to be added?

For now, the `DaemonSetsController` workqueue is  `rateLimitingType`.   Replace it with `PriorityQueue`, and this work item priority reference to spec.template.priorityClassName.

### Why is this needed?

There are some system-node-critical components (e.g. CNI,CSI) which deployed by daemonset. The node `Ready` condition depends on CNI Initialization.

The DaemonSetsController concurrent is 2, the burst created replicas in one reconcile is 250. When we have 6~8 daemonset in cluster, when scaling hundreds of nodes,  the controller will delay to create CNI pod. And the node will delay to be `Ready`.

title: Suppress console window for exec auth command on Windows (or expose a method for the caller to do so)
body:
If a GUI application is built for Windows which uses this library connect to Kubernetes clusters; and if the user of that application is connecting to a cluster for which authentication is handled via an exec plugin (for example, an EKS cluster); then every time the application needs to refresh its credentials, a console window flashes on screen for as long as it takes the exec plugin to return the credentials.

This behavior can be suppressed by setting setting some Windows-specific `sysProcAttr`s on the `cmd` struct, however, because the command execution is buried deep inside the library code, there's not currently any way for the calling application to do this.

One way to handle this would be to allow the calling application to supply `sysProcAttr` values to use with auth exec commands; alternatively, it might be appropriate to simply handle setting the necessary `sysProcAttr`s within the library itself, when running on Windows (I'm not sure if the current "briefly flash a console window on screen in certain circumstances on a specific platform" behavior is something that needs to be maintained under the aegis of "backwards compatibility"? It seems unlikely).

title: Terminating Pods will get their empty dir volumes unmounted when kubelet restarts
body:
### What happened?

Workloads which do not shutdown instantly on SIGTERM but start a graceful shutdown behavior to delay the shutdown of the container for some additional time will be in the Pod-Phase "Terminating" after the SIGTERM was received.

If the kubelet on a node that hosts such a "Terminating" pod is restarted (e.g. during k8s version patching) mounted emptydir volumes will be unmounted and not added to the pod again. As a consequence there will no directory be mounted under the configured mount path.





### What did you expect to happen?

Terminating Pods (which can be basically fully operational workloads) should not end up with removed emptydir volumes and missing mounted directories when the kubelet restarts. Mounted emptydir volumes should behave just like pvcs.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Example Pod with both (empty dir + pvc):

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: copy-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: ed-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: worker
      image: eu.gcr.io/gardener-project/gardener/ops-toolbelt:latest
      command:
        - bash 
        - -c
        - while true; do echo $(date); sleep 5d; done
      volumeMounts:
      - mountPath: /var/tmp/data
        name: worker-data
      - mountPath: "/copy"
        name: copy-vol
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 3600
  volumes:
  - emptyDir: {}
    name: worker-data
  - name: copy-vol
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: copy-pvc
```

- Send SIGTERM to pod, pod should be in "Terminating" now
- Restart Kubelet
- Check directory /var/tmp/data (try creating a new file there)

title: topologySpreadConstraints: Proposal to add whenUnsatisfiable: PreemptOrSchedule
body:
Right now, topologySpreadConstraints have only two possible behaviors when the constraint can not be satisfied: DoNotSchedule or ScheduleAnyway

However, these behaviors do not consider the possibilty that there may be lower priority pods which can be preempted in order to satisfy the constraint.

I propose adding a third value to 'whenUnsatisfiable' - let's name it PreemptOrSchedule. This will first try to preempt lower priority pods to allow the constraint to be satisfied, but it can't find pods to preempt, it will schedule the current pod anyway.

A typical use case is when we create negative priority 'headroom' pods whose only purpose is to reserve space in the cluster to allow for faster autoscaling.

Consider the case where we have a topologySpreadConstraint with maxSkew:1 to balance across two availabilty zones. Zone A has 5 pods and Zone B has 6. We now want to schedule another pod. Zone A does not have enough free space, while Zone B does have free space. There are two scenarios:
1) Zone A has some negative priority 'headroom' pods which could be preempted to free space
2) Zone A does not have any more pods that can be preempted (e.g. They all have already been preempted and are Pending waiting for the cluster autoscaler)

With whenUnsatisfiable:ScheduleAnyway, the new pod will be scheduled on Zone B even though we have plenty of 'headroom' on Zone A.

With whenUnsatisfiable:DoNotSchedule scenario 1 will indeed preempt the headroom pods in Zone A in order to schedule the new pod. However, for scenario 2, it leaves the new pod Pending and we will need to wait for the cluster autoscaler to add resources.

What I would like is an option where in scenario 1,  we will preempt the headroom pods in order to satisfy the constraint. However, in scenario 2, I would rather have the pod scheduled anyway and not need to wait for the cluster autoscaler

title: e2e framework: remove dependency on k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/api/v1/pod
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Several test/e2e/framework/* packages have k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/api/v1/pod as their only dependency on k/k. The following functions are shared that way:

 - IsPodAvailable returns true if a pod is available; false otherwise.
 - IsPodReady returns true if a pod is ready; false otherwise.
 - VisitContainers invokes the visitor function with a pointer to every container spec in the given pod spec with type set in mask. If visitor returns false, visiting is  short-circuited. VisitContainers returns true if visiting completes, false if visiting was short-circuited.
 - AllFeatureEnabledContainers returns a ContainerType mask which includes all container types except for the ones guarded by feature gate.

The feature gate check in AllFeatureEnabledContainers is problematic. E2E tests don't know what the feature gates in the cluster are.

The rest of the functions look like something that could be moved into  k8s.io/api/v1/pod == staging/src/k8s.io/api/core/v1/pod.

### Why is this needed?

- Having the functions in k8s.io/api makes it clearer that the checks only depend on aspects of the public API.
- Reduces dependencies of e2e/framework on k/k, in case that we want to move it into staging.
- Prevents accidentally using checks that only work in-tree (like feature gates).

title: Make it easy to request kube-apiserver and kubelet to support strong TLS configurations
body:
This is similar to #91444 and #81145 but the issue here is not what is _possible_ but what is _easy_ for an admin to say.

Currently kube-apiserver and kubelet (like [etcd](https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/14906)) default to accepting anything that go does.  My local security scanner objects to some of those ciphersuites.  I get a list of offending ones.  If there were a command line flag or config file field that I could use to _exclude_ the offending ciphers, that would be an easy reactive way to handle this.

Additionally or alternatively, it would be great if there were a simple way to request a stronger-than-go's-default configuration, that would be great too.  We may not want to be in the business of authoring that configuration ourselves, but FIPS has already done this.  How about a `--fips-tls` command line flag?  Or a `--boring-crypto` command line flag?

Our use case is a desired uniform distribution of pods which reside in different namespaces - think of multiple instances of an app which belong to different teams. title: docs: inotify behavior on atomic configMap/secret volumes is not documented
body:
**Background:**
Kubernetes [automatically updates](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/#mounted-secrets-are-updated-automatically) files on mounted `secret` and `configMap` volume types, as respective Secret/ConfigMap resources change.

**Problem:**
When someone runs a program on Kubernetes watching filesystem updates on `secret` and `configMap` volume types volumes (which is typically done using [inotify(7) syscall](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/inotify.7.html) on POSIX systems), they will be getting only "file deleted" (IN_DELETE_SELF) inotify event when the files are updated. (This is because how Kubernetes/kubelet uses [AtomicWriter](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/volume/util#AtomicWriter) to make updates to these files.)

This behavior is quite different than what the program would see when it's running outside Kubernetes, since a normal filesystem would return inotify events like IN_CLOSE_WRITE (file opened for writing closed) or IN_MODIFY (file written) events. Furthermore, "file deleted" event causes the inotify monitor to break. Therefore, the code needs to handle this to re-establish the inotify watch upon deletion (otherwise it would only receive the one delete event, and nothing else).

This caveat is not documented.

**Solution:**
Since this behavior might break existing programs that watch files when the program is migrated to run on Kubernetes, it would be ideal to note this pitfall in the project documentation ([this page?](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/#mounted-secrets-are-updated-automatically)).

It currently seems that this information is tucked away in some blog posts [[1]](https://william-yeh.net/post/2019/06/inotify-in-containers/), [[2]](https://medium.com/@xcoulon/kubernetes-configmap-hot-reload-in-action-with-viper-d413128a1c9a), [[3]](https://ahmet.im/blog/kubernetes-inotify/) and would be good to surface in official documentation as well.

/kind bug
/area do

title: Expose Pod cgroup path as part of `status` field
body:
### What would you like to be added?

We would like pod's cgroup path to be exposed in the Pod `status` (or other metadata field in the Pod object).  

### Why is this needed?

This would allow accessing pod's cgroup paths in a way that is independent of the container runtime, or cgroup driver, etc, and that doesn't require installing additional tooling. 

Here are some use cases utilizing pod cgroup paths:

- Cilium uses pod cgroup paths to identify pods for eBPF datapath events related to observability, load-balancing, etc. 

- Per-cgroup [BPF LSM](https://docs.kernel.org/bpf/prog_lsm.html) programs to implement security policies.

- Ability to install BPF cgroup programs on a per pod basis based on cgroup hierarchies to control how network traffic is processed.

- There are other open source projects like [DataDog](https://github.com/DataDog/datadog-agent/blob/67ce06c03e207193ac6d9f38481755e323cdb1f6/pkg/util/cgroups/reader.go#L123), [Pixie](https://github.com/pixie-io/pixie/blob/98189f6e939a9e7787ab31feca7ce3f7633a44ed/src/shared/metadata/cgroup_path_resolver.cc#L79), [Inspektor gadget](https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/blob/a219c9c29c67d07e41b36bd762d8330915f554db/pkg/container-utils/cgroups/cgroups.go#L99) with use cases such as for monitoring, observability, events/stats collection, etc. 

**Current limitations with retrieving pod's cgroup path:**

Following are the possible ways of getting this information, all with their own limitations. 

- Tools such as [crictl](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cri-tools/blob/master/docs/crictl.md): It's a CLI tool for container runtimes that runs on k8s nodes.
This is an example of how you can retrieve the cgroup path for a pod:
 
```
$ sudo crictl inspectp -o=json $POD_ID | grep cgroupsPath
"cgroupsPath": "/kubepods/burtsable/podd7f4b509-cf94-4951-9417-d1087c92a5b2/7ccf55aee35dd16aca4189c952d83487297f3cd760f1bbf09620e206e7d0c27a"
```

Cons: The tool may not be installed

title: kubectl message says "<object> deleted" before it actually deletes.
body:
> What is actually going on under the covers? It appears that the command immediately prints "<object> deleted" and then hangs, but actually it is waiting. It seems like the messaging is incorrect. It should say "deleting" and if --wait is the default it should only print "deleted" when the object is actually deleted.
> 
> The way it works right now it seems like kubectl deletes things and then hangs for no reason, and it doesn't give any indication that a state change has actually happened when the command finally terminates. (However ctrl-c and inspecting with kubectl get shows what is going on.) It's also a little surprising that the whole operation is async and ctrl-c doesn't stop it.)

_Originally posted by @lukeschlather in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/42594#issuecomment-955090666_

I've also had this issue where I `ctrl-c` before the `--wait` finished and even though `namespace mynamespace deleted` was printed, the namespace wasn't actually deleted, and was actually stuck in the `Terminating` state.

title: When requesting `cpu: "1.2"`, then `kubectl apply` always shows "configured" in output
body:
### What happened?

When creating a deployment and requesting `cpu`, then there are some cases when the output of `kubectl apply` (when doing it more than once) shows `configured` rather than `unchanged`:

Examples:

* `cpu: "1.2"` (but `"1200m"` works fine)
* `cpu: "1000m"` (but `"1"` works fine)

The error seems to occur when the `cpu` format is not as expected.

~~This is an issue when we request `cpu`, but not when we request `memory`.~~ This is also an issue when requesting `memory`.

deployment.yaml:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: busybox-deployment
  labels:
    app: busybox
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: busybox
  template:

    spec:

        image: busybox:1.36
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "1.2"
```

```console

title: APIServices can be deleted at the apiserver startup
body:
### What happened?

Initially reported at 1.24.10, but it seems to be present in master as well:

We observe that a part of apiservices objects have been removed by "system:apiserver" right after the kubernetes upgrade.

It looks like there is race between "autoregister controller" [1] deleting apiservices and "crd-autoregister controller" populating a map of desired apiservices, i.e. in logs we see:
```
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070841Z Starting autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070858Z Waiting for caches to sync for autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.071116Z Starting crd-autoregister controller

The unwanted APIServices delete happened at 14:21:35.438 GMT so between crd-autoregister sync and autoregister controller.

It looks like we attempt to wait with "autoregister controller" for crd-autoregister to initialize here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5c1d2d4295f9b4eb12bfbf6429fdf989f2ca8a02/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/aggregator.go#L148-L154

title: VolumeMount support in ephemeral containers with kubectl debug
body:
### What would you like to be added?

At present, I cannot attach an ephemeral container with a volume mount by using "kubectl debug".
I would prefer to have some way to create an ephemeral container with volume mount using kubectl debug.
It could be something similar to [patch command](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-kubernetes-objects/update-api-object-kubectl-patch/#alternate-forms-of-the-kubectl-patch-command)

I don't know if it's already possible to do it.[Blog](https://iximiuz.com/en/posts/kubernetes-ephemeral-containers/) indicates one way of doing it with API call, but kubectl debug would be much easier.





### Why is this needed?

Real world use case would be - 
Use case - I have a statefulset with a PVC where I store all the data related to the application. When the app crashes and it needs to be investigated, it is only possible to share net and pid namespace. If I want to investigate the file system it's just not possible as containers use different mount space.
By using the same volume mount as the crashing container of the pod, it is possible to check the data present in the PVC.  There might be security concerns also with this , but it needs to be explored

title: k8s.io/kubernetes/cmd/kubeadm/app/cmd/phases/workflow TestBindToCommandArgRequirements fails in Go 1.21
body:
### What happened?

`FORCE_HOST_GO=y make test WHAT=./cmd/kubeadm/app/cmd/phases/workflow` fails with the latest Go 1.21 dev branch, with:

```
+++ [0520 15:18:01] Setting GOMAXPROCS: 48
+++ [0520 15:18:01] Running tests without code coverage and with -race
--- FAIL: TestBindToCommandArgRequirements (0.00s)
    --- FAIL: TestBindToCommandArgRequirements/leaf_command,_no_defined_args,_follow_parent (0.00s)
        runner_test.go:406: The function pointers where not equal.
    --- FAIL: TestBindToCommandArgRequirements/container_cmd_expect_none,_custom_arg_check_for_leaf (0.00s)
        runner_test.go:406: The function pointers where not equal.
FAIL
FAIL	k8s.io/kubernetes/cmd/kubeadm/app/cmd/phases/workflow	0.016s
FAIL
```



### What did you expect to happen?

Test should pass but it fails.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Build the latest Go tree from source (or wait for Go 1.21 rc1). Then run:

    FORCE_HOST_GO=y make test WHAT=./cmd/kubeadm/app/cmd/phases/workflow

### Anything else we need to know?

This test is in `cmd/kubeadm/app/cmd/phases/workflow/runner_test.go`.

It is comparing function pointers by using reflect on the function value and then checking .Pointer. This typically does work for ordinary functions, but the test is comparing closures instead. If the closures were created by calling the same function twice, they may be different closures. This is why Go does not support function equality directly at all (which is why the test is resorting to reflect and non-guaranteed behavior).

The closures appear to come from, among other places, cobra.ExactArgs:

```
% go doc -src cobra.ExactArgs
package cobra // import "github.com/spf13/cobra"

// ExactArgs returns an error if there are not exactly n args.
func ExactArgs(n int) PositionalArgs {
	return func(cmd *Command, args []string) error {
		if len(args) != n {
			return fmt.Errorf("accepts %d arg(s), received %d", n, len(args))
		}

body:
### What happened?

Followup feedback from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/117019#discussion_r1165009267

In a few e2e node tests (e.g. tests of deletion grace period) we have some busybox pods that wait for SIGTERM and perform some action like a small sleep to simulate SIGTERM taking some time. These tests follow the pattern of `while true; do sleep 5; done` -- see https://sourcegraph.com/search?q=context:global+repo:%5Egithub%5C.com/kubernetes/kubernetes%24+file:%5Etest/e2e_node+while+true%3B+do+sleep+5%3B+done&patternType=standard&sm=1&groupBy=path

title: CronJobs should support timezones
body:
I couldn't find any discussion of this after searching for "cron timezone", "cronjob timezone", or "scheduledjob timezone".

The CronJob spec makes reference to https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron. That page suggests that cron would respect the timezone for a given user. The controller manager runs in a single time zone under a single user so I can't use different time zones for each job. I have jobs that run based on the schedule of external entities that observe daylight savings time. So, if I define that CronJob in UTC I will be forced to update that job from time to time (generally not something one remembers to do after just losing an hour of sleep).

I see two options for how this support might work in kubernetes:

1. Add some new field to the `CronJobSpec`, like `timezone: "Americas/Chicago"`.
2. Use an extended cron syntax that includes timezone, e.g. `30 6 * * 1 Europe/Stockholm`

title: client-go prints a klog warning by default in library code which is not allowed
body:
**What happened**:

A code change was merged that used `klog.Warningf` in library code by default (`NewDefaultClientLoadingRules` changed in a way that impacted all code in the world which uses that default, which is pretty common), which is not allowed by convention in Kube because client libraries may be used in UIs that wish to control output (klog is not consistent with other output).  The code change should have had a callback that allowed clients to optionally decide to print, not print to Warningf by default.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/78185#issuecomment-685765692

We should also document the convention for other reviewers that logging by default in client libraries is disallowed.

For instance, a callback would have allowed kubectl to print a human readable message `warning: KUBECONFIG does not exist` in general, and in specific cases (like `kubectl config` or login flows where KUBECONFIG not existing is totally reasonable) not print a message.

title: Better mechanism to decide Retry-After header
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Make the value for Retry-After header of APF-rejected responses dynamic or user-adjustable instead of being constant 1

### Why is this needed?

When `kube-apiserver` APF rejects a request, it sets the HTTP response header with `Retry-After` of value 1 (ie. retry in 1 second). There was a TODO in https://github.com/kubernetes/apiserver/blob/master/pkg/server/filters/maxinflight.go#L38 to improve this since many years ago. 

Retry-After being 1 seems less reasonable to many cases when the kube-apiserver is heavily overloaded. 

As suggested in the TODO:

* one naive way to improve this is simply making it user-adjustable . 
* alternatively, it can be dynamic by recording count of 429s in past X mins and decide the Retry-After value up to what users have specified. The implementation needs more thoughts if we think the naive one is not good enough.

title: use ipsets in iptables proxier
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The IPVS proxy mode leverages IPSets to significantly decrease the number of iptable rules. Currently, IPTables proxier doesn't use IPSets and can benefit from them.

[there is a kep for nftables proxy mode](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3824) which might replace iptables and ipvs proxier with nftables, [but that might take time](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3824#discussion_r1096604360).



### Why is this needed?

Taking an example from the current IPTables proxier, the following rule will be written **n times** _(n being the number of cluster IPs)_. We can replace the n rules with a single one, IPSets with specialized data structures can efficiently match against the set which will significantly increase the packet throughput.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bb67eb5bd237334d6d0343aa382b351002653404/pkg/proxy/iptables/proxier.go#L1076-L1083

[EDIT]
Performance won't increase significantly for clusters with few but long-lived connections as conntrack will kick in after the connection/flow is established bypassing all proxy rules.

[EDIT-2]
This has been raised before(but not discussed) https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108460#discussion_r960895453

title: PV recycler fails if too many files in top-level directory
body:
### What happened?

PV recycler pod fails to remove files if there are `>67567` files in the directory. 

Error in the pod logs:
```
› kl recycler-for-pv-040
2023-04-10T08:17:49.426784970Z /bin/sh: 1: rm: Argument list too long
```

Apparently one hits ARG_MAX due to too long command line. 
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/11289551/argument-list-too-long-error-for-rm-cp-mv-commands



### What did you expect to happen?

PV is recycled successfully

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Claim and NFS pv, create `>67567` files.

```
for i in {001..67568}
do
    echo hello > "/tmp/test/file${i}.txt"
done

# rm /tmp/test/*
-bash: /usr/bin/rm: Argument list too long
```




### Anything else we need to know?

In my testing I have provided my template and replaced the [current command](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/plugins.go#L1068) 

```
test -e /scrub && rm -rf /scrub/..?* /scrub/.[!.]* /scrub/*  && test -z "$(ls -A /scrub)" || exit 1
```

with:
```
test -e /scrub && find /scrub -mindepth 1 -delete && test -z "$(ls -A /scrub)" || exit 1
```

and recycle was successful. 


Maybe I am missing something but the `find -delete` was able to clean up everything (files, folders) and we also need to exclude the `/scrub` folder name.

`debian-base:v2.0.0` already has the `find` command, no changes to image needed.

title: Warn users about CRD alias naming conflicts
body:
Issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/94860 was closed as stale so opening a new one.

Another case in which this happens is with `kubectl get img` if both Knative Serving and kpack are installed.

Calling `kubectl api-resources` shows that a kpack Image resource should have four aliases:
```
$ k api-resources | grep kpack | grep -i image
images                            cnbimage,cnbimages,img,imgs   kpack.io/v1alpha2                           true         Image
```

Three of these aliases work:
```
$ k get cnbimage
NAME     LATESTIMAGE                                                                                                      READY
manual   gcr.io/fe-ciberkleid/demo/app@sha256:c3a9f2e8f8eced4f6779aa99419642c164665768872960c9c7737bd1146cd044   True

$ k get cnbimages
NAME     LATESTIMAGE                                                                                                      READY
manual   gcr.io/fe-ciberkleid/demo/app@sha256:c3a9f2e8f8eced4f6779aa99419642c164665768872960c9c7737bd1146cd044   True

$ k get imgs
NAME     LATESTIMAGE                                                                                                      READY
manual   gcr.io/fe-ciberkleid/demo/app@sha256:c3a9f2e8f8eced4f6779aa99419642c164665768872960c9c7737bd1146cd044   True
```

However, one of the aliases (`img`) does not work:
```
$ k get img
No resources found in default namespace.
```

I think it is important to inform the user that the `img` resource may refer to more than one type. The above results are misleading and can cause users to draw incorrect conclusions about what is or isn't running.

Aside: I had originally logged this under `kpack` but was advised that it is a `kubectl` issues, hence bringing it up here. For reference, the `kpack` issue is https://github.com/pivotal/kpack/issues/929.

_Originally posted by @ciberkleid in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/94860#issuecomment-1061063514_

title: Improve exponential backoff in reflector
body:
Currently, reflector uses two backoff managers: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/2a5f18df73b70cb85c26a3785b06162f3d513cf5/tools/cache/reflector.go#L223
One is used for initial list call and other for watch call. 

Imagine following scenaraion when k8s apiserver is under very heavy load:
1. At the beginning, reflector spams k8s apiserver (with exponential backoff) with `List` calls until one of them succeeds (due to APF throtling and receiving `429`)
2. Reflector tries to run `Watch` request and uses separate backoffManager - so again spams k8s apiserver with `Watch` requests
3. If Watch does not succeed during Etcd compaction window (2.5 - 5 minutes usually) at some point it will receive `resourceVersionTooOld` and go back to point 1, spamming k8s apiserver again with List calls (because first backoffManager for List got reseted after 2 minutes of retries for Watch requests)

I propose we combine these two backoff managers into one. 
If we combine these two backoffManagers into one, it will work like this:
- At the beginning, reflector spams k8s apiserver (still with exponential backoff) with `List` calls until one of them succeeds
- Tries to make first watch call instantly (as there is no backoff on this path)
- If it fails, it will makre retries every (30, 60)s
- If watch request fails all the times during Etcd compaction window it will go back to List call, but already being throttled with (30, 60)s window. 

/sig scalability

title: Reflector retains initial list result for a long time
body:
### What happened?

The result of initial list in Reflector is kept in the memory until the last element in the items list hasn't been changed. 

In practice this can be a long time, e.g. there can be some stable pod that are running for days, in configmaps there is a kube-root-ca.crt which stays there forever.

This problem is described here: https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro#a-possible-gotcha

IIUC this affects both:
* clients using informers/Reflectors
* kube-apiserver which is using the same Reflector to initialize watch cache

This means e.g. when all (but 1) elements are frequently updated, the memory usage is 2x the state size (the initial size + current size).

### What did you expect to happen?

When the objects are deleted from the cluster, the memory consumption of the Reflector drops.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Create cluster with 1GB state of significant size (e.g. by creating 1000 configmaps of size 1M each)
* Start informer (e.g. I was using https://gist.github.com/mborsz/8964c84b298ee63c7153190d608a7464)
* Observe memory usage (it should be around ~1GB as expected)
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197553760-cfd8a8f0-0996-4ee7-8f8c-5ea72e06bf8d.png)
* Remove 99% of the state
* [issue] Observe memory usage (it stays around ~1GB, despite state taking ~10M)
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197555163-adff7e50-e0db-4c75-8397-929b08dc9c08.png)
* Recreate the state (with the same name)
* [issue] The memory usage grows to ~2G
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197557325-f3aef1f3-c003-4f17-83db-5aac06ab5643.png)


### Anything else we need to know?

This seems to be consequence of the:
* ConfigMapList using []ConfigMap type (not []*ConfigMap)
* Reflector taking pointer to those objects https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fe9d04763b94366a7a80a1ef3d9f83337eac722e/stag

Would you happen to know if this is expected? I wanted to store the cluster state in a DB and update the cluster only when the list ResourceVersion is different.

Do you know if the resourceVersion for the list is only helpful for watching events and cannot be used for my use case?

title: Allow setting an environment variable to some fraction of a resource field
body:
**What would you like to be added**:

It would be nice to pass a process a number that is a bit lower than the container memory limit so that its garbage collection or memory management can use that limit.

For example:

- setting `GOMEMLIMIT` or setting `NODEMEMLIMIT`
- setting `NODE_OPTS=--max-old-space-size=$(NODEMEMLIMIT)` would be useful.
- setting `JAVA_MEM_LIMIT` and passing `-Xmx$(JAVA_MEM_LIMIT)M`

Currently you can use `envFrom.resourceFieldRef` to "copy" a resource request or limit to an environment variable, but you can only multiply the value by some power of 1000 or 1024 by specifying `divisor`.

**Why is this needed**:

This would make it possible to pass a memory limit into a process inside the container that is based on the container resource request or limit but less.

For example, when specifying node's `--max-old-space-size` or Java's `-Xmx` parameter, setting it equal to the memory limit of the container will be a problem, because the process actually uses more memory than what you provided as a parameter.

**Potential Solutions**

- If we could specify a `divisor` like `1.5Mi` then it would result in a number of megabytes equal to roughly 2 thirds of the available memory, leaving some extra for the other heaps.
- Add another field like `scale` or `multiplier` to `enfFrom.resourceFieldRef` which is multiplied by the input value to get the env var value
- (moonshot?) allow using a go template or some simple templating/expression language to actually fill out the env var with prefix and suffix, like `--max-old-space-size={{ value * 800 }}M`

title: CVE-2023-2878: secrets-store-csi-driver discloses service account tokens in logs
body:
A security issue was discovered in [secrets-store-csi-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/secrets-store-csi-driver) where an actor with access to the driver logs could observe service account tokens. These tokens could then potentially be exchanged with external cloud providers to access secrets stored in cloud vault solutions. Tokens are only logged when [TokenRequests is configured in the CSIDriver object](https://kubernetes-csi.github.io/docs/token-requests.html) and the driver is set to run at log level 2 or greater via the -v flag.

This issue has been rated **MEDIUM** [CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N) (6.5), and assigned **CVE-2023-2878**

**Am I vulnerable?**

You may be vulnerable if [TokenRequests is configured in the CSIDriver object](https://kubernetes-csi.github.io/docs/token-requests.html) and the driver is set to run at log level 2 or greater via the -v flag.

To check if token requests are configured, run the following command:

```shell
kubectl get csidriver secrets-store.csi.k8s.io -o jsonpath="{.spec.tokenRequests}"
```

To check if tokens are being logged, examine the secrets-store container log:

```shell
kubectl logs -l app=secrets-store-csi-driver -c secrets-store -f | grep --line-buffered "csi.storage.k8s.io/serviceAccount.tokens"
```

**Affected Versions**

- secrets-store-csi-driver < 1.3.3

**How do I mitigate this vulnerability?**

Prior to upgrading, this vulnerability can be mitigated by running secrets-store-csi-driver at log level 0 or 1 via the -v flag.

**Fixed Versions**

- secrets-store-csi-driver >= 1.3.3

To upgrade, refer to the documentation: [https://secrets-store-csi-driver.sigs.k8s.io/getting-started/upgrades.html#upgrades](https://secrets-store-csi-driver.sigs.k8s.io/getting-started/upgrades.html#upgrades)

title: Pods keep being created by Deployment with match-all "NoSchedule" toleration until node shutdown when using graceful node shutdown
body:
### What happened?

When graceful node shutdown is triggered, kubelet will taint the node with "not-ready", set "spec.unschedulable" to true, and set running pods' phase to "Failed" (I'm using 1.23.6 and 1.24 where the phase will be set to "Failed" according to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/106900).

Meanwhile, the shutdown manager also will reject any new pod with "Failed" phase which is scheduled to the node due to the code I believe at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.24/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager_linux.go#L143-L154.

With above behavior, if a controller instance like Deployment with match-all "NoSchedule" toleration (toleration without setting the key), the Deployment will create a new pod once the old one is set to "Failed" and the scheduler may still schedule the new pod to the node being shutting down because of the toleration. As the kubelet rejects the new coming pod and also set its phase to "Failed", the former procedure just repeats leading to a lot of rejected pods being created until node truly shutdown. And we know those pods will stay until garbage collection or other entity kick-in to clean up.

This may leave a certain way to exhaust the cluster resource as the pod creating can be much faster than cleaning up.

### What did you expect to happen?

(Since this) I'm aware of that have a match-all "NoSchedule" toleration on things like Deployment is a bad idea but sometimes it can just happen. And I also know there is back-and-forth discussion on whether the phase should be set to "Failed" on the pod during graceful node shutdown (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/104531) and there is still work ongoing (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/108991).

Our case is we still need the new pod instance can be created after node reboot (so completed pod staying forever is not fine for us either), but at the same time hope it won't be scheduled to the same node being shu

title: client: shared informer SetX functions are racy
body:
### What happened?

The functions SetWatchErrorHandler and SetTransform are racy with ShareInformer factory


Consider the following example:
```go
	informerFactory := informers.NewSharedInformerFactory(client, 0*time.Second)
	go func() {
		informerFactory.Start(stop)
	}()
	serviceInformer := informerFactory.Core().V1().Services().Informer()
	serviceInformer.SetWatchErrorHandler(func(r *cache.Reflector, err error) {
		// ...
	})
```

In the real world, the goroutine running Start is likely entirely decoupled from the rest; the code here is fairly obviously "wrong".

This has both a data race (I have a PR ready for this) and a logical race. There is no safe way to call these functions unless the entire application is sequenced in a manner such that all informers are created before Start is called. In our real world case, we have some informers that start after application start, which leads to races with other components calling Start().

### What did you expect to happen?

SetWatchErrorHandler and SetTransform can be called without races. That is, I can make an informer from a shared informer factory, set a watcher handler and transform, and ensure they are applied.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See incoming PR which has a test case

title: kube-proxy in LocalModeNodeCIDR mode may cache stale Node.PodCIDR if the Node object is recreated
body:
### What happened?

If `LocalModeNodeCIDR` is true, kube-proxy reads the `Node.PodCIDR` value and uses it to determine whether or not traffic is local to the Node.

In certain cases (e.g. when kube-proxy runs before the Node information has been completely updated), it is possible for kube-proxy to read and store a stale `PodCIDR` value. This will cause kube-proxy to route traffic incorrectly as the local traffic determination is no longer correct.

Note: PodCIDR is immutable once set but it is possible to delete and recreate the Node object to get into this state. (yes, this can happen)

/sig network

### What did you expect to happen?

kube-proxy should detect this state and reconfigure/restart with the newly updated `PodCIDR`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Recreate the Node object with a different PodCIDR after kube-proxy has started on the Node.

### Kubernetes version

Impacts all current versions that support `LocalModeNodeCIDR`

### Cloud provider

<details>
Observed for GCE preemptible/spot VMs, but is a generic problem.
</details>

After running k8s conformance testing on kubernetes v1.27, we have leftover custom resources of the `foo*.mygroup.example.com` format that should not exist.  For example)

foofq2kkas.mygroup.example.com                        2023-05-22T20:43:50Z
foom64ghas.mygroup.example.com                        2023-05-22T20:50:34Z

...

```
docker run --rm -v "/tmp:/tmp" --entrypoint cp gcr.io/k8s-staging-test-infra/kubekins-e2e:latest-master -r /workspace /tmp

We run serial conformance tests as follows.
```
export KUBERNETES_CONFORMANCE_TEST=y
$kubetest_binary --provider=skeleton --test --test_args="--ginkgo.noColor --ginkgo.flakeAttempts=2 --ginkgo.focus=\[Serial\].*\[Conformance\] --ginkgo.skip=\[Disruptive\] --num-nodes=${NUM_NODES} --check-version-skew=false --dump="${k8s_conformance_e2e_results_directory}" > "${k8s_conformance_e2e_results_serial_file}"

title: Support startup dependencies between containers on the same Pod
body:
/kind feature
/sig node 

This is a proposed kubernetes feature to address an issue we're seeing on Istio. I'm definitely open for alternative approaches, but I feel that this may be a generally useful feature for Kubernetes.

Background: 

Istio pods have a sidecar container (called "istio-proxy") which runs an Envoy proxy. All traffic in and out of the pod is redirected (via iptables) through Envoy. Kubernetes starts both the application and istio-proxy at the same time, and as soon as the application shows "healthy", it can start receiving traffic. However, if Envoy has not yet received its initial configuration from Pilot (the configuration service), the service will experience temporary traffic loss until Envoy is configured. 

We're currently recommending that developers solve this problem themselves by running a startup script on their application container which delays application startup until Envoy has received its initial configuration.  However, this is a bit of a hack and requires changes to every one of the developer's containers.

Proposal:

In my mind, this situation would be better if we could make the startup of one container on the Pod dependent on a healthy status of another container.  This way, we can provide an Envoy health check that confirms that it's received configuration from Pilot, thus triggering the startup of the application container automatically.  No custom scripts, or manual steps at all.
