title: undeprecate kubelet --provider-id flag
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Un-deperecate the `--provider-id` kubelet flag, as this option is typically set per-node similar to `--node-ip` (which is not deprecated).

Or more generally, consider not deprecating fields available in config that make sense to set per-node.

### Why is this needed?

I noticed this while trying to ensure KIND moves towards not setting any deprecated flags, this one is tricky because it's not a fixed value.
https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kind/pull/2764

For a lot of kubernetes users, kubeadm is used for bootstrapping, and kubeadm supports supplying additional kubelet flags when configuring each node, but the kubelet config is cluster-wide, created during setting up the first node and uploaded to a configmap then used for all nodes.

In the future kubeadm may have the ability to do per-node kubelet config, but that effort will probably be involved and isn't staffed at the moment.

_technically_ you could run kubeadm in phases and then modify the config, but this is more complex to implement.

It's possible this won't be necessary if kubeadm patches can be extended to kubelet which may be a smaller feature change for kubeadm, but personally I think being able to configure simple per-node strings with a flag override is desirable for implementing clusters, and we've had the flag for many years with no trouble ...

 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubeadm/issues/1682#issuecomment-1124027039


The actual deprecation seems to be due to a blanket deprecation on things possible to set in config, and not targeted at this flag in particular.

See discussion in https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1652465646070179

title: Stateful Indexed Job
body:
### What would you like to be added?

An automated way of creating PVCs for the individual pods of Indexed Job. This is similar to PersistentVolumeClaimTemplate in StatefulSets.

### Why is this needed?

Many long running training workloads use checkpointing to recover from failures. In some cases, the individual workers create node-local checkpoints. To ensure that on failure the replacement pod restarts fast, it should be scheduled on the same node as the failed pod. At the same time, if the node itself fails and gone, the replacement pod is free to schedule on any available node.

title: kubelet: PreStop Hooks can hang termination of a pod beyond pod's termination grace period
body:
### What happened?

Termination grace period includes the termination time of prestop hooks and containers in the pod. The total time that the pod terminates should always be < termination grace period seconds.

A misconfigured pod with a preStopHook that hangs indefinitely and pod ignoring SIGTERM can result in the pod taking 2X (double) the termination grace period seconds to terminate.
 

### What did you expect to happen?

The time to terminate the pod should always be <= termination grace period seconds including prestop hook execution time as documented in https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks/#hook-handler-execution

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1) Apply the following pod

```
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: prestop-repro
  labels:
    pod: prestop-repro
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec:
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 999999"]
    image: k8s.gcr.io/e2e-test-images/nginx:1.14-2
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - |
        _term() {
            echo "Caught SIGTERM signal!"
            while true; do sleep 5; done
        }
        trap _term SIGTERM
        while true; do sleep 5; done
```

2) 

```
$ time kubectl delete pod prestop-repro
pod "prestop-repro" deleted

real    2m1.035s
user    0m0.172s
sys     0m0.077s
```

3) Observe it actually took ~120s to terminate the pod not ~60s as would be expected.

### Anything else we need to know?

The kubelet logs for the pod https://gist.github.com/1f76e54b32bc51f1a9525cc8b707f820

title: CVE-2023-2431: Bypass of seccomp profile enforcement
body:
### What happened?

A security issue was discovered in Kubelet that allows pods to bypass the seccomp profile enforcement. This issue has been rated LOW ([CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N)) (score: 3.4).

If you have pods in your cluster that use [localhost type](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.27/#seccompprofile-v1-core) for seccomp profile but specify an empty profile field, then you are affected by this issue. In this scenario, this vulnerability allows the pod to run in “unconfined” (seccomp disabled) mode. This bug affects Kubelet.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This can be reproduced by creating a pod with following configuratoin - 

```
        seccompProfile:
          type: Localhost
          localhostProfile: ""
```

https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.27/#seccompprofile-v1-core

### Kubernetes version

**Affected Versions**
v1.27.0 - v1.27.1
v1.26.0 - v1.26.4
v1.25.0 - v1.25.9
<= v1.24.13

**Fixed Versions**
v1.27.2
v1.26.5
v1.25.10
V1.24.14

To remediate this vulnerability you should upgrade your Kubelet to one of the below mentioned versions.

title: Indexed Jobs can break with high number of parallelism or completions
body:
### What happened?

Currently, the maximum number of completions is MAX_INT32, around 2e9 and the maximum parallelism is 1e5.

When using these values, and assuming a very unlucky case, the field `.status.completedIndexes` can fill up the maximum size for objects in etcd (around 1.5Mi)

/sig apps
/sig scalability

### What did you expect to happen?

An Indexed Job with the maximum number of completions and parallelism to be correctly tracked.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sample-job
spec:
  completionMode: Indexed
  completions: 2000000000
  parallelism: 100000
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: bad
        image: python
        command:
        - python3
        - -c
        - |
          import os
          import time
          id = int(os.environ.get("JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX"))
          if id > 1000000000 and id % 3 == 0:
            time.sleep(10000)
      restartPolicy: Never
```

In other words, every index multiple of 3 takes too long to terminate.

### Anything else we need to know?

In the example above, the number of characters needed by the `completedIndexes` field is:

`(10+1)*2*1e5`, roughly 2Mi, where:
- 10 is the number of characters for a number
- 1 for the separating character.
- 2 for the consecutive numbers
- 1e5 for the number of "holes" in the `completedIndexes`, based on the parallelism.

### Kubernetes version

1.21 and newer (when IndexedJob was introduced)

title: Online pvc resize stuck
Cleanup the Job controller exponential backoff delay
body:
/sig apps

The code around Job controller exponential backoff delay has a lot of heritage. The purpose of this issue is to collect and discuss cleanup ideas. It was initiated by the backoff discussion under the KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3967#discussion_r1219690984.

Some fixes initiated by the discussion and small cleanups are already handled by the PR: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/118470.

The source of the issue might be that the “backoff” delay is used in two different contexts:
- Value of the exponential backoff delay is computed based on the number of consecutive failures. It’s main purpose is to throttle pod creation rate when the pods fail: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1415-L1419. 
- Value computed by the number of requeues in the queue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1546-L1564

First, I suggest splitting the naming of these two different backoffs. Let’s use “api error backoff delay” and “pod failure backoff delay”. It would be good if the naming in the code reflected this difference.

Second, the “api error backoff delay” is used in non-obvious places:
- When handling a pod which is transitioning to failed phase: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4c40d749006a8895f6718f2b624a3dbe975988ab/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L321 (seems ok to drop)
- Where there is API conflict: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4c40d749006a8895f6718f2b624a3dbe975988ab/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L879

Also, I suggest having the following methods to requeue `syncJob` to make the intention clearer to the reader:
- `enqueueControllerImmediately(key)` - no delay
- `enqueueControllerDelayed(key)` - delayed by `max(1s, api error backoff)`
- `enqueueControllerDelayedByApiErrors(key)` - delayed by `max(1s, api error backoff)` [not sure we need it sin

title: Change default HPA downscale policy from 100% pods to 25% pods
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Change the [default HPA downscale policy](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale/#default-behavior) from allowing 100% pods to be removed in a single step to allowing a smaller percentage (maybe 25%?). This will result in annealed downscaling.

### Why is this needed?

The current default downscale policy means that after the stabilization window has passed the downscale recommendation is applied in a single step, regardless of how severe it is. HPA can downscale e.g. from 500 replicas to 1 in a single go.

Such rapid downscaling comes with risks:

a) It's a rapid increase of per-instance load that may have impact on application performance.
b) Potential incorrect (too low) recommendation gets actuated directly. Scaling down step by step (annealed) means calculating a new recommendation in each step, based on new input data, which may fix the bug symptom. It also gives a bit more time for human response.

OTOH rapid downscale is beneficial for some workloads, e.g. batch processing, queue processing. There is a trade-off between cost efficiency and reliability and IMO we should favor reliability by default. Users can override the default to favor efficiency if their use case requires it.

title: Kubelet's volume manager called NodeUnpublishVolume for a volume which is being referred in a running pod, leading to I/O error
body:
### What happened?

Kubelet's volume manager reconciller called UnPublish on a pvc which was being referred in a running pod due to which pod started getting I/O error on that volume.

Reason -
Upon kubelet restart, before marking hasAddedPods = true Kubelet's volume manager populates it's desired state of world (dsw) and waits for first run of populatorLoop() to complete without checking an error. Ref - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c9ed04762f94a319d7b1fb718dc345491a32bea6/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/populator/desired_state_of_world_populator.go#L152

Hence even  if the dsw population failed for a pod and  it's volumes were not added to dsw cache, since hasAddedPods will be set as true, rc.Sync() will be run (ref - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c9ed04762f94a319d7b1fb718dc345491a32bea6/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler/reconciler.go#L40) which will later lead reconciller to UnPublish the volume that is being referred in a running pod. 

Proof from logs -

title: Detaching volume forcefully is extremely dangerous
body:
### What happened?

We see the output of the following code snippet in our production log:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/741bd5c3823344b3fc4a38cae9846cdda1941bb4/pkg/controller/volume/attachdetach/reconciler/reconciler.go#L274

### What did you expect to happen?

We should not forcefully detach a volume in this scenario or at least leave the choice to the user.
 
The result may be a non-working node. The reason is that if kubernetes forcefully detach a volume, which has in-flight I/Os that did not flushed.  Linux kernel won't be able to flush the journal or I/O unless the node rebooted because of underneath device does not exist any more.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

If the PV/PVC can't be detached for any reason, and Pod still have I/O operation, this issue should happen.

In our environment, this happened during cluster upgrade.

title: Cleanup Job controller unit tests for requeuing with delay
body:
/sig apps

In many unit tests we set `DefaultJobBackOff` and `syncJobBatchPeriod` to 0. However, this is problematic, because the mechanism works differently when the delay is 0 and when it is >0. When the delay is 0 the delay is immediate and the unit tests can assert if the requeueing was immediate, which makes them easier to right, but making them far from the real running system. 

Examples:
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fa78f28f0a011e9922cf12145dd602c5a63981e8/pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go#L3473
-  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fa78f28f0a011e9922cf12145dd602c5a63981e8/pkg/controller/job/job_controller_test.go#L3110

One complication though with simply passing the fake clock is described here, and may result in flakiness, so this should be done carefully: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114944#discussion_r1069179801

title: wait.PollUntilContextTimeout with immediate=true does not invoke condition function at least once
body:
### What happened?

Calling wait.PollUntilContextTimeout with immediate=true does not invoke the passed condition function if context has already been cancelled.



### What did you expect to happen?

wait.PollUntilContextTimeout with immediate=true should invoke the passed condition function at least once even if context has already been cancelled as wait.PollUntilContextCancel documentation says:

> If immediate is true, condition will be invoked before waiting and guarantees that condition is invoked at least once, regardless of whether the context has been cancelled.

Note that wait.PollUntilContextTimeout wraps wait.PollUntilContextCancel, so the above should be applied to wait.PollUntilContextTimeout as well.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```go
package main

import (
        "context"
        "time"

        "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait"
)

func main() {
        err := wait.PollUntilContextTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second, 0, true, func(context.Context) (bool, error) {
                return true, nil
        })
        if err != nil {
                panic(err)
        }
}
```

This program panics because context ctx.Err is checked before invoking the passed function.


### Anything else we need to know?

The deprecated wait.PollImmediateWithContext does not have this kind of issue.
If wait.PollUntilContextTimeout is the replacement of wait.PollImmediateWithContext, it should exhibit the same behavior.

title: Pod graceful deletion hangs if the kubelet already rejected that pod at admission time
body:
### What happened?

We observed the following series of events:

1) Pod is created with some attributes that later result in the pod being rejected at kubelet admission time
2) The pod is scheduled to a node
3) The pod is gracefully deleted by a controller, i.e. a deletion timestamp is set on the pod
4) The pod is rejected at kubelet admission time
5) The pod never gets deleted and is stuck: despite having the deletion timestamp set. It seems that kubelet does not issue the final force delete for the pod.

This is problematic in many scenarios, but one specific case it was hit was when the pod is backed by a daemonset controller. This issue manifested in way where since the pod never got deleted in step 5 above, the daemonset controller did not create a new pod to run the on the node and thus node was was not running a replica of the daemonset controller pod.

This seems to a be regression in k8s 1.27, I was not able to repro this behavior in 1.26.

### What did you expect to happen?

It is expected at during the series of events above, after the pod is failed at kubelet admission time, since the pod has a deletion timestamp set, the kubelet should forcefully delete the pod. The pod should not hang in deletion forever. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a 1.27 kind cluster:

```
kind delete cluster


kind_config="$(cat << EOF
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
networking:
  ipFamily: ipv4
nodes:
# the control plane node
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
  kubeadmConfigPatches:
  - |
    kind: JoinConfiguration
    nodeRegistration:
      kubeletExtraArgs:
        v: "4"
        read-only-port: "10255"
EOF
)"

kind create cluster --config <(printf '%s\n' "${kind_config}") --image  kindest/node:v1.27.1@sha256:b7d12ed662b873bd8510879c1846e87c7e676a79fefc93e17b2a52989d3ff42b

title: ProgressDeadlineExceeded not set outside of Deployment rollouts
body:
I'd floated #93933 earlier with a PR attempting to address this, and more recently opened [rhbz#1983823][1].  Here's a third try at pitching this proposal 🤞.

/sig apps

#### Proposal

When a Deployment has a single underlying ReplicaSet that had previously completed, but which now lacks the target count of ready replicas, and the underling ReplicaSet fails to make progress for more than `progressDeadlineSeconds`, the Deployment controller should set `Progressing=False` with `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`.

##### Benefits

Deployment owners get a clear signal that the Deployment controller (via the delegated ReplicaSet controller) is struggling to recover the desired state.  In situations where the Deployment controller continues to be unable to make progress, additional disruption will eventually push us into `Available=False`.  But `Progressing=False` with `ProgressDeadlineExceeded` is a way the Deployment controller can request assistance before things get bad enough to go `Available=False`.

##### Downsides

Maybe someone depends on the current behavior and would be broken by the proposed pivot.  Feedback welcome, if anyone can think of a use case that might be vulnerable.

#### Context

The only `Progressing` condition in kubernetes/kubernetes is `DeploymentProgressing`, so we don't have to worry about changes to the Deployment controller's handling being inconsistent with other core controllers.

The dev-facing godocs for Deployment's `Progressing` [is][2] and [has been since it landed][3]:

> Progressing means the deployment is progressing. Progress for a deployment is considered when a new replica set is created or adopted, and when new Pods scale up or old Pods scale down. Progress is not estimated for paused deployments or when progressDeadlineSeconds is not specified.

"when new pods scale up or old pods scale down" is the fuzzy bit where this proposal is working.

title: Warn when new clusters are turned up using the `.local` DNS TLD
body:
### What would you like to be added?

xref #82381

.local has meaning that doesn't really apply to Kubernetes.  We never should have used it.  We may not be able to change the default (maybe not now, maybe not ever), but we can make it more obvious to people.

1) Update docs to make it clear that `.cluster.local` is the default, but something like `.cluster.lan` is probably better.
2) Update examples to use a different name (2a: decide on a better name; 2b: use it)
3) Update tools which implement that default to issue warnings (non-fatal) 

### Why is this needed?

.local has meaning that doesn't really apply to Kubernetes.  We never should have used it.

title: DaemonSet does not recreate failed pods when they have deletionTimestamp
body:
/sig apps

When a terminal pod (Failed or Succeeded) has a deletionTimestamp it is ignored by DaemonSet and not recreated, because of this check: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go#L822-L824.

It was observed when working on what was isolated to Kubelet issue, that Kubelet would not force-delete pods in some scenarios: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118472. 

The below reproduction steps use the 1.27.2 version with affected kubelet by the bug:

1. create kind cluster using 1.27.2 with config in `kind-config.yaml`

```yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
```

```sh
kind create cluster --config kind-config.yaml --image kindest/node:v1.27.2
```

2. create daemonset with the following spec:
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
 name: issue-daemonset
 namespace: default
spec:
 selector:
   matchLabels:
     name: issue-label
 template:
   metadata:
     labels:
       name: issue-label
   spec:
     os:
       name: "windows"
     containers:
     - name: ubuntu
       image:  gcr.io/google-containers/ubuntu:14.04
       command: ["/bin/sleep"]
       args: ["infinity"]
```

title: imagePullSecrets should log warning if secret does not exist
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


#### What happened:

imagePullSecrets can added to a pod manifest to reference a secret containing registry credentials. Currently, if you add the name of a secret that does not exist, there is no warning or error. 

#### What you expected to happen:

I would expect there to be an error and a failed deployment if the secret does not exist/cannot be found in the namespace. 
If people are pulling public images, they may still wish to authenticate to a registry, for example dockerhub, before pulling the image, in order to utilise their subscription account rate limits. Currently if they use imagePullSecrets and the referenced secret does not exist, they may assume they are authenticating to their account when they are not, and will still be able to pull public images without any warning that authentication is not taking place. 

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

Add `imagePullSecrets: myfakesecret` to a pod spec, and pull images from docker.io.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

There is a case where if user updates image of a running container that desires resource resize, it gets restarted with desired values that has not been granted by kubelet. This will cause image update to fail. We need to use checkpointed resourcesAllocated values in this case.

Please see review comment: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102884#discussion_r932998061

### Why is this needed?

We need this to allow image update when a desired resize has not been admitted by kubelet.

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Add /resize subresource to request pod resource resizing
body:
### What would you like to be added?

In-place Pod vertical scaling [feature](/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102884/) currently relies on PATCH verb applied to Pod objects. This issue tracks a task to design and implement /resize subresource for Pods as opposed to PATCH, add RBAC controls to it, and additionally consider supporting it for Pod superset objects such as Jobs, RS, Deploys etc.

This came up during KEP discussions with Tim Hockin as we revisited first version of the API.
Please see the following discussion threads for context:
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1883#discussion_r459156714
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1883#discussion_r464627665
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1883#discussion_r448752659
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1883#discussion_r555668219
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1883#issuecomment-814273899




### Why is this needed?

It may be cleaner and more desirable to use /resize subresource to request a desired resize, and such a resource can be optionally supported on objects such as Deployments, Jobs etc.

title: DRA: delayed allocation: deallocate after use
body:
When a ResourceClaim:
- uses delayed allocation
- does not get created for a specific pod (i.e. not from a template)

then it currently gets allocated and remains allocated until:
- scheduling of a pod fails because the node originally chosen for the allocation isn't suitable, in which case the scheduler triggers deallocation via `claim.status.deallocationRequested`
- the user deletes the claim

What we want instead is that deallocation gets triggered when the last user of such an allocated claim gets removed from `claim.status.reservedFor`. To avoid races, deallocation must be done through `deallocationRequested`.

This can be implemented either as a controller or directly in the API server.

title: Allow setting an environment variable to some fraction or multiple of a resource field
body:
**What would you like to be added**:

It would be nice to pass a process a number that is a bit lower than the container memory limit so that its garbage collection or memory management can use that limit.

For example:

- setting `GOMEMLIMIT` or setting `NODEMEMLIMIT`
- setting `NODE_OPTS=--max-old-space-size=$(NODEMEMLIMIT)` would be useful.
- setting `JAVA_MEM_LIMIT` and passing `-Xmx$(JAVA_MEM_LIMIT)M`

Currently you can use `envFrom.resourceFieldRef` to "copy" a resource request or limit to an environment variable, but you can only multiply the value by some power of 1000 or 1024 by specifying `divisor`.

**Why is this needed**:

This would make it possible to pass a memory limit into a process inside the container that is based on the container resource request or limit but less.

For example, when specifying node's `--max-old-space-size` or Java's `-Xmx` parameter, setting it equal to the memory limit of the container will be a problem, because the process actually uses more memory than what you provided as a parameter.

**Potential Solutions**

- If we could specify a `divisor` like `1.5Mi` then it would result in a number of megabytes equal to roughly 2 thirds of the available memory, leaving some extra for the other heaps.
- Add another field like `scale` or `multiplier` to `enfFrom.resourceFieldRef` which is multiplied by the input value to get the env var value
- Allow arithmetic in the existing env var expansion system - where currently you can only do `$(SOME_VAR)` in the command line, additionally support something like `$(SOME_VAR - 100)`
- Allow using a go template or some simple templating/expression language to actually fill out the env var with prefix and suffix, like `--max-old-space-size={{ value * 800 }}M`

**Workarounds**

- Create an admission webhook that does one of the above without changing the kubernetes core features
- If the container uses bash, you could run a command like `bash -c 'NODE_OPTIONS=---max-old

title: StatefulSet with `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` should create pods in parallel
body:
### What would you like to be added?

When `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` is set, StatefulSetController should issue create requests for replicas in batches (similar to how other controllers work, e.g. ReplicaSetController) when creating pods for the first time and scaling up.

### Why is this needed?

Currently even with `Parallel` podManagementPolicy StatefulSet the replicas are still _created_ sequentially, even though they can start to _run_ in any order.

This severely limits pod throughput when working with large StatefulSets (~thousands of replicas). For example, 10 StatefulSets with 5k pods each achieve a total of ~6 pods/s, while 1k StatefulSets with 50 pods each allows for creating ~120 pods/s. 

`Parallel` policy suggests the pods can be created sequentially (https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/stateful-set-v1/#StatefulSetSpec): 

>The alternative policy is Parallel which will create pods in parallel to match the desired scale without waiting, and on scale down will delete all pods at once.

Relevant code (`Parallel` policy controls the value of `monotonic`): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L424)

title: Feature: Container level control of active deadlines
body:
### What would you like to be added?

A client wants the ability to control active deadlines on a container-by-container basis.  

Currently you can set active deadlines on a pod basis and at the job level.  I don't believe it is possible to say that I want to restrict a particular container (or init-container) to be restricted to run under a particular amount of time.  

This would probably need a new API in the Container API and some thoughts on what kind of control we would want to provide.  

### Why is this needed?

Users would like to control how long init containers run.  They would want to set a deadline for init containers that normal containers don't have to obey.  

Other areas that could fall under this is to only apply an active deadline if the Pod is running.  A relevant issue could be https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/111948.

title: kubectl wait on arbitrary jsonpath with unknown value
body:
### What would you like to be added?

#83094 describes the `kubectl wait` functionality that allows to wait for a JSONPath expression condition to match a value. For example, the following command waits for a pod with the name `busybox1` reaching "Running" phase:

```bash
kubectl wait pod/busybox1 --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Running
```

The proposal is to extend the syntax of the command by supporting _any non-empty_ values. The extended syntax will look like the following:

```terminal
jsonpath='{JSONPath expression}'[=value]
```

In the new syntax if the `=value` is provided, the behavior will be, as today, to return when the JSONPath expression matches the value. If `=value` is omitted, the behavior will be to return when the JSONPath expression exists and has _any non-empty_  value.



### Why is this needed?

Unfortunately, the use of current syntax of the JSONPath conditions is limited because it is not always possible to know in advance the value that the JSONPath expression will get. For example, if we would like to wait for a LoadBalancer service with the name `loadbalancer1` to get IP "10.0.0.1", we will run the following command:

```bash
kubectl wait service/loadbalancer1 --for=jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[].ip}'="10.0.0.1"
```

However, there is no guarantee that the service will get this IP. It can get any other. So, if we want to wait until the LoadBalancer service will get an IP, any IP, we cannot use `kubectl wait` command. Like this, we cannot wait for annotations and labels that are dynamically assigned when their value can vary.

Today DevOps engineers are forced to compose scripts where they implement the waiting logic by calling `kubectl get` in loops (e.g. [this question][1] on Stackoverflow).

[1]: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/66114851/kubectl-wait-for-service-to-get-external-ip

title: When publishNotReadyAddresses is set to true, Services route traffic to not-ready Pods anyway
body:
### What happened?

When creating a set of pods behind a service facade (with **_publishNotReadyAddresses=true_**), from which only one pod is marked as ready (albeit they're all running), traffic hitting the service IP gets routed to all pods, not just the ready one(s).

It's possible this is a side-effect of hard-wiring the _**ready**_ attribute in _EndpointSlice_ to _**true**_ (as documented [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices/#ready)).

It seems to me that traffic should only be routed to the pods if _**both**_ _ready_ and _serving_ are _**true**_. The observed behavior contradicts the [documentation of the publishNotReadyAddresses flag](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/dns-pod-service/).

### What did you expect to happen?

Service traffic to only be routed to pods in Ready status.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1) create a stateful set or deployment whose pods will randomly mark themselves as ready, and those marked as ready will listen on a given port (using **_nc -kl 8000_** or **_python3 -m http.server_**)
2) create a service that will route traffic to those pods, and set _publishNotReadyAddresses=true_
3) attempt to access the service's IP + Port repeatedly, observe how "connection refused" errors occur sporadically, evidencing that traffic is being routed to pods that aren't listening.

### Anything else we need to know?

The pods' startup and liveness probes are successful, but only one of the pods' readiness probe succeeds. Regardless, traffic is attempted to be served out to all pods.

title: WaitForAttachAndMount might delay pod terminating.
body:
From comment https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/100047#issuecomment-796980046

syncPod is waiting for volumes to finish mounting. before calling WaitForAttachAndMount, it checks if the pod is terminated before entering. However, if the pod is terminated after that check, then we are stuck in in WaitForAttachAndMount until it times out, a little over 2 minutes.

The call probably needs to be enhanced to return early if the pod is deleted. It doesn't seem like pod deletion is captured as a pod error. In fact, we seem to pop all errors if the pod is deleted.

title: `kubectl expose` fails for apps with same-port, different-protocol
body:
Given this deployment:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: multiport
spec:
  replicas: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: multiport
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: multiport
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: k8s.gcr.io/serve_hostname:v1.4
        name: c1
        ports:
        - containerPort: 93
          protocol: TCP
        - containerPort: 93
          protocol: UDP
```

```
$ k expose deploy multiport
The Service "multiport" is invalid: spec.ports[1]: Duplicate value: core.ServicePort{Name:"", Protocol:"UDP", AppProtocol:(*string)(nil), Port:93, TargetPort:intstr.IntOrString{Type:0, IntVal:0, StrVal:""}, NodePort:0}
```

Looking at staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/expose/expose.go, it builds a `protocolsMap` which reduces those 2 ports to one protocol.  It should probably just return a list of {proto, port} or even {proto, port, name} which it extracts from the target.

title: dynamic resource allocation: delete generated ResourceClaims
body:
At the moment, dynamic resource allocation relies on the garbage collector to delete a ResourceClaim that was created from a template for a specific pod. But that garbage collection only happens when the pod actually gets deleted.

That means that for pods that linger after having failed or completed (manually created test pods, jobs), resources remain allocated for extended periods of time although they are not needed anymore and could be reused for other claims.

The solution outlined in the KEP is to make the `resourceclaim` controller also responsible for deleting ResourceClaims when it detects that a pod no longer needs the claim.

title: DRA resource driver API: batching Pod resource claims for allocation, deallocation, resource preparation and unpreparation
body:
### What would you like to be added?

API for resource driver Allocate and Deallocate calls should handle list of resource claim allocations like the NodePrepareResource and NodeUnprepareResources do, and DRA helper code should send all resource claims that belong to the same pod scheduling context in the same list for allocation and deallocation.

API for resource driver preparation and unpreparation of resources should also batch all the resource claims that can be prepared and unprepared at the same time by given driver based on the Pod being handled by kubelet.

### Why is this needed?

At the moment resource driver has no easy means to know all resource claims of the Pod when the Pod is being scheduled, the allocate call handles one claim at a time, which makes optimizations of resources during allocation sub-optimal and more complicated - resource driver has to keep track of what resource claims are part of particular Pod scheduling context to judge which of the previously allocated resource claims could have been sent for resource preparations, and which were not and thus can still be adjusted for resource optimization. 
In kubelet plugin as well, preparation of resource can sometimes be setting the actual HW in a state when no more additional changes can be done until previous changes are undone, making preparation of future  requests impossible, and at the moment there has to be additional logic in resource-driver kubelet-plugin forecasting which resource claims could be coming in consecutive calls to batch-prepare resources.

title: [Umbrella] Skip Filter plugins when coupled PreFilter plugin returns `Skip` status
body:
### What would you like to be added?

It's spawned from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107556.

After https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114125 gets merged, the scheduler skips the plugin in Filter, if that plugin return `Skip` in PreFilter. In other words, the plugin can return `Skip` when it doesn't do anything on Pod's scheduling.

For example, if the pod doesn't have any inter-pod affinity, the inter-pod affinity plugin PreFilter can return Skip, and the scheduler won't run the inter-pod affinity plugin Filter. 

Here, I just listed all filter plugins, **not all of them may not need to return Skip in PreFilter though.** Assignee, please make sure your plugin really needs to return `Skip` or not.
Please feel free to assign what you'd like to work on. And please comment in this issue before starting to work on so that we can avoid many people from working on the same thing!

- [x] InterPodAffinity @sanposhiho https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114889
- [x] NodeAffinity @sanposhiho https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114125

title: controller_util_test.go does not follow similar patterns as other unit tests in the repo.
body:
### What would you like to be added?

During implementation of KEP 3393 (PodReplacementPolicy for Jobs) we found that the unit tests of [controller_util_test.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/controller_utils_test.go) do not follow common patterns established in k/k.  

1) The tests are not written using table driven design (https://dave.cheney.net/2019/05/07/prefer-table-driven-tests).

2) The tests use `Differences` rather than `Cmp.Diff`.

This probably should be done as two separate PRs but wanted to highlight some areas that could use some cleanup. 

### Why is this needed?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/117015#discussion_r1254470573

Not using `Cmp.Diff` means that we don't see diffs in the unit tests that makes this difficult.  

And not using table driven tests makes it difficult to add new test cases as it usually is brought up during review that we should use a table-driven test but the entire file does not obey this format.

title: Do contextual logging for scheduler
body:
The kube-scheduler is currently difficult to debug through logs. Logging is inconsistent and sparse, and critically helpful information is in some spots logged at too high of a level to be practically accessible (such as [node scores](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b618411f1edb98afe807866fb3a607356d72ba24/pkg/scheduler/core/generic_scheduler.go#L703), which are `V(10)`. At this level logs are flooded with low-level information too quickly to even grep).

**What would you like to be added**:
Standardize scheduler logging to useful, documented levels to improve debuggability and diagnoses of scheduling anomalies. This information should be accessible at reasonable levels so as not to be flooded by irrelevant low-level process and network logs (ie, `v=2,3,4..`) and consistent across the scheduler.

Specifically, information that is necessary includes, but is not limited to:
* Filter plugins
  * Per plugin/per node
* Preemption attempts (/postfilter plugins)
* Score plugins
  * Normalized results
    * Per plugin/per node
* Nominated node result
(sub-lists to indicate potential logging hierarchies. these are just some examples)

In addition, these logs should be able to be easily traced through a scheduling cycle. That is, all logs related to a specific scheduling cycle should have a unique identifier so that relevant information can be efficiently gathered with common search tools like grep.

**Why is this needed**:
The most common issues with the scheduler are questions related to the scheduling cycle ("Why did/didn't my pod get scheduled here/there?"). While the scheduler does currently report `FailedScheduling` events, these can lack information (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/91340, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/91601) and do not provide any insight to successful scheduling that does not land on the expected node (eg, scoring interference).

title: Feature request: Upgrade buckets in statefulsets
body:
What is the ask?
If we were to assume all replicas of a Statefulset can be bucketed into a fixed number of 'upgrade buckets', can Statefulset controller support rolling update based on these 'upgrade buckets'

What is the benefit?
* Shorter upgrade times
* Constant time upgrade regardless of number of replicas

How does this work?
If we have hundreds or thousands of replicas in a sts, a simple rolling update can take a very long time.
If we were to bucket all replicas into a fixed number of buckets where the application deals with building redundancy across buckets vs replicas, we believe the upgrades can be shortened a lot and also can be made constant time.

xref #108794

title: Document address family of listening INET sockets, given config
body:
The docs are ambiguous on whether a socket will be limited to either the IPv4 or IPv6 address familiy. 
E.g., https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-apiserver/
 contains 

> `--bind-address` string     Default: 0.0.0.0
> --
>  The IP address on which to listen for the --secure-port port. The associated interface(s) must be reachable by the rest of the cluster, and by CLI/web clients. If blank **or an unspecified address (0.0.0.0 or ::), all interfaces will be used**.

This wording in bold suggests that when `bind-address` is 0.0.0.0, the API server will listen on IPv6 addresses too, potentially. That would be incorrect and prevent limiting the address family from the config (to enforce single-stack). According to a report to me, indeed this incorrect behavior is the case. In any case, the wording is ambiguous.

Moreover, the source code base contains quite a few `0.0.0.0` literals that aren't accompanied by `::`, suggesting that IPv4 is assumed in some paths. Unless ... Kubernetes has this special algorithm that equates either {0.0.0.0} or {::} with {0.0.0.0, ::}.

title: StatefulSet ignores OnDelete update strategy
body:
### What happened?

According to the official documentation https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/#update-strategies, when using the OnDelete strategy, the update of the pods should be done when the user deletes the pod. However, I found a case where StatefulSet tries to update volumes of an existing pod.

It is also worth noting that if StatefulSet gets an error when trying to update volumes in an existing pod (e.g. because the Volume field cannot be changed in an existing pod), StatefulSet will interrupt service to other pods.

### What did you expect to happen?

When using the OnDelete strategy, the StatefulSet will update the pod only when the pod is deleted.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create an instance of StatefulSet without PVC and wait until all pods are created
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: test-sts
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test-pod
  serviceName: ""
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test-pod
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: test-container
          image: busybox
          command:
            - sleep
            - "3600"
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  updateStrategy:
    type: OnDelete
```
2. Delete the created StatefulSet, but leave its pods
```shell
kubectl delete sts/test-sts --cascade=orphan
```

3. Create a new StatefulSet with PVC, for example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: test-sts
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test-pod
  serviceName: ""
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test-pod
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: test-container
          image: busybox
          command:
            - sleep
            - "3600"
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          volumeMounts:
            - mountPath: /mnt

title: Introduce JSON logging format for kube-proxy
body:
#### What would you like to be added:

Structured logging support in k8s allows specifying logging in JSON. Many k8s components like apiServer, scheduler have support for json. This issue tracks adding JSON logging support for kube-proxy.  

#### Breakdown of the task

To get json logging support, changes have to be made in kube-proxy and Kind e2e script (for Prow/CI runs) which uses KubeProxyConfiguration 

1. Introduce logging-format (--logging-format string  ) option in kube-proxy. Currently there is none. ([link](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-proxy/))
2. Introduce an option in [KubeProxyConfiguration](https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-proxy/blob/v0.22.1/config/v1alpha1/types.go#L104) so that kubeadm/kind can specify logging-format. Whether this "configuration option" is something generic or specific to logging needs input from a kube-proxy domain expert.
3. Update Kind to make use of the above 2 and specify the logging format similar to how we do for control-plane components. 
4. Prow/test-infra CI runs will have json logging enabled for kube-proxy.

#### Why is this needed:
To get the benefits of structured logging.

/sig network
/cc @serathius 
/cc @BenTheElder

title: PVCs capacity can exceed request.storage resource quota
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Make Kubernetes validate correctly the CSI volumes capacity allocated. 

### Why is this needed?

## Reproduce

- Create a resourcequota as
  ```yaml
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ResourceQuota
  metadata:
    name: default-quota
    namespace: default
  spec:
    hard:
      requests.storage: 1Gi
   ```
- Create a first PVC as
  ```yaml
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
  metadata:
    name: first-pvc
    namespace: default
  spec:
    accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
    resources:
      requests:
        storage: 1Mi
    storageClassName: gce-pd-ssd
   ```
- Create a second PVC as
  ```yaml
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
  metadata:
    name: second-pvc
    namespace: default
  spec:
    accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
    resources:
      requests:
        storage: 1Mi
    storageClassName: gce-pd-ssd
   ```
- Check PVCs provisionning
  ```shell
  $ k get pvc -n app-k8s-demo-ppd
  NAME       STATUS   VOLUME                                     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
  first-pvc  Bound    pvc-3f341049-c5f6-46e9-92aa-bb288e0d124e   1Gi        RWO            gce-pd-ssd     1m
  second-pvc Bound    pvc-7bda0b63-59f0-442f-9bdf-3cd40d262c07   1Gi        RWO            gce-pd-ssd     1m
  ```

## Actual behavior

- There is no limitation on the minimum of requested storage
- Kubernetes is doing its validation on this resource.request.storage field which breaks the quota enforcement

## Expected behavior

- gcp-compute-persistent-disk-csi prevents me from creating PVCs with 1Mi request as the minimum capacity is 1Gi

## Additional details

This can be bypassed using a LimitRange but this one applies to all the PVCs in the cluster, there is no way of making it per CSI/StorageClass AFAIK

title: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
body:
### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from there on. So basically Kubernetes wouldn't do much in terms of scheduling, but takes over from there.

### What did you expect to happen?

TBH I expected it to fail and it did. The resource claims won't work, since the scheduler plugin isn't getting a chance to do its thing.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Just use DRA with Pod spec nodeName field, one needs a DRA driver obviously.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Export `loadConfigFromFile` as a public function `LoadConfigFromFile`
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I want `loadConfigFromFile` to be exported as a public function `LoadConfigFromFile` 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/746b88c6ff442185589640885228ef100811083a/cmd/kube-scheduler/app/options/configfile.go#L33-L40
 

### Why is this needed?

* [Kubernetes cluster-autoscaler](https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/tree/master/cluster-autoscaler) imports scheduler code and runs scheduler simulations for `Pending` pods to decide which nodegroup should be scaled up. 
* consider this case:
  1. a user is running a scheduler with custom scheduler config
  2. the user wants cluster-autoscaler to run scheduler simulations based on the custom scheduler config
 
For ii default scheduler config is used in cluster-autoscaler scheduler simulations. Right now, it is not possible to use custom scheduler config for cluster-autoscaler scheduler simulations  but I am working on a PR (https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/pull/5708) to support this feature. For this feature, I need to parse scheduler config. [I have custom code based on `loadConfigFromFile`](https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/pull/5708/files#diff-03046c2a86c17ed94a0d62f14449afb658d5a297113cbf894f3a1150858d0203R122-R141). It would help if we can have  `loadConfigFromFile` exported as `LoadConfigFromFile` (just like [`ValidateSchedulerConfiguration`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/746b88c6ff442185589640885228ef100811083a/pkg/scheduler/apis/config/validation/validation.go#L40)) so that programs which need to parse scheduler config can use the exported `LoadConfigFromFile` function directly instead of writing custom code.

title: meaning of sync_proxy_rules_iptables_total given MinimizeIPTablesRestore
body:
The `sync_proxy_rules_iptables_total` metric is defined as "Number of proxy iptables rules programmed".

In the past, that effectively meant "the total number of rules in iptables that kube-proxy owns". But post-`MinimizeIPTablesRestore`, it now ends up being "the number of iptables rules that changed in the last sync". (FWIW this is only a change for the `nat` half of the metric; currently we always rewrite all `filter` rules, even in a partial sync, so the `filter` half of the metric is still "correct".)

There are arguments for either meaning, but I think the traditional ("total number of rules in iptables that kube-proxy owns") is more useful?

One possibility would be to only set the metric during full syncs, but in that case we might go a very long time without updating it, and it would get out of date.

Another possibility would be that instead of setting that metric from the `iptables-restore` _input_, we could set it from the `iptables-save` _output_. This would mean that it would always lag by (at least) one sync (since it would be set based on the rules we are replacing rather than the rules we are creating) but that would at least be more up-to-date than waiting for the next full resync. (In `largeClusterMode`, it would lag a bit more, only getting updated once every `syncPeriod` (default 30s).)

If we think it's important to have it always be up-to-date then we could try to figure out some way to calculate the right value during a partial update... in that case we'd have to run through the code that currently gets bypassed during a partial update, and have it decide what rules are needed, but not actually try to write them.

/sig network

body:
### What happened?

I was trying to add volume expansion support to an out-of-tree CSI driver (https://github.com/apalia/cloudstack-csi-driver), then when I actually tried to expand a volume which I had created, I saw an error message from kube-controller-manager saying "didn't find a plugin capable of expanding the volume; waiting for an external controller to process this PVC".
After some debugging, I found that the `ProbeExpandableVolumePlugins` function in app/plugins.go does not call `csi.ProbeVolumePlugins()`, like the `ProbeAttachableVolumePlugins` function does. Instead, it creates a list of legacy volume plugins and a few hard-coded ones, but CSI is missing from that list:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c2a7bfd6b4f147b40c3b2132aae003ff21a142bb/cmd/kube-controller-manager/app/plugins.go#L73
Later on, when trying to expand a volume, the `FindPluginBySpec` function in volume/plugins.go will return the error "no volume plugin matched" because CSI is not in its list of plugins.

Was CSI intentionally omitted? The [CSI developer documentation](https://kubernetes-csi.github.io/docs/volume-expansion.html) says that CSI drivers can implement volume expansion, so it seems odd that `ProbeExpandableVolumePlugins` does not include CSI in its list.

title: Promoting some flowcontrol metrics to Beta
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Some flowcontrol metrics in kube-apiserver have been around for a long time and are very high value signals for how APF is impacting apiserver latency. With APF graduated to Beta in 1.20 and on-going work to get to GA, I wanted to open an issue to discuss graduating some of these metrics to Beta ([or Stable because we skip Beta?](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/1209-metrics-stability/kubernetes-control-plane-metrics-stability.md#beta-stability-level)), specifically ones that are high value signals for apiserver latency with many users depending on them already. Here are metrics that I personally think would benefit from graduation to Stable based on their usage at Google:
* request_wait_duration_seconds
* request_concurrency_in_use
* request_concurrency_limit
* rejected_requests_total
* dispatched_requests_total
* current_inqueue_requests
* current_executing_requests 

For other metrics, I propose we leave as alpha for now as they pertain to internals details of APF that most users will likely not care about and mostly catered to maintainers who are looking to optimize implementation details.

### Why is this needed?

Promoting widely adopted metrics to Beta/Stable will provide stronger guarantees on their compatibility going forward.

title: [Proposal] k-proxy support zero trust network
body:

Motivation
===========

Due to business security requirements, developers need to switch the TCP/HTTP services exposed by service to TLS/HTTPS without any impact. However, the current k-proxy does not provide this capability by default. Although ServiceMesh enhances the functionality of Kubernetes Service in the field of service (including governance, security, observability, etc.), it is quite heavy to introduce an additional sidecar if users only focus on security-related capabilities. ===========

Integrating the universal network security capabilities of zero trust network into the k-proxy or other independent components, allows users of k8s to use it out of the box. The k-proxy/Daemonset with zero trust network architecture is as follows:

title: Not possible to tolerate domain loss in TopologySpreadConstraints and keep capacity after addition of minDomains
body:
### What would you like to be added?


When working with `TopologySpreadConstraints` it used to not be possible to control how pods got placed in the scenario where a node pool had to be scaled up from 0 nodes and, whilst it has not yet scaled to the point where the maximum number of domains that the agent pool can provide is reached, the scheduler will not be aware of them and hence make scheduling decisions contrary to what the developer might expect.

https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3030 solved this by adding `minDomains`. Nonetheless, if one is to use this new setting, while it will be possible to ensure that all require domains are present before making scheduling decisions that might result in domain inbalance, it will degrade the workload's ability to operate in failure conditions. 

To make a clear example, in a scenario where we are working with the `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` or `failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone` domains. There can be a clear requirement to:

1. Ensure that we have N zone redundancy for the workload
2. Allow the workload to keep up with the required capacity ( be able to scale up, restore lost capacity due to failure ... ) 

In a failure scenario where we are expecting 2 zones to be available but there is a zone failure where we lose the nodes in one of the zones this is how things would play out in my head.

To accomodate (1) we would use `minDomains` as the setting is intended to solve that precise problem. Nonetheless, the moment we do that, we would limit (2) as, per the behaviour of that field, we would only be able to have as many pods as `maxSkew` dictates.

title: Mismatched URLs for service-account-issuer-discovery and Open API Spec's swagger.json
body:
### What happened?

When I use the official Kubernetes Java Client (version 18.0.0) from within a pod using `Config.defaultClient()` to build an `ApiClient` and then access `getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDConfiguration` in the `WellKnownApi` I get the following error:

```json
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "forbidden: User \"system:serviceaccount:test:user\" cannot get path \"/.well-known/openid-configuration/\"",
  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403
}
```

The same happens with the `OpenidApi#getServiceAccountIssuerOpenIDKeyset`.

However, the problem does not happen when I call the `/.well-known/openid-configuration` endpoint using the pod's service account and curl.

The problem is that the generated Open API spec indicates that the client should call `/.well-known/openid-configuration/` instead of `/.well-known/openid-configuration` (and similarly `/openid/v1/jwks/` instead of `/openid/v1/jwks`). While the API Server seems to resolve these endpoints just fine, the `ClusterRole` defined in the code does not have the trailing slashes and therefore rejects the requests with a 403:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a75e7c40cab5a0d96d815c3aa976dc98b4b0972/plugin/pkg/auth/authorizer/rbac/bootstrappolicy/policy.go#L521-L530

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected to be able to access these APIs from within a pod that has a mounted service account because this [documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-account/#service-account-issuer-discovery) suggests all that is required is a service account and because all clusters get this `ClusterRoleBinding` and this `ClusterRole` by default:

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  annotations:
    rbac.authorization.kubernetes.io/autoupdate: "true"
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/bootstrapping: rbac

Currently pv_controller  has its own resync loop which periodically list all PVCs/PVs and put them into the queue. title: Cron job staggering / randomization / concurrency limiting
body:
<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->

**What would you like to be added**: CronJobs should have fields allowing for their start time to be randomized (as systemd's Timers have), or even distributed within a range to spread out in equal intervals with other CronJobs of a set. At the very least, it would be useful to specify concurrency policies like "do not run more than two Jobs with the selected annotation", so that scheduling will be postponed until that policy could be met.

**Why is this needed**: I have a cluster with very few cores, and KubeApps adds a CronJob to sync every repo in the cluster, one for each repo, each one scheduled to run every 10 minutes. This would only take a few seconds per repo, but when it tries to run the CronJob at the same time for every repo, it causes a "Three Stooges effect", and most of the synchronization jobs end up timing out for lack of available processing. If I could stagger these synchronizations, they could all succeed, and my cluster wouldn't be momentarily starved of resources while it happens.

title: Debug endpoint to dump currently executing requests
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The currently available debug endpoints for APF are for dump_priority_levels, dump_queues, and dump_requests. These commands provide useful information primarily about the state of APF queues, including the the FlowDistinguisher, ArriveTime, UserName, Verb, and APIPath of requests waiting in queues. To help debug APF-related issues, it would be valuable to provide similar information about requests which have been dispatched by APF and are currently occupying 1 or more seats. The existing commands for dump_priority_levels and dump_queues give a count for the number of executing requests per PriorityLevelConfiguration or queue but there is not enough information available to identify which requests those are without also using information available from audit or apiserver logs.

### Why is this needed?

This new debug command, which could be called something like dump_executing_requests, could assist with live-debugging of APF issues. Situations where this would be useful:
1. General APF debugging to see which problematic requests are using a majority of seats per PriorityLevelConfiguration. This would aid in live-debugging in situations where the given request type is not included in the cluster's audit policy or if verbose apiserver logging is not enabled. Situations where a relatively low number of requests use a large number of seats could be debugged quicker (for example if listing 100k+ event objects is taking around 60 seconds).
2. APF issues with stuck requests. For example, this previous issue with broken CRD could've been quickly reproduced if we knew which watch request was stuck executing, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109603. title: Job: Pod backoff calculation should not depend on failure policy
body:
### What happened?

Pod backoff calculation excludes pods that match an `Ignore` rule in the failure policy:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/847f1758748ac357e79094c5e85029a10428e65f/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1365

This could lead to fast retries, overwhelming the control plane, if most failures match an `Ignore` rule. The semantics of `Ignore` is not to count towards the limit, but the backoff should still be respected.

/sig apps

### What did you expect to happen?

Recreations to be throttled.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job with failure policy that matches every kind of failure.

Volume can be detached successfully after the node goes down, and new Pods can be created successfully on another node, which means Pod can failover successfully.

body:
### What happened?

As part of our product we use [extended resources](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/#extended-resources) to add a capacity to certain nodes for use by special pods.  I found that if I add a capacity (`22` in my particular test case) to a node and then I try to schedule a `Deployment` with exactly that number of pods, each using 1 resource, one of the pods persistently fails to schedule.  

### What did you expect to happen?

All 22 slots should be used.  The 22nd pod should schedule no problem.

* Patch a node with an extended resource (I used a value of 22). **NB** when setting an extended resource capacity a PATCH operation must be used, at time of writing the feature in our product (1 year ago), `kubectl edit` didn't work.
* Create a deployment with 22 pods that each claim one of the resource and a nodeSelector targeting only the one node.

title: remove support for legacy debug profile for pre-1.22
body:
It looks like the returned ec references is only used for two reasons:

1) to print a debugging message, which could easily be changed
2) for compatibility with pre-1.22 APIs, which we probably don't need anymore

Maybe we should just get rid of returning a pointer to the ephemeral container and just return the name instead?

The section might read a little more clearly with an immediate pod copy, something like:

```
name := o.computeDebugContainerName(pod)
copied := pod.DeepCopy()
i := len(copied.Spec.EphemeralContainers)
copied.Spec.EphemeralContainers = append(copied.Spec.EphemeralContainers, corev1.EphemeralContainer{
		EphemeralContainerCommon: corev1.EphemeralContainerCommon{
			Name:                     name,
			Env:                      o.Env,
			Image:                    o.Image,
			ImagePullPolicy:          o.PullPolicy,
			Stdin:                    o.Interactive,
			TerminationMessagePolicy: corev1.TerminationMessageReadFile,
			TTY:                      o.TTY,
		},
		TargetContainerName: o.TargetContainer,
	})
ec := &copied.Spec.EphemeralContainers[i]
```

Both of these suggestions are optional, feel free to disregard or fix in a follow-up.

_Originally posted by @verb in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/114280#discussion_r1083991162_

title: Jobs create replacement Pods as soon as a Pod is marked for deletion
body:
### What happened?

When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted, the job controller creates a replacement pod immediately, even if parallelism is set to 1 and backoffLimit is set to 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

This depends on the use case, but some applications fail when there are more than one pod.

For example, tensorflow fails with:

```
 /job:worker/task:4: Duplicate task registration with task_name=/job:worker/replica:0/task:4
```

This applications will benefit from a delayed Pod creation until the original Pod is marked as Failed/Succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job that takes some time to clean up on SIGTERM. You can use `gcr.io/k8s-staging-perf-tests/sleep` with `-termination-grace-period 1m`
2. Delete the pod.
3. Observe that there are two pods running.

While here we do a manual DELETE, it could come as a result of preemption from kube-scheduler or a Node maintenance event, which could be common.

### Anything else we need to know?

IIUC, the existing behavior is similar to that of ReplicaSets and it's the behavior that Jobs had from the beginning.

A comment from an internal discussion with @erictune:

> This non-locking behavior was chosen when Job was designed.  At that time, there was no completionMode: Indexed.  Without an index, even if we waited for complete termination, the user would still need to do their own locking/coordination process, or ensure idempotence.  So it would just slow down the Job controller with no benefit.  

Also, at that time there was no PodFailurePolicy. If the user sets a rule for FailJob, we might be creating a replacement pod before being able to act on the policy (related to point 3 in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-apps/3329-retriable-and-non-retriable-failures#marking-pods-as-failed kubernetes/enhancements#3329).

So I propose that we treat this as a bugfix for Jobs (Indexed or NonI

title: Elastic Indexed Job
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently we validate that `spec.completions` is set when `completionMode=Indexed` for job. I suggest we relax this validation. 

This will require the following changes:

1) We need to update the job controller to look at `spec.parallelism` instead of `spec.completions` when calculating the range of indexes.
2) When reducing parallelism, we should remove the higher indexes first (otherwise the controller will eventually do that anyways to ensure that the pods have a continuous range).

both changes only apply when `spec.completions=nil`

### Why is this needed?

The use case is jobs with workers that require a form of autoscaling, like Ray, Spark or Horovord. By modeling these as jobs with `spec.completion=nil`, `spec.parallelism` can be used to scale the job.

While such jobs could be modeled as a StatefulSet, the job API offers batch-specific features that makes it a better fit (like [retriable and non retriable failures](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-apps/3329-retriable-and-non-retriable-failures))

title: Node lease leak caused by lease controller swallowing error
body:
### What happened?

Hello,

We have a cluster that's showing a constant increase in node lease objects. One particularity of the leaked leases is that  they don't have an OwnerReference.

Looking at the code, the ownerReference is set by this kubelet function [`SetNodeOwnerFunc`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dad95e1be65d4e74d33c810f4395596a22115717/pkg/kubelet/util/nodelease.go#L32) which is called by the lease controller in [`newLease`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dad95e1be65d4e74d33c810f4395596a22115717/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go#L230-L233). 

Note that  `newLease` returns `lease` even if the call to `newLeasePostProcessFunc` fails. The means `lease` is returned despite being potentially without an ownerRef.

Looking at `newLease()` call site in [`retryUpdateLease`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/dad95e1be65d4e74d33c810f4395596a22115717/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go#L187) we see that the returned error is swallowed meaning the controller will make calls to `c.leaseClient.Update` with an incomplete lease.

We don't have access to the worker nodes or the kubelet logs but this explanation match what we are seeing when looking at the audit logs where the call which creates the lease without ownerRef is an Update call.


### What did you expect to happen?

Node lease should always be created with an ownerRef

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To repro, setup a cluster with a worker node, delete the worker node object (but keep the node+kubelet running):
```
kubectl delete no ip-192-168-212-28.us-west-2.compute.internal
```
Then look at the lease, the original one will be removed by the GC but kubelet will eventually re-create it without an ownerRef:
```
$ kubectl -n kube-node-lease get lease ip-192-168-212-28.us-west-2.compute.internal -o json

body:
### NCC-E003660-RKV: Path Traversal in Namespace Specifier
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
By specifying a namespace of `..` in _list_ requests to the Kubernetes API, a user can
discover the full path of some objects they do not have access to, and possibly retrieve
CRD objects they do not have access to.

**Description**
The Kubernetes API will accept a directory traversal sequence ( `..` ) as the namespace in a
request, and this leads to some access control bypasses, as it widens the scope of the
etcd lookups which are constructed on the back end. For a variety of reasons, the extent to
which this issue can be exploited for unauthorized access to resources appears to be
relatively limited, but it does represent a significant flaw in access controls, and it is
possible that further methods of exploitation may exist, which have not been identified
during this assessment.

A single dot is also accepted as the namespace identifier, although this has less serious
consequences for security. Note that neither `..` nor `.` are accepted for other path
components in the URL (e.g. resource names) - these are checked by the
[NamespaceKeyFunc](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.24.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go#L245-L262) method and will be rejected.

In what follows, note that when a request is received with a namespace of `..` , RBAC
checks will be performed as normal, and so the requesting user will need to have
appropriate cluster-scoped permissions against the resource type being requested. For
example, a GET request to `/api/v1/namespaces/../pods` will require _get_ permission on
pods at cluster scope. The vulnerabilities here relate to being able to use such requests to
also access differ

restrictions on and between pods to provide isolation. However, their design and behavior
result in several drawbacks that significantly limit their applicability. In general, the
`networking.k8s.io/v1` `NetworkPolicy` type attempts to present a lowest common
denominator specification for traffic filtering. It is not, however, required that a CNI

useful isolation features than are supported by the standard `NetworkPolicy` type.
Additionally, while network policies may be partially or fully unsupported, there is no
mechanism to determine if an applied `NetworkPolicy` will be enforced. Instead, it is left to
administrators to validate the intended behavior. In general, the risk of this facet of network
policy behavior is low given that production CNIs tend to support network policies.

controls, whereby a range or “entity” that is allowed cannot be disallowed. Furthermore, network policies are, in the general use case, effectively opt-in, as rule application is performed via label matchers. title: NCC-E003660-YVU: Incorrect Handling of Proxy Authentication Headers
body:
### NCC-E003660-YVU: Incorrect Handling of Proxy Authentication Headers
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
If custom values have been set for the authentication proxy header names, an attacker can
assert arbitrary group memberships to extension API servers, leading to privilege
escalation opportunities.

**Description**
The proxy authentication scheme supported by the Kubernetes API server adds custom
HTTP headers to proxied requests to specify username, groups and extra values. These
header names default to `X-Remote-User`, `X-Remote-Group` and `X-Remote-Extra-xxxx`, but
can be changed using command line arguments. The implementation of proxy authentication used by the aggregation layer strips these headers out of incoming requests (to avoid the obvious header spoofing attack), but this code does not take account of the fact that the header names are configurable - instead, it assumes the default values. This means that if the header names _have_ been changed, it will be possible for an attacker to add these headers to a request sent to the Kubernetes API server, and when it is proxied onwards (e.g. to an extension API server) they will not be stripped. The extension API server (assuming that it has been configured with the same header names, as would be expected) would then make security decisions based on these spoofed values: if following the guidance in the Kubernetes documentation, it would include the spoofed information in the `SubjectAccessReview` sent back to the main API server.

title: minimum-image-ttl-duration is not working after restart kubelet

### What happened?

When a node is under disk pressure, restarting kubelet will lead to image gc immediately, even if we set a long `minimum-image-ttl-duration`.

image gc honor `minimum-image-ttl-duration` when we restart kubelet of a node under disk pressure.

2. make sure node is under disk pressure, e.g. nodefs utilization 85%+ (without imagefs)
3. pull new image on disk pressure node, make sure there are unused images on this node
4. restart kubelet

title: Pod volume configuration miss match between config map and secrets
body:
### What happened?

Configuration of specifying the `ConfigMap` and `Secret` as a volume for `Pod` are not consistent with each other.
In K8S Pod key to specify a `ConfigMap` in volumes is `name`, but key to specify a `Secret`  name is `secretName`. 

As all the other configuration to set a volume as ConfigMap and Secret are same, the key name should be same as well to avoid confusion. 


### What did you expect to happen?

While setting the `Secret` as volume in `Pod`, change the key of Secret to `name` from `secretName`

AS IS:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: nginx
  name: secret-vol
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: secret-vol 
      secret:
         secretName: test-secret
  containers:
  - image: nginx
    name: nginx
```

TO BE:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: nginx
  name: secret-vol
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: secret-vol 
      secret:
         name: test-secret
  containers:

    name: nginx
```
