title: Use of a third party library maintained by a Sanctioned Entity
body:
### What happened?

The [easyjson](https://github.com/mailru/easyjson) library is maintained by Mail.ru. This is owned by VK, which is owned by Gazprom Media, and thus is subject to EU and [USA Sanctions](https://sanctionssearch.ofac.treas.gov/Details.aspx?id=20296) 

This is a dependancy via [https://github.com/go-openapi/swag](https://github.com/go-openapi/swag/issues/68) which is used by the client-go library.

I suspect Kubernetes want to either fork easyjson, or migrate to a library that isn't maintained by a sanctioned entity.

I did attempt to report this via the process documented at <https://kubernetes.io/security> but didn't get a response for weeks.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes to rely on libraries that aren't maintained by entities subject to U.S.A. and E.U. sanctions

body:
### What happened?

The kubectl auth can-i command behaves differently when using the --user and --as options.
The --as option only checks the explicit permissions granted to the user via roles and bindings. It does not check the permissions which a user acquires through its associated group.
The --user option works correctly (provided the user is in the kubeconfig file)

### What did you expect to happen?

The --as option should also check the permissions that a user acquires through its associated group.

Either a minikube or kubeadm cluster with kubectl installed. openssl is needed to generate CSRs.

```
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: example-cluster-admin
roleRef:

  kind: ClusterRole
  name: cluster-admin
subjects:
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Group
  name: example:masters
EOF
```

2. Create a new user and associate it with the `example:masters` group
```
openssl genrsa -out poweruser.key 2048

title: [Umbrella] Skip Score plugins when coupled PreScore plugin returns Skip status
body:
### What would you like to be added?

It's much similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114399.
In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114827, we support Skip in PreScore/Score as well. (Thanks @kidddddddddddddddddddddd)
So, the plugin can return Skip in PreScore when it doesn't do anything in Score in that scheduling cycle.

For example, if the pod doesn't have any preferred inter-pod affinity, the inter-pod affinity plugin PreScore can return Skip, and the scheduler won't run the inter-pod affinity plugin Score.

Let's change our in-tree Score plugins to return Skip.

Here, I just listed all score plugins, **not all of them may not need to return Skip in PreScore though**. Assignee, please make sure your PreScore/Score plugin really needs to return Skip or not.

title: Expose metrics for the `/godebug/non-default-behavior/*` go runtime metrics
body:
Recently, as part of go1.21's [extended backwards compatibility changes](https://go.dev/blog/compat), the [runtime/metrics](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/metrics) packages [exposes metrics](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/metrics#hdr-Supported_metrics) on the usage of codepaths that depend on non-default values of GODEBUG settings (see metrics of the form /godebug/non-default-behavior/*).

These metrics, IMO, are an excellent addition complementing the new minimum 2 year period of GODEBUG settings, and can help give users confidence in moving away from non-default GODEBUG settings eventually based on these metrics.

In the past, we've added custom metrics in Kubernetes for tracking usage of these non-default GODEBUG settings: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109024. Once these go runtime metrics are exposed, we can deprecate the metrics added in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109024.

This will be done in 2 stages:
- [ ] Add the `/godebug/non-default-behavior/*` metrics to the go collector in `client_golang`: https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/issues/1337
- [ ] Use these newly added metrics in the go collector in the metrics [registry](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/973ea2d376267d2fe1017f2f1dca94390dab702d/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/legacyregistry/registry.go#L54C1-L55)

title: [discussion] potential bug in the scheduling path when one PreFilter plugin returns `Unschedulable`
body:
Move @sanposhiho 's https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119769#pullrequestreview-1563700339 here as a new discussion thread:

Kensei pointed out a potential bug in the scheduling path when we hit Unschedulable result in one of PreFilter plugins:

> - pluginA returns Unschedulable in its PreFilter.
> - (Because pluginA returns unschedulable, RunPreFilterPlugins() is aborted at that point and pluginB PreFIlter isn't executed)
> - a Pod is claimed as unschedulable (failed by pluginA)
> - calling a pluginB's AddPod/RemovePod during preemption, sometimes will abort the whole preemption as the logic tries to read info from cycleState.

/sig scheduling

title: Higher CPU usage when pods are placed in a single namespace
body:
### What happened?

When @afcollins was testing with [benchmarking](https://github.com/cloud-bulldozer/kube-burner/blob/master/cmd/kube-burner/ocp-config/node-density-heavy/node-density-heavy.yml) runs, it was observed that we if place the pods in a single namespace the reported CPU usage is much higher than if we just distribute those pods across multiple namespaces. 

e.g. When all 6006 pods are created in the same namespace, the kubepods.slice exceeds 12 cores.
However, when dividing the same 6006 pods across 4 namespaces (capping each namespace to 2000 pods), the node's CPU maxes out at 5 cores.


![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/12152047/b4bffcb2-7ea5-4b89-bc20-30a66fe26dd3)

Corresponding prometheus query - `prom query:
sum by (id) (( rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{ job=~".*", id =~"/system.slice|/system.slice/kubelet.service|/system.slice/ovs-vswitchd.service|/system.slice/crio.service|/system.slice/systemd-journald.service|/system.slice/ovsdb-server.service|/system.slice/systemd-udevd.service|/kubepods.slice"}[$interval])) * 100 * on (node) group_left kube_node_role{ role = "worker" } )
`

This becomes an issue on smaller cloud nodes with 8vCPU, where the excessive CPU use causes the nodes to thrash, skip metrics collection, and presents as a poorly-performing workload. Changing the config to break iterations into namespaces allows the workload to run on the smaller cloud nodes.

The goal here is to understand why the CPU usage compounds when pods are focused in a single namespace and if that points to any performance improvements we can make.

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/12152047/1856bfa0-8a5c-41c0-95ae-61e3e584f4ae)

Prometheus query - `sum( rate( (node_cpu_seconds_total{ mode != "idle" } * on (instance) group_left label_replace( kube_node_role{ role = "worker"} , "instance" , "$1" , "node" ,"(.*)") )[$interval:] ) ) by (instance) * 100
`

title: Default settings for EvictionHard do not include imagesfs.inodesFree.
body:
It is possible to deploy Kubernetes with a separate filesystem.  We default the settings for EvictionHard [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blame/master/pkg/kubelet/eviction/defaults_linux.go).

A concern is that if users are using the default settings and separate filesystem for images, we are effectively turning off monitoring for INodes on the imagefs.  This means that we won't have disk pressure if inodes run out on the ImageFs.  

The fix can be to add 

```
var DefaultEvictionHard = map[string]string{
	"memory.available":  "100Mi",
	"nodefs.available":  "10%",
	"nodefs.inodesFree": "5%",
	"imagefs.available": "15%",
        "imagefs.inodesFree": "5%",
}
```
To default settings.

This doesn't seem to be a regression as these defaults were added 5 years ago (k8s 1.12) but this could be a potential bug if either users mount a separate filesystem to their container runtime storage or they configure their runtime to store their images on a separate filesystem.

title: RoleBindings deleted by namespace finalizer before other objects using those permissions finish stopping/finalizing
body:
### What happened?

When you delete a Namespace, Kubernetes automatically deletes all the objects in that namespace. 

However, if you have a workload in that namespace (e.g. a custom resource) AND the workload has a finalizer AND the controller that manages that finalizer is granted permission by a RoleBinding in the same namespace, then when the Namespace is deleted, the workload object and the RoleBinding are deleted at roughly the same time. So the finalizer controller may (often) deadlock, unable to use the permissions that have been revoked and unable to remove the finalizer on the workload object. This then also blocks the namespace finalizer and namespace deletion.

The only way to recover fromt his situation is the manually remove the finalizer on the workload object. But removing finalizers manually is often unsafe and can cause memory leaks or worse. Worse, namespace tenants won't be able to delete the finalizer either, because their RoleBindings will have been deleted too; a cluster admin would have to do it.

### What did you expect to happen?

This behavior is expected, given the current implimentation, but it could be improved and the problem solved by delaying the deletion of RoleBindings (and probably also Secrets, ServiceAccounts, and Roles) until after all other objects in the namespace are fully deleted (not found).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This problem was observed while testing a new feature in Config Sync called deletion propagation, which deletes managed objects that have previously been applied, when the RootSync or RepoSync is deleted. To reproduce that exactly would require deploying Config Sync from HEAD of main.

But conceptually, you would follow these steps:
1. Create a Namespace "X"
2. Create a RepoSync in namespace X
3. Create a Secret, Role, and RoleBinding as required for the RepoSync's "reconciler" (a Deployment spun up in another namespace by Config Sync to manage the object

title: Projected Service Account Tokens: Ability to specify multiple Audiences
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The Property `Audience` of  `ServiceAccountTokenProjection` is currently a `string`. (see [here]( https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/projected-volumes/#serviceaccounttoken) and [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-auth/1205-bound-service-account-tokens/README.md#api-change))

Would be helpful if this could be an array of type string (`Audiences []string`)
  






### Why is this needed?

1. If the token is passed to a service for authentication and that service uses exactly that token to authenticate on the k8s token review api endpoint, then at least two audiences are necessary. First for the service itself and second the k8s api server audience. (Example Hashicorp Vault K8s Auth Plugin: see [here](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault-plugin-auth-kubernetes/blob/6f9c733333c1d5f86166db8db0016eda7bfb21bf/path_login.go#L456) and [here](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault-plugin-auth-kubernetes/blob/6f9c733333c1d5f86166db8db0016eda7bfb21bf/token_review.go#L71))

2. To be consistent with the manual `TokenRequest` api, which also allows to create tokens with multiple audiences (see [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-auth/1205-bound-service-account-tokens/README.md#api-changes))

title: `NetworkPolicy`: connection-oriented semantics are undocumented
body:
### What would you like to be added?

It is undocumented (on e.g., https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/ or https://network-policy-api.sigs.k8s.io/reference/spec/#policy.networking.k8s.io%2fv1alpha1) that `NetworkPolicy` rules result in a `conntrack` rule, i.e., that `NetworkPolicy`s are connection-oriented rather than packet oriented, for TCP.

For example, the egress key in the last `NetworkPolicy` is redundant:

```yaml
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: defaultdeny
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
    - Ingress
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: http
spec:
  egress: # This entire key is redundant.
    - ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: '1024-65535'
  ingress:
    - ports:
        - port: '80'
          protocol: TCP
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/component: webservice
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
```

The docs are misleading, for example:

https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/ 

> A pod is isolated for egress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and has "Egress" in its policyTypes; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for egress. When a pod is isolated for egress, **the only allowed connections from the pod are those allowed by the egress list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to the pod for egress**. The effects of those egress lists combine additively.

In truth this refers to **the only new, unestablished connections ...**.

Indeed, given https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109672 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/120214 it seems this design choice for TCP is not protocol-independent and an undeliberate architectural design.

title: Topology Aware Routing: Unable to allocate minimum required endpoints to each zone without exceeding overload threshold
body:
### What happened?

Given that we have 3 availability zones and even spread of nodes/CPU across all of those topology domains, we end up with a cpu ratio of `[0.333, 0.333, 0.333]`

Given that the workload has `HorizontalPodAutoscaler`, it can scale up and down with random assignment to zones but never with a skew of more than 1.

The workload had a spread of `[4, 4, 3]` across topology domains (a total of 11 `Pods` / `EndPoints`). This leads to an error of `Unable to allocate minimum required endpoints to each zone without exceeding overload threshold (11 endpoints, 3 zones)`

Given the [code logic here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/755b4e2bc493518f916e1b1ba11652a44b9fdc58/staging/src/k8s.io/endpointslice/topologycache/topologycache.go#L315C46-L331):
- `cpuRatiosByZone` of `[0.333, 0.333, 0.333]`
- `numEndpoints` of 11
- => `remainingMinEndpoints` ends up being `-1`
- => removes hints

![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/9448877/f10b8d01-44c6-4b14-b145-f706df94dc3b)



### What did you expect to happen?

Spread of `[4, 4, 3]` is capable of handling same zone traffic so I would expect the hints to not be removed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Set up nodes across 3 zones
- Setup a Deployment or StatefulSet with 9 replicas evenly spread across zones (can use `topologySpreadConstraints` of `DoNotSchedule` with `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` key and `maxSkew` of 1)
- Observe a spread of `[3, 3, 3]` across zones
- Observe that hints are created
- Scale to 11 replicas to force a spread of `[4, 4, 3]`
- Observe that hints are removed

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Exceeding the ephemeral storage limit not causing eviction in critical pods
body:
### What happened?

As per my understanding, when containers exceed their memory or cpu limits, they are restarted. But when they exceed ephemeral storage limit, the pod itself has to be destroyed and recreated (by eviction). Also, critical pods would not be evicted.
We have some pods marked as critical which at times consume ephemeral storage exceeding their limit (potentially filling up the disk). We have marked them as "critical" as we dont want them to become victim in case of any node pressure. At the same time, we would not want the pod to be evicted when they cross the configured limit. Is there any way we could achieve this?

### What did you expect to happen?

Pods (even critical ones) have to be evicted when they consume more storage than the configured ephemeral storage limit.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We can reproduce the issue by the following,

1. Define ephemeral limit for any container in a pod.
2. Mark the pod as critical by using setting priority class (priorityClassName: system-cluster-critical)
3. Consume disk space from the container using dd if=/dev/urandom of=test 
or alternately configure very small ephemeral limit.

title: Resource Quotas: Possibility to not enforce limits.cpu per pod
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently, for cpu (and memory) resources, ResourceQuotas enforce that every (new) pod in that namespace sets a limit for that resource.

There should be a new option for the limits.cpu ResourceQuota at namespace level:
`enforceLimitPerPod: true (default) / false`

If false, it's optional to define limits.cpu for each pod in this namespace. `limits.cpu` of the namespace minus `limits.cpu` of each pod (where defined) should be used to limit CPU usage across all other pods in this namespace.

### Why is this needed?

According to https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/,
you can limit the total sum of compute resources that can be requested in a given namespace. limits.cpu for the namespace ist computed as follows: Across all pods in a non-terminal state, the sum of CPU limits cannot exceed this value.

This is a problem with workloads which have a low base CPU usage with short cpu spikes randomly distributed across pods and time. A lot of assigned CPU is wasted in such case.
For such workload scenarios, it would make more sense to limit only the sum of CPU usage of all pods in the namespace instead of limiting each pod separately.

Example: 
limits.cpu namespace: 8
16 containers with limits.cpu 500m

Each of these containers are limited to 500m CPU which could affect application performance negatively.  If specification of limits.cpu is not enforced in this namespace, each pod could use up to 7.985 CPU If each other pod in the observed timeslot currently has a CPU usage of 1m.

title: Device plugin allocatable resource overwritten when kubelet restart
body:
### What happened? Device plugin allocatable resource is set to capacity temporarily instead of actual value from device plugin when kubelet restart. This is because when kubelet restarts, device plugin manager `func (m *ManagerImpl) GetCapacity` [link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L280) used by node status update may get run *before* `func (m *ManagerImpl) Start`[link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L375). `func GetCapacity` will return empty result when ManagerImpl is not started, causing device plugin allocatable resource set to capacity of last node status just like other resource [link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/nodestatus/setters.go#L354). There is no guarantee that `updateRuntimeUp` which calls `Start` runs before `syncNodeStatus` which calls `GetCapacity`. These functions are executed in goroutines asynchronously in `func (kl *Kubelet) Run`. In our case, `updateRuntimeUp` is always the slower one leading to false allocatable resource every time. After device plugin ManagerImpl is started, allocatable resource is set correctly. ### What did you expect to happen? Device plugin allocatable resource should always be set correctly when kubelet restart. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. watch node source kubectl get node -ocustom-columns=Name:.metadata.name,capc:.status.capacity."com/resource",alloc:.status.allocatable."com/alloc" -w 2. restart kubelet meawhile 3. watch output, alloc set to cap ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version v1.20.6, related code remains unchanged up to master ### Cloud provider
### OS version
```

title: Take dataSource topology into account when scheduling a pod using unbound WFFC storage
body:
### What happened?

I have some dynamically provisioned storage that uses WFFC like the included csi-hostpath. I have a multi node cluster. When I attempt to do a csi clone using that storage, the scheduler does not take the topology of the dataSource into account when scheduling the pod. Example:
- I have 3 nodes.
- I have 1 bound volume (source) on node01.
- I create a new PVC with a dataSource of source.
- The scheduler schedules the pod on node02, and the clone can not succeed because the source is on a different node.
- Same thing happens if my dataSource is a snapshot of a volume on a different node than where the pod is scheduled.

### What did you expect to happen?

I am expecting the VolumeZone plugin to take the topology of the dataSource of a PVC Into account when filtering nodes. A snapshot restore or csi clone cannot succeed if the source volume doesn't exist in the same topology as the node. I am fairly certain the offending piece of code is [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumezone/volume_zone.go#L135-L138) where it just skips checking unbound WFFC PVCs.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create a multi node cluster
- Use the csi hostpath provisioner in distributed fashion
- Create a PVC, and run a pod to bind the PVC to a PV on a node
- Create another PVC with a dataSource that is the PVC from the previous step
- Create a pod that uses the new PVC, it may or not get scheduled on the same node. If it is scheduled on a different node, the pod will remain pending because the csi clone will fail.

Similar to the above setup, but add an intermediate step of making a snapshot of the first PVC, and set the dataSource to that snapshot will yield the same result. You will need a version of the csi-snapshot sidecar/controller that includes https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/external-snapshotter/pull/585 so the snapshots are properly created o

title: Kubelet should prevent failed volume mounts from resulting in containers writing to host filesystem
body:
### What happened?

A PVC failed and the FS became unmounted. A container restarted and the replacement container ended up mounting the mountpoint directory from the host filesystem and continuing to operate without realizing it.

### What did you expect to happen?

In a perfect world, the replacement container would entirely fail to restart, and the pod might even be killed, but that's not something trivial for kubernetes to solve. However, it is at least very possible for kubernetes to prevent this leading to data loss by setting `chattr +i` on the underlying mountpoint to make it immutable and `chmod 0` to make it so that listing the directory fails for non-root users in the container.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

You can potentially reproduce this by force-detaching a PVC from an XFS EBS volume, waiting for it to become unmounted, and then restarting a container in the pod, but I don't think anyone should waste time reproducing this end-to-end since there's a clear fix for any scenario. You can instead manually unmount the source path that containers bind mount for PVCs and then restart a container in a pod using that PVC, applications on that container will then write to the host filesystem instead of the PVC.

### Anything else we need to know?

I'm guessing this might be challenging to fully implement in kubelet itself because volume plugins don't necessarily need to mount anything at all, they can do something simple like extracting a `.tar.gz` file at the path that kubelet tells them to mount something at.

However, for something like a PVC, subpath mounts, etc kubelet layers a bunch of bind mounts on top of each other and the underlying mountpoints for all of those could be made immutable in case one of the intermediate mounts breaks, and device plugins could set mountpoints as immutable on their end if they want to.

If it is too hairy to do this in kubelet, then kubelet could at least enable volume plugins t

title: configure pluginMetricsSamplePercent or CycleState.recordPluginMetrics from outside of scheduler
body:
### What would you like to be added?

We have `pluginMetricsSamplePercent` which indicates the percentage of plugin metrics to be sampled. But it's `const` and we cannot change the value from outside.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e30f66c300c76ce21c0ca0e8bc4bf4a45e028f/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L65

It would be nice if there was a way for this to be set up externally.
There are several possible ways to achieve this:
- add `pluginMetricsSamplePercent` to KubeSchedulerConfiguration.
  -  we need to implement new [`Option`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e30f66c300c76ce21c0ca0e8bc4bf4a45e028f/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L143) to set `pluginMetricsSamplePercent` as well.
- create new [`Option`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95e30f66c300c76ce21c0ca0e8bc4bf4a45e028f/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L143) to pass a function to set `CycleState.recordPluginMetrics` in each scheduling cycle.
  - default should be `rand.Intn(100) < pluginMetricsSamplePercent` not to break the current behavior.
- Add function to set `CycleState.recordPluginMetrics` in each scheduling cycle to `Scheduler` field like `NextPod` or `Error`.
- just change `pluginMetricsSamplePercent` to `var` and expose it to be able to be changed value from other package.
- (... do you have other good way?)

/kind feature
/sig scheduling

### Why is this needed?

In sigs/kube-scheduler-simulator, we want to set `pluginMetricsSamplePercent` 100 to see the metrics of all scheduling.
https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kube-scheduler-simulator/issues/60

Also, users may want to increase this value for some detailed/accurate performance measurement or may want to set to 0 when not using metrics at all.

title: Scheduler will run into race conditions on large scale clusters
body:
### What happened?

The scheduler has a [30s timeout](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L231) for the bind operation to succeed; if we don't get a response within 30s, the in-memory assignment of pod to node in the [scheduler cache expires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0fefe4e605ba05793e919598c09390769c127b3c/pkg/scheduler/internal/cache/cache.go#L720).

A race condition will happen in the follow case:

1. pod1 is assigned to a node, scheduler cache is updated with the assignment, bind operation issued to apiserver.

1. if the apiserver is under huge pressure, bind takes more than 30s, scheduler expires the cached pod-to-node assignment.

1. bind eventually succeeds, but because the apiserver is under huge pressure, the pod update with the node name takes a long time to propagate to the scheduler.

1. because the pod update took a long time to propagate and the cache entry expired, the scheduler is not aware that the assignment actually happened, and so it had no problem assigning a second pod to the same node that would otherwise not fit if the scheduler was aware that the first pod was eventually assigned to the node.

On the scheduler side, what we need to do is make the 30s longer for large clusters, and ideally adaptable to cluster state.

/sig scheduling

### What did you expect to happen?

No race conditions.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a large scale cluster.

title: Pod startup errors bork StatefulSet rolling update
body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

/kind bug

I'd like to think this is a bug, but I fear it may actually be a feature request.

**What happened**:

Pod startup failed during creation of or rolling update to a StatefulSet (for any of a number of reasons, e.g., a typo in an image name, or just a crash bug in the code being run).  Rollout remains stalled even if the update is rolled back or if the StatefulSet is updated again with a corrected image.  The only way to recover is via manual intervention (e.g., delete the pod that was failing, causing it to be recreated in the corrected state, and allowing subsequent pods to start).

**What you expected to happen**:

I expected updating the StatefulSet configuration with a corrected or reverted image spec to correct the problem.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

(1) Define and create a StatefulSet with 2 replicas of a single container pod with some **non-working** image.
(2) Observe that StatefulSet comes up with pod 0 in a restart loop (e.g., Waiting: CrashLoopBackOff) and pod 1 does not start.
(3) Patch the StatefulSet to update the image to a **working** image.
(4) Observe that the condition of the pods does not change, even though the StatefulSet is now configured with the new, corrected image.
(5) Manually delete pod 0.
(6) Observe that pods 0 and 1 now both come up successfully running the new image.

Alternatively:

(1) Define and create a StatefulSet with 2 replicas of a single container pod with some **working** image.
(2) Observe that StatefulSet comes up with pods 0 and 1 both running successfully.
(3) Patch the StatefulSet to update the image to a **non-working** image.
(4) Observe that pod 1 is updated to the new image and goes into a restart loop (e.g., Waiting: CrashLoopBackOff) while pod 0 remains running the old image.
(5a) Patch the StatefulSet again to update the image to a third, **working** image.
(5b) Revert the image change

title: Memory QoS should not be affected by CPU requests/limits
body:
### What happened?

I had a discussion with @kad during KubeCon about some unexpected behavior we observed testing Pod Quality of Service and its relation to OOMKills.  The kubernetes documentation [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/node-pressure-eviction/#node-out-of-memory-behavior) talks about the kubelet's setting of `oom_score_adj` based on QoS for the pod.

For Pod's with memory request == limit and CPU request == limit, we see the `oom_score_adj` == -997 as expected.
For Pod's with memory request == limit and CPU request < limit, we see the `oom_score_adj` == 998 as it is then calculated as a bustable QoS.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would not expect CPU settings to have any bearing on the memory QoS and subsequently the `oom_score_adj`. There is a lot of debate ongoing about whether to limit CPU. However, this debate should have no bearing on the way we treat a pod in relation to Node Memory Pressure. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a pod with memory request == limit and CPU request == limit and exec into to the pod. `cat /proc/<process_num>/oom_score_adj` and validate the score is -997.

Create a pod with memory request == limit and CPU request < limit and exec into to the pod. `cat /proc/<process_num>/oom_score_adj` and validate the score is not -997 as expected.

title: Dangling volume mechanism for CSI does not exist
body:
The dangling volume mechanism we currently use for recovering volumes that are incorrectly attached will not work for CSI.

This mechanism is in use by Cinder and EBS drivers at present - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L338 and solves real issues where a volume may be erroneously attached to the node. 

In past building exact state of the world after controller-manager recovers from a crash was kinda not very precise which results in bugs like this. I am wondering if for CSI we should be able to use `VolumeAttachment` objects to rebuild the state and workaround/fix problems like this.

title: Calculate oom_score_adj in a CPU-agnostic way, taking in consideration Pod Priority too
body:
**What would you like to be added**:

I would like to start a conversation to understand if we may improve `GetContainerOOMScoreAdjust` to:

1. Calculate the `oom_score_adj` in a CPU-agnosticy way
2. Take in account Pod Priority too


**Why is this needed**:

Currently, the `kubelet` sets a `oom_score_adj` value for each container based on the Pod QoS:

- `Guaranteed`: `-998`
- `BestEffort`: `1000`
- `Burstable`: `min(max(2, 1000 - (1000 * memoryRequestBytes) / machineMemoryCapacityBytes), 999)`

The QoS class depends both on the CPU and memory requests/limits, which means the `oom_score_adj` also depends on the CPU resources and not just on the memory resources, while OOM score is a purely memory management thing. Moreover, `oom_score_adj` is also Pod priority agnostic (except that critical pods always get `-998`, regardless their QoS class) which can cause higher priority pods to get evicted before lower priority pods under node memory pressure.

title: An Indexed Job mode that allows every index to execute
body:
### What would you like to be added?

A mode of operation for Jobs with `.spec.completionMode="Indexed` that allows every index to execute. 

Currently this is not possible because when a job reaches its `.spec.backoffLimit`, active pods will be deleted; moreover, the job is declared failed and so no new pods are created for the indices that didn't execute yet (happens more often when parallelism < completions).

I can think of two open issues:
1. How to decide when to stop retrying a failed index. One approach is to consider backofflimit at the index level, this will be challenging to track per index in the job status, but one solution is to have the backofflimit with min semantics: each index is guaranteed to at least `backofflimit` retries, we track that in the job-controller memory for each index, and in status we only track which indexes reached the limit as a bitmap.
2. Job failure status: in the simplest case we could just declare the job failed if at least one index failed, but we could also introduce an API to allow users to tune that (perhaps based on a percentage or a min number of indexes).

Related comment to this issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109131#issuecomment-1088328034


### Why is this needed?

There are cases where the indexes represent independent operations, and so it is desired to continue and execute all of them before declaring the job complete.

title: apiserver: Make the default scheduler name configurable
body:
### What would you like to be added?

From https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/scheduling/config/#multiple-profiles:
> If a Pod doesn't specify a scheduler name, kube-apiserver will set it to `default-scheduler`. Therefore, a profile with this scheduler name should exist to get those pods scheduled.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f4abde9e57cc30efcc8f79c9ebd791d15f4164c4/pkg/apis/core/v1/defaults.go#L205-L207

Currently when you configure multiple scheduling profiles and you cannot change cluster-wide the default scheduler name.

You have to implement a custom mutating webhook that sets the Pod `.spec.schedulerName` to the wanted scheduler.

I would expect the default scheduler name that is used by the kube-apiserver (currently hard-coded to `default-scheduler`) to be configurable in the apiserver via command line flag (for example `--default-scheduler-name`).

### Why is this needed?

To allow the default scheduler to be changed easily without the need to write, deploy and maintain a custom mutating webhook.

title: Introduce ClusterSecret for (among others) wildcard certificates
body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

/kind feature


**Details**

In cert managers developers are [struggling to deploy](https://github.com/jetstack/cert-manager/issues/494) wildcard certificates that can be shared among applications in different namespaces. A natural solution to this would be introduction of `ClusterSecret` in similar spirit to `ClusterIssuer` or `ClusterRole`.

This is an alternative to cross-namespace secret referencing rejected in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/57325

Another use case is defining `kubernetes.io/dockercfg` so deployments in different namespaces can access shared private docker repository with secret managed in one place

Feature of ClusterSecret could include:

- ability ot expose secrets to all namespaces
- ability to expose secrets to some namespaces with `matchLabels` or `matchExpressions`
- seamless integration with Secret resource where it can be used 

**Example definition of clustersecret that is visible to namespaces with `domain: example.com` label**

```
apiVersion: v2
kind: ClusterSecret
type: kubernetes.io/tls
metadata:
  name: default-wildcard-certifiate
matchLabels:
  domain: example.com 
data:
  tls.crt: ...
  tls.key: ...
```

Example usage:

```
...
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts:
      - myhost.example.com
      secretName: default-wildcard-certifiate
...
```

**Example definition of docker credentials shared to all namespaces:**

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ClusterSecret
type: kubernetes.io/dockercfg
metadata:
  name: private-docker-registry
data:
  .dockercfg: ...
```

Example usage:

```
...
imagePullSecrets:
  - name: private-docker-registry
...
```

/sig auth

title: Bind mounting Kubelet root-dir causes staging volumes to never be cleaned up for ReadWriteMany PVCs
body:
### What happened?

For various reasons I have an installation of Kubelet on all nodes in a cluster bind mounted to another location on disk. When a volume is staged on a node this causes the staging volume to appear twice when running the `mount` command. Here's an example of such an instance with a pod on the node,

```
~$ mount | grep pvc-my-volume
<scrub>:/volumes/csi/csi-vol-uuid on /some/path/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/pv/pvc-my-volume/globalmount type <scrub>
<scrub>:/volumes/csi/csi-vol-uuid on /var/lib/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/pv/pvc-my-volume/globalmount type <scrub>
<scrub>:/volumes/csi/csi-vol-uuid on /some/path/kubelet/pods/pod-id/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pvc-my-volume/mount type <scrub>
<scrub>:/volumes/csi/csi-vol-uuid/pod-id on /var/lib/kubelet/pods/pod-id/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pvc-my-volume/mount type <scrub>
```

How ever when the pod is deleted you would expect all of these mounts to be removed since no pods are on the node anymore requiring the volume, and `NodeUnstageVolume` should be called on the CSI.

If you take a look in the logs you'll see an error (only the error is here to scrub info from the log)
`kubelet[6307]: 6307 nestedpendingoperations.go:301] Operation for "{volumeName:kubernetes.io/csi/<scrub> podName: nodeName:}" failed. Error: "GetDeviceMountRefs check failed for volume \"pvc-my-volume\" (UniqueName: \"kubernetes.io/csi/<scrub>\") on node \"my-node\" : the device mount path \"/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/pv/pvc-my-volume/globalmount\" is still mounted by other references [/some/path/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/csi/pv/pvc-my-volume/globalmount]"`

This is caused by this check
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2c6c4566eff972d6c1320b5f8ad795f88c822d09/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L947-L955

Which fails on a false flag that the mount is itself the reference. This seems to only happen on `ReadWriteMany` volumes, and we particularly noticed

### What happened?

This is the same issue as #79773

The `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` condition `ScalingLimited`  can have an incoherent status even if the `currentReplicas`/`desiredReplicas` is within the range of requested `minReplicas`/`maxReplicas`:

```

title: Add a presubmit to restrict test only libraries from linking into prod binaries
body:
We have many "test only" packages through out the project, containing fixtures, helpers, utilities, etc... These test libraries are not intended for use in production binaries. They often lack rigorous review and sufficient testing for use in production binaries. We should make sure they don't accidentally get pulled in.

Strawman proposal, test only packages must import "testing". Blank import is sufficient:

```golang
import (
  ...

  // Restrict to tests
  _ "testing"
)
```

Then write a presubmit that fails if we find `testing.init` symbol in the release binary.

```console
$ go list -json ./cmd/kubectl | jq 'any(.Deps[]; . == "testing")'
true
```

This approach is trivial and fairly effective although a more sophisticated approach could print a dep chain.

title: Publish the pod index as a label and annotation for Statefulset and indexed Job
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently the only way for a statefulset pod to identify its own index is by parsing the pod name, this is not convenient, it is easier if we set that as an annotation that users can set as an env var using the downward api. We already do this for Indexed Job.

Also, for both Indexed Job and StatefulSet it is useful to have the index set as a label as well so that it is simpler for filtering and selection.

### Why is this needed?

Setting the index as an annotation makes it easier to plumb that as an env var using the downward api.

Setting the index as a label allows for filtering and selecting the pods based on their index.

/sig apps

title: Mutable Pod scheduling directives when gated
body:
### What would you like to be added?

We introduced PodSchedulingReadiness in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/3521-pod-scheduling-readiness; 

The main use case for this feature was to enable building external resource controllers (like extended schedulers, dynamic quota managers) to make a decision on when the pod should be eligible for scheduling by kube-scheduler.

This feature proposes to make pod scheduling directives (nodeSelector, affinity) mutable as long as the pod is gated. This is similar to what we did for suspended Job: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/2926-job-mutable-scheduling-directives

### Why is this needed?

This allows external resource controllers to not only decide when the pod should be eligible for scheduler, but also where it should land.

/sig scheduling

title: Critical: Node reboot could lead to data loss due to broken volume lifecycle management
body:
### What happened?

In certain situations, rebooting a Kubernetes node could lead to:
- Best case: A volume not getting mounted, despite it being a healthy volume
- Worse case: A volume getting mounted in an (ephemeral) empty host directory
- Worst cast: The wrong volume getting mounted inside the pod

### What did you expect to happen?

The right volume must be mounted in the right pod.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create a PVC, and make sure all ongoing pod creations happen on the same node
- Create a deployment with long termination grace period, say 600 seconds, that uses that PVC, wait for it to become Ready
- Delete the deployment, which should result in the pod getting stuck in `Terminating` state
- Create another deployment that uses the same PVC
- Reboot the underlying node

After the reboot, one of the two happens:
- CSI node driver receives `NodePublishVolume` before receiving any `NodeStageVolume` requests, meaning the CSI will try to `Publish` using an invalid stage directory, which could lead to the CSI not being able to publish it (Best case) or it mounting the wrong volume (Worst case)
- CSI node driver does not receive any requests, and kubelet goes ahead and mounts the empty directory inside the pod, leading to the "Worse case" scenario described above.

These steps almost always results in one of the undesired outcomes to happen.

### Anything else we need to know?

After realizing that the issue was a regression, we bisected it, and it looks like this was first introduced in 1.23.15. We've verified that the issue disappears after downgrading node's kubelet to 1.23.14, but 1.23 and 1.24 have reached their EOL already.
Based on the history of changes on kubelet's volume manager code, the issue might've had been introduced in [this commit range](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/75b8b1ebfd55e1c5042cdc33d3f30d8080bd707e%5E...390fc21359561b9094eff93e60176e244f3af54

title: Metric process_start_time_seconds is not defined for /metrics/slis
body:
### What would you like to be added?

/metrics/slis was added for several components (apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, kubelet, cloud-controller-manager) in https://kep.k8s.io/3466

This is to propose adding metric `process_start_time_seconds` to these components  for /metrics/slis to support cumulative metric `kubernetes_healthchecks_total`

### Why is this needed?

Missing start time metric in metrics/slis will result in inaccurate cumulative metrics.

Even though the start time metric is available in /metrics, it requires the metrics collector to scrape two endpoints at once and sync them to prepare the cumulative metric data.

title: Add the skip return status support for PreEnqueue, and won't run PreFilter if PreEnqueue returned a Skip status

Add the skip return status support for PreEnqueue, and won't run PreFilter if PreEnqueue returned a Skip status

### Why is this needed?

We have skip status for PreFilter to return, and when we skip prefilter, the following filter will not run, but we don't have skip choice for PreEnqueue, we'd better add this.

When we skip for the preEnqueue, we can skip add the pod to activeQueue, it's more reasonable and saving time for plugin customer scheduler to optimize.

title: Duplicate OwnerReferences Can Deny Service To SSA Clients
body:
### What happened?

When some actor manages to add duplicate `OwnerReferences` to an object, any other client attempting to use server-side apply to mutate the object will fail client-side.

Consider some `Service`:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2020-07-10T22:57:31Z"
  name: service-name
  namespace: service-namespace
  ownerReferences:
  - apiVersion: group.whatever.com/v1
    blockOwnerDeletion: false
    controller: false
    kind: SomeKind
    name: someName
    uid: 1ea7605c-001a-11ea-9a90-027feb72be7e
  - apiVersion: group.whatever.com/v1
    blockOwnerDeletion: false
    controller: false
    kind: SomeKind
    name: someName
    uid: 1ea7605c-001a-11ea-9a90-027feb72be7e
  resourceVersion: "304470743"
  uid: 8cf44d74-d698-450f-abb6-b52f3511a85b
spec:
  clusterIP: 172.30.249.81
  clusterIPs:
  - 172.30.249.81
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  ipFamilies:
  - IPv4
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ports:
  - port: 443
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 5443
  selector:
    app: whatever
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: ClusterIP
status:
  loadBalancer: {}
```

When a client attempts to send a server-side apply PATCH, client-side validation fails:

```
E0131 12:33:54.677801       1 queueinformer_operator.go:319] sync {"update" "service-namespace/service-name"} failed: failed to create manager for existing fields: failed to convert new object (service-namespace/service-name; /v1, Kind=Service) to smd typed: errors:

  .metadata.ownerReferences: duplicate entries for key [uid="1ea7605c-001a-11ea-9a90-027feb72be7e"]
```

title: Scheduler:  Share `frameworkImpl.waitingPods` among profiles
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I hope to share the `waitingPods` among multiple profiles, instead of creating a new `waitingPods` in each profiles with the current implementation.

In other words, `waitingPods` is only instantiated once in a scheduler app.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a1ffdedf782edf1472102b0b99c1467d4ed39753/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L253-L258


@Huang-Wei @ahg-g  PTAL, Is there any negative impact of this change that I didn't consider, thanks.

### Why is this needed?

In some scenarios, I need to traverse `all pods` waiting in the permit stage within the current scheduler app, rather than the pods that using the current profile for scheduling and waiting in the permit stage.

For example, we want use [coscheduling](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/scheduler-plugins/blob/master/pkg/coscheduling/README.md) to achieve `all-or-nothing`. And we have abstracted the concept of a `Cluster`, where there are two deployments under each cluster. Each deployments use different scheduler profile, and one cluster corresponds to one podGroup, as following:
![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/18323315/256ffd20-6adc-4dc5-b249-d6ffcafed303)

Then, we want pods in one cluster (podA1, podA2, podB1) to be scheduled succeed/failed together. 

We assume that all pods can pass through the filter plugins, and `podA2` is the last to be scheduled. At this point, `podA1` and `podB1` are both waiting in the permit stage. Afterwards, we traverse the `waitingPods` to complete the permit waiting for `podA1` and `podB1`. However, from an implementation perspective, now we can only see `podA1` in `waitingPods`, `podB1` cannot be seen, because`podA2` & `podB1` use different scheduling profiles. Which will cause `podB1` timeout during the permit phase, even if all pods within the podGroup are successfully scheduled.

title: Kubelet didn't respect --resolv-conf when resolv.conf is empty or full of comments
body:
### What happened?

When I passing `--resolv-conf` to kubelet, it did not respect the option, and still copy the `/etc/resolv.conf` to the pod.

What makes it special is that the `resolv.conf` provided by myself is empty.

> https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/

After skimming the code, I found the logic here is problematic:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.28.2/pkg/kubelet/network/dns/dns.go#L225-L274

Because `resolv.conf` is empty, an empty array and no error is returned. Then, if the dnsPolicy is `default` (that is the default config for CoreDNS deployment), the `podDNSType` turns to be `podDNSHost`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.28.2/pkg/kubelet/network/dns/dns.go#L316-L317

Then, containerd will get an empty `dns_config`, so it will copy `/etc/resolv.conf` from the host to the container:

https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/v1.7.6/pkg/cri/server/sandbox_run_linux.go#L282-L287

Finally, CoreDNS reports forwarding loop error.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should refuse to use the wrong empty `resolv.conf` to create a pod, and complains with errors.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Pass `--resolv-conf` to kubelet, and make sure the specified `resolv.conf` file is empty.
2. Check the output of CoreDNS, and its `/etc/resolv.conf`.

title: ReplicaSet naming is inconsistent
body:
### What happened?

When kubernetes is creating a ReplicaSet automatically through a deployment, the suffix added to the deployment name has an inconsistent length. Although this is not necessarily a bug, this can lead to issues in trying to identify ReplicaSets that were created through deployments using, for instance, RegEx.

[This code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9754e404390a8d4e969e17e339586376b6f6ad8f/pkg/controller/controller_utils.go#L1201) is responsible for creating a suffix string to add to the deployment name to create the ReplicaSet name. The number created by `podTemplateSpecHasher.Sum32()` is any number from 0 to 4,294,967,295. This means the suffix string after the number goes through `rand.SafeEncodeString` ([link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/rand/rand.go#L121)) will have a length of 0 to 10.

### What did you expect to happen?

ReplicaSet names should always have a suffix of consistent length when created automatically via a deployment.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a number of deployments that will in turn create ReplicaSets. On average, 23% of these ReplicaSets will have suffixes of length 9 or shorter instead of the expected 10.

### Anything else we need to know?

An easy solution would be to simply change the code as follows:
```
return rand.SafeEncodeString(fmt.Sprintf("%0*d", 10, podTemplateSpecHasher.Sum32()))
```
There is no risk to a solution like this as it will only go into effect when new ReplicaSet revisions are created and will only make ReplicaSet names more consistent. Any names that would be generated out of a number like 1,234,567 will instead be generated by 0,001,234,567, i.e. there is the same number of possible suffixes as before.

### Kubernetes version

Doesn't really matter but:

$ kubectl version

title: Allow ratcheting validation on custom resources
body:
(hoisted from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/94060#issuecomment-677644185)

To support improving validation on a custom resource definition when there is existing persisted custom resource data that only passes the old less restrictive validation, allow a CR update that fails custom CRD schema validation IFF the existing object fails the custom CRD schema validation with identical errors (object-level ratcheting)

---

original description:

<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->

**What would you like to be added**:
The ability to make updates to certain fields that are used in the deletion flow (like (ownerReferences, finalizers, managedFields) ), on objects that would otherwise fail validation.

**Why is this needed**:
For the VolumeSnapshot CRDs, we wanted to introduce stricter validation on some fields, but found it very difficult to accomplish this in a way that could retain backwards compatibility. The procedure we came up with was:

1. Introduce a validating webhook for an existing v1beta1 version that does ratcheting validation - existing invalid objects continue to be invalid while new objects or updates to valid objects that would cause them to be invalid are rejected. Proactively detect and reach out to consumers to clean up their invalid objects.
2. 1+ releases later, add v1 as a serving version, but keep v1beta as the storage version, so that we have the ability to rollback the CRD schema to drop v1 if that's causing trouble in the controllers.
3. Once we are 100% sure no invalid objects exist in the cluster, update the storage version to v1.

The main challenge right now is that we cannot upgrade the storage version to v1 until we are absolutely sure no invalid objects exist in the cluster. Otherwise, updates like removing finalizers would fail validation.

xref: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1902#discussion_r468782652

title: MissSchedule event will never be produced
body:
#### What happened:

No `MissSchedule` event produced when a cron schedule is missed due to `startingDeadlineSeconds`.

#### What you expected to happen:

When a `CronJob` schedule is missed because of `startingDeadlineSeconds` I would expect the `MissSchedule` event to be produced per this [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/62011) and the [code for the controller](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/edc7f023a4bfafc36b5cf452fdd30106ebbccf80/pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controller.go#L286-L288)

#### Anything else we need to know?:

However, it appears it will _never_ be produced because the code that produces the list of missed schedules for the `startingDeadlineSeconds` check will exclude any times outside of `startingDeadlineSeconds` if it is set: [link to code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/edc7f023a4bfafc36b5cf452fdd30106ebbccf80/pkg/controller/cronjob/utils.go#L113-L119)

In the code we see that because it uses `startingDeadlineSeconds` as the bound for missed schedules considered, then we will not find any that are older than `startingDeadlineSeconds` and thus the event will not be emitted.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

You need to engineer a situation where CronJobs will be delayed by more than `startingDeadlineSeconds`. I guess setting `startingDeadlineSeconds` less than `10` will produce it. In our scenario it is sometimes being caused by a large number of cronjobs and with potential additional latency via a webhook so that the cronjob controller loop takes a longer time to iterate over all cronjobs than allowed by the `startingDeadlineSeconds` value.

#### Environment:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):

Experienced on `1.184`, but a browse of the code in github shows the bug is still present in master (links embedded above), and looks to also be present in the v2 controller because the source of the issue is in the shared `utils.go` file.

title: Rollback ResourceQuota changes in admission if persisting to etcd fails
body:
### What happened?

In our cluster, we encountered an issue below:
The ResourceQuota `status.used` showed:
```
status:
  used:
    configmaps: "10"
    services: "10"
    ...
```

But when we got the actual `svc` or `cm` count, they were just:
```
configmaps: "1"
services: "1"
```

After debugging the mismatch, we found that it is the apiserver `Create()` with `QuotaAdmission` would +1 (`UpdateQuotaStatus`) every time, even if the `Create()` returned err.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c84d0864ddebbd0d36ce295cf74a447f24d7b3ec/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/resourcequota/controller.go#L275-L278

In the `resource_quota_controller`, if the resyncPeriod > 0, will do a full recalculation across all quotas, then the mismatched `status.used` will be consistent with the actual resource num.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c84d0864ddebbd0d36ce295cf74a447f24d7b3ec/pkg/controller/resourcequota/resource_quota_controller.go#L289-L294

### What did you expect to happen?

Check apiserver `Create()` return err, if err not nil, then should do the rollback (-1) logic with the quota.
To keep the ResourceQuota `status.used` consistent with actual resource num.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

In the controller logic, call the apiserver `Create()` many times with the same resource, ignore the `IsAlreadyExists` error,
then we can check the mismatch between the ResourceQuota `status.used` and the actual resource num.

title: Allow scaling up to meet PDB constraints
body:
**What would you like to be added**:

Currently if you have a PDB spec like `minAvailable: 1`, and a HPA defining minReplicas=1 and maxReplicas=N, you may end up in a scenario where disruptions get "stuck" if the HPA has scaled to 1. At any point an increase in load could cause the HPA to scale up to 2+, allowing the PDB to be satisfied, which leads to a weird scenario where a disruption can only occur if there is high load.

Ideally, the PDB would be able to trigger the HPA to scale up to meet constraints. For example, if I have 1 replica and a disruption is triggered, scale up a new replica first, then terminate the old one. Given an HPA is in place, I have already clearly specified I am OK with my pod being scaled up, so this shouldn't have negative impact on stateful workloads.

Some more context: https://github.com/istio/istio/issues/12602

title: [kubeadm] Apparently, it's not possible to change the Node CIDR Mask Size
body:
### What happened?

BACKGROUND
I'm trying to create a small HA kubernetes cluster with 'kubeadm" following the topology "stacked control plane nodes" described here [1]. Considering I want to have 3 worker nodes, my infra looks as the following:
 - 6 nodes in total ( 3 control plane and 3 worker ).
 - All 6 nodes are within a GCP /28 subnet. In GCP, the first 2 and last 2 IPs of a subnet are unusable for the user. Meaning my cluster can run up to 12 nodes (16 - 2 - 2).
 - I'm also running an internal TCP Load Balancer with an internal IP within the same /28 subnet to distribute the traffic within the 3 control plane nodes, that leaves a total space of 11 nodes for the cluster.
 - Moving on, I decided to have a maximum number of pods per node of 64. For that, I have created a /20 secondary IPv4 range in the subnet, that I can divide into up to 16 /26 alias IP ranges for each node of my cluster.

title: CVE-2020-8562: Bypass of Kubernetes API Server proxy TOCTOU
body:
CVSS Rating: **Low** ([CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N))

A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where an authorized user may be able to access private networks on the Kubernetes control plane components. Kubernetes clusters are only affected if an untrusted user can create or modify Node objects and proxy to them, or an untrusted user can create or modify StorageClass objects and access KubeControllerManager logs. 

This issue has been rated Low (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) and assigned CVE-2020-8562.
 
As mitigations to a report from 2019 and CVE-2020-8555, Kubernetes attempts to prevent proxied connections from accessing link-local or localhost networks when making user-driven connections to Services, Pods, Nodes, or StorageClass service providers. As part of this mitigation Kubernetes does a DNS name resolution check and validates that response IPs are not in the link-local (169.254.0.0/16) or localhost (127.0.0.0/8) range. Kubernetes then performs a second DNS resolution without validation for the actual connection. If a non-standard DNS server returns different non-cached responses, a user may be able to bypass the proxy IP restriction and access private networks on the control plane.

### Affected Versions:
Kubernetes <= v1.21.0
Kubernetes <= v1.20.6
Kubernetes <= v1.19.10
Kubernetes <= v1.18.18

### Fixed Versions
There is no fix for this issue at this time.

### Mitigations
If this issue affects your clusters’ control planes, you can use dnsmasq for name resolution and configure the min-cache-ttl and neg-ttl parameters to a low non-zero value to enforce cached replies for proxied connections. 

### Detection
This issue is not known to be directly detectable, but proxied calls will appear in the Kubernetes API Audit log. Kubernetes will respond with “address not allowed” when the validation successfully prev

title: Namespace resource reservation per node
body:
### What would you like to be added?

An object named NodeReservation :
- with one CPU entry
- if one pod of a namespace wants to be scheduled on a node the latter must have NodeReservation.cpu non requested and free CPU
- if at least one pod of this namespace run on a node, any pod of another namespace cannot consume the CPU reserved
- sum of all pod CPU limits of the namespace concerned by the NodeReservation, per node, cannot be greater than the NodeReservation.cpu
- CPU throttling of these pods happens if they try to consume more CPU than the NodeReservation.cpu
- pods of this namespace are never evicted

### Why is this needed?

Many applications are migrated to kubernetes.
Often these applications avoid to be evicted because they have not been originally designed to relaunch interrupted tasks or the cost to rerun a long task can be considered too high.
Also these applications come from the VM world, where there's no CPU limit per process but a global VM CPU capacity is shared between all processes running inside.
When migrating to kubernetes, finding good pod CPU limits and dealing with CPU throttling can be difficult to address.
It is not obvious to take a global VM CPU capacity an convert it to per pod CPU limits.

Some operators/developers would like their main application pods without CPU limits but also avoid them being evicted.

Is there a way to reserve a CPU capacity per namespace per node ?

Such a feature may not be desirable from a kubernetes point of view, but I am also curious to have hints to how address this issue differently with such applications without rewriting them from scratch or chose an oversized pod request = limit to either avoid eviction and CPU throttling. 

By the way, happy new year !

title: Kubelet does not respect container-log-max-size on time, during heavy log writes from container
body:
### What happened?

We are running a Statefulset that logs pretty aggressively on disk. The rate is around 6M/second. The kubelet configs around container log management are set to:
- container-log-max-files: 5
- container-log-max-size: 50Mi

We are running with containerd as the CRI on Kubernetes version 1.20. 


For this specific workload, we notice that the logs DO NOT get rotated upon hitting the 50Mi limit. Instead, the rotation happens at a much later size, depending on the number of containers/Pods on the node. In some extreme cases, if there are several Pods that are aggressively logging to disk, on the same node, then the kubelet lets the log size grow up to several tens of GBs before noticing that the log size has grown out of control. Then, it steps in to rotate the logs (compress and replace). 

This problem is letting nodes consume Terabytes of disk space, as opposed to a few hundred MBs of data for logging. 

### What did you expect to happen?

container logs should be rotated out as specified in the container-log-max-size kubelet configuration.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

My coworker (Venkata Gunapati) has a simple repro for the issue using the following Statefulset spec.

Upon applying this spec, we observe that the Pod/container's log file grow beyond 50Mi to uptown 256Mi, before rotating the logs. It is obvious how the problem gets extreme when dozens of such Pods run on the same node.


```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: logging-test
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: logging-test
  serviceName: "logging-test"
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: logging-test
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 10
      containers:
      - name: logging-test
        command: ["sh", "-c", "i=1; while [ $i -le 100  ]; do j=1; while [ $j -le 2000 ]; do echo 2022-06-16T20:02:18,308+0000 2gEAAAABu0zlAy3NjPX1DPttWcZsBs

title: Make `fmt.Errorf` use `%w` to wrap error instead of `%v`
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Make it canonical to use `%w` for all `fmt.Errorf` to wrap error. If it's believed a good idea, we can add lint check.

### Why is this needed?

According to [fmt.Errorf doc](https://pkg.go.dev/fmt#Errorf), verb `%w` will make it return a new error wrapping the operand error, which allows using `errors.As()`. Many error [handling functions](https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/v0.29.1/pkg/api/errors/errors.go#L546) in k8s rely on `errors.As()`. However, the majority of `fmt.Errorf` in current k8s code is using verb `%v`, which may lead to false assumption in using `errors.As()`.

There might be good reasons to use `%v` to abstract the implementation details as well, but it should be rare.

title: Deprecation and removal of the `SecurityContextDeny` admission plugin
body:
**tl;dr** the `SecurityContextDeny` admission plugin is going to be removed because it's outdated and now replaced by the `PodSecurity` admission.

#### Context

While digging on PodSecurityPolicy history, I came across this 2015 PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/7343 that added the `SecurityContext` field in containers spec. It also added a new admission plugin called **scdeny**. In fact, this PR was remade after ServiceAccounts were added, it was first proposed here https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/6287 and a comment asked for adding the admission control part (with a deny all and an allow all, for testing purposes), which should be enabled by default https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/6287#issuecomment-95715700. 

In the end, when https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/7343 was merged, only scdeny was added and it was disabled by default. At this time `SecurityContext` was only composed of the pre-existing `Capabilities` and `Privileged` fields and the newly introduced `RunAsUser` and `SELinuxOptions`. scdeny blocked the use of the new `RunAsUser` and `SELinuxOptions` fields. There was an issue opened afterward on enabling scdeny by default https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16456.

This admission control plugin survived until now, [is still available]( https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/15d12e713f82672ac8951ed14cb5e83ad3288d8b/plugin/pkg/admission/securitycontext/scdeny/admission.go) and was, for example, updated in 2019. Its code is super small and its [validate function](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/15d12e713f82672ac8951ed14cb5e83ad3288d8b/plugin/pkg/admission/securitycontext/scdeny/admission.go#L54) is short enough to be easy to understand by just reading it.

With the new ephemeral containers subresource, this plugin misses its security context. I asked about that topic in a [Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C019LFTGNQ3/p1658755949311999) in si

title: [StructuredAuthorizationConfig] Implement reloading of configuration
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Implement reloading of configuration in a loop at defined time intervals.

- Replace active authorizer on successful load and validation pass.
- Log and metric on failure

From the KEP:
The API server will periodically reload the configuration at a specific time interval. If it or any of referenced files change, and the new configuration passes validation, then the new configuration will be used for the Authorizer chain. The reloader will also check if the webhook is healthy, thereby preventing any typo/misconfiguration with the Webhook resulting in bad Authorizer config. If healthcheck on the webhook failed, the last known good config will be used. In the next iteration of reload, if webhook is found to be healthy, the new config will be used. Logging and metrics would be used to signal success/failure of a config reload so that cluster admins can have observability over this process. Reload must not add or remove Node or RBAC authorizers. They can be reordered, but cannot be added or removed.



### Why is this needed?

Implements https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-auth/3221-structured-authorization-configuration

title: Serving watch requests takes large memory space in goroutine's stack
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Optimize the memory usage of goroutine stack for serving watch requests. According to the [traceback](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117777#issuecomment-1723055664) of handling a watch request, the stack memory is 0x3768, which is very close to 16 KiB and Golang runtime will double it to 32 KiB once exceeded. In fact, it does exceed if we print the traceback deeper and take the fact that extra stack memory reserved by Golang itself into consideration. 

A naive optimization is to run as much as preparation handlers in a separate goroutine and then move the actual serving to another goroutine, so the former routine can free the stack memory earlier and make it more memory efficient.

### Why is this needed?

Given the extensive use of watch requests, 32 KiB per watch could add up to a very high amount of memory overhead for `kube-apiserver`. A typical watch request commonly lasts for 30s or longer, which means this memory will be active for quite long. I see a great improvement in memory efficiency to do this optimization.

title: support PreBind for scheduling extender
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add PreBind and Unreserve verbs to scheduling extender.  The logics of Bind operation could be moved to the Prebind method of extenders. If there are any problem during the prebind/bind stages, the Unreserve method of successful extenders will be called.


### Why is this needed?

For now, only one scheduling extender could enable bindVerb and perform binding operations. However, we have multiple extenders which all need to do something, such as updating annotations, just before binding in the bind method.

For example, ExtenderFoo is for extended resource exmaple.com/foo, and ExtenderBar for example.com/bar.

1. For pods requesting no exmaple.com/foo neither exmaple.com/bar, none of ExtenderFoo/ExtenderBar will be called.
2. For pods requesting exmaple.com/foo or exmaple.com/bar, ExtenderFoo or ExtenderBar will be called.
3. BUT if ExtenderFoo and ExtenderBar both needs some operation during Binding, it's NOT possible now， because configuring multiple Bind hooks for extenders is not possible
4. Furthermore, in our cluster, there are some pods requesting both exmaple.com/foo and exmaple.com/bar.

One possible solution is to rewrite our extenders with scheduling framework. But this needs lots of effort. And some customers use their own schedulers and their schedulers can integrate with our extenders easily, and no need to share the code with them.

title: HPA to support AND operation
body:
Currently, HPA only supports metrics with an OR relationship, meaning that if any one metric exceeds the threshold, scaling up will occur. Scaling down will only occur if all metrics are below the threshold. 

## Support request
I have a requirement where I only want to scale up if both TPS and CPU exceed the threshold. 
Since if only the CPU exceeds the threshold, it may be due to a memory leak, and scaling up will not help to solve the underlying issue. Also if only TPS exceeds the threshold, it means current replicas are able to serve the increased traffic and no need to scale up either.

So would like to ask if anyone has a similar requirement and how you have addressed it. I have tried using PromQL with ‘and’ operators, such as `avg(cpuUsage{_namespace_="perfmon", pool="r1obfsvc"}) > 27 and avg(tps{_namespace_="perfmon", pool="r1obfsvc"}) > 80`. However, the problem with this approach is that when both the CPU and TPS are below threshold, 27 and 80, the query will not return any data, making it impossible for the HPA to carry out a scale down operation.

title: Add resource `MultiplePodDisruptionBudget` to support mutiple pdb constraint of per pod in EvictionAPI
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to create a new resource`MultiplePodDisruptionBudget` to  support multiple pdb rule of one pod. the API may be defined as follows:
```apiVersion: policy/v1beta1
kind: MultiplePodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: test-multi-pdb
spec:
  ruleGroups:
    - name: "rule1"
      maxUnavailable: 1
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app.kubernetes.io/instance: test
          app.kubernetes.io/group-name: "0"
    - name: "rule2"
      maxUnavailable: 25%
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app.kubernetes.io/instance: test
status:
  ruleGroupStatus:
    - name: "rule1"
      currentHealthy: 1
      desiredHealthy: 1
      disruptionsAllowed: 1
      expectedPods: 1
      observedGeneration: 1
    - name: "rule2"
      currentHealthy: 1
      desiredHealthy: 1
      disruptionsAllowed: 1
      expectedPods: 1
      observedGeneration: 1
```



### Why is this needed?

I think multiple PDBs is meaningful. For example, the following scene.

_A service is sharded, it has 10 groups and each group has 2 replicas. For each replica under the group I only allow 1 unavailable, and for instances under the all groups, I allow 25% to be unavailable._
```
pod-0-0
pod-0-1
...
pod-9-0
pod-9-1
```

Multiple PDBs can solve the above problem, but for prior discussion see [113891](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113891) and [75957](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/75957). The main problem is multiple parallel eviction attempts target debiting the same budget due to the lack of transactions.

title: Kubernetes API server memory usage spikes when stopping a large number of watches
body:
#### What happened: I was performing some scalability testing focusing on how secret read latency was affected when watching a large number of secrets (~85K) with many watchers (anywhere from 5K up to ~30K). After I had gathered my data, I stopped my watchers and then saw the memory usage on the master nodes spike dramatically: ![screenshot_024](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/15820709/119373881-29e57b00-bc76-11eb-9a42-19591b035d60.png) EDIT: The graph above is missing some data because the memory usage spiked enough to trigger kernel OOM killing, which locked up the node for a while. title: kube-controller-manager: resource leak
body:
### What happened? In our environment we have a namespace with ~3k deployments and ~10k pods in it. Most of the deployments are updated simultaneously. We observed that during this mass-rollout time kube-controller manager in some situations starts to consume more than 100GB of memory and significant amount of CPU. Collected cpu and memory profiles (attached) point that significant amount of time is spent in https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/kubernetes/client-go@04ef61f72b7bc5ae6efef4e4dc0001746637fdb3/-/blob/tools/cache/thread_safe_store.go?L281 Our assumption is that it leads to unbounded growth of https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/kubernetes/client-go@04ef61f72b7bc5ae6efef4e4dc0001746637fdb3/-/blob/tools/cache/shared_informer.go?L872-877 which is called from https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/kubernetes/client-go@04ef61f/-/blob/tools/cache/listers.go?L60 ![cpu](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6113489/230208662-e6f626aa-42dc-4458-83f4-aeefeb6ae2f2.svg) ![mem](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6113489/230208670-e67de67e-d761-48da-b465-a039b8828250.svg) ### What did you expect to happen? No exponential memory growth is expected. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Create 3k deployments with 10k pods in a single namespace, update deployments simultaneously. ### Anything else we need to know? It looks like most of the time is spent in map lookups in https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/kubernetes/client-go@04ef61f72b7bc5ae6efef4e4dc0001746637fdb3/-/blob/tools/cache/thread_safe_store.go?L292 ### Kubernetes version
