title: kubelet: Evicted and force deleted pods get their full termination grace period when they should not
body:
### What happened?

When pods are evicted, i.e. with a hard eviction, the grace period is intended to be `0s` (i.e. do not respect the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`). 

However, currently, evicted pods receive their full termination grace period seconds.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod is evicted immediately and the termination grace period is not respected 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy the following pod which has an ephemeral storage limit of 5Mi and uses `dd` to fill the disk

```
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: evictdiskpod
  labels:
    pod: evictdiskpod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: k8s.gcr.io/e2e-test-images/nginx:1.14-2
    resources:
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: 5Mi
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - |
        _term() {
            echo "Caught SIGTERM signal!"
            while true; do sleep 5; done
        }
        trap _term SIGTERM
        sleep 10
        dd if=/dev/zero of=file bs=1M count=10
        echo 'write done'
        while true; do sleep 5; done
```

2. Observe the pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds was respected when it should've not been

title: Compatibility between `k8s.io/component-base` and latest `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/prometheus`.
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like `k8s.io/component-base` to be compatible with the latest version of `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/prometheus`.

### Why is this needed?

In version `0.48.0` of the `github.com/prometheus/common` library, the `expfmt.FmtText` constant [was made private](https://github.com/prometheus/common/commit/05d7387306aee31a5a9776899b1baf2267667e81#diff-60c3dc651d46ce2018a3e3c97b4bcddd42d132f134c1e592efa28aa4f589090aL45). This directly impacts its compatibility with `k8s.io/component-base`, which uses this constant, leading to issues with the latest Prometheus libraries, such as `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/prometheus`.

title: Enabling `publishNotReadyAddresses` causes proxy to direct traffic to NotReady pods.
body:
### What happened?

Documentation states that enabling `publishNotReadyAddresses` will cause DNS records to appear for pods, even if `NotReady`. Documentation does not state that enabling this flag will cause incoming traffic to be directed to pods that are `NotReady`.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected DNS records to be created, nothing beyond that.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create HTTP Server deployment with initContainer -> `sleep 30`
2. Create service for that deployment with `publishNotReadyAddresses` set to `true`
3. Continiously call HTTP Server
4. Scale HTTP Server to 10 Replicas
5. Observe incoming errors

### Anything else we need to know?

It can be easily fixed by changing condition for building topology from `isReady` to `isServing && !isTerminating`.

title: topologySpreadConstraints not working as expected if the topologyKey is not set in the nodes
body:
### What happened?

When setting topologySpreadContraints with ScheduleAyway whenUnsatisfiable param set the scheduling is not working as it expected if multiple constraints are set at the same time
Instead of splitting workload among all available workers , all workloads goes to the same node or they are note evenly distributed.

No other affinities nor nodeSelector are set

### What did you expect to happen?

All the replicas should be evenly distributed among all available workers

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create any deployment with the following topologySpreadConstraints:

```yaml
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: foo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: foo
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: foo
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
        whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: foo
```

Check created pods are not evenly distributed

### Anything else we need to know?

**It seems if we remove the zone constraint, the scheduler works fine again**

Important note: it only fails if the nodes doesn't have the label which is configured in the constraint present

title: Kubernetes conflicts with AppLocker on Windows PCs
body:
Dear Kubernetes Team,
We have a considerable number of users who utilize your software tools such as kube forwarder, k9s, kubectl etc. for a variety of tasks, a number that is consistently growing.
However, we are encountering recurring issues due to conflicts between your software and our security solutions, notably AppLocker, Microsoft's application control feature. 
This primarily stems from the fact that you have opted not to sign your software or situate it within program files. As a result, we are compelled to authorize the software based on its filehash, but this obviously changed at each software update.
This situation is not only causing administrative difficulties for us (Without a doubt other customer as well), but it is also proving problematic for the developers who use your software tools.
I hope you will consider this, as it will make your software way more enterprise friendly.
BR

title: bug: kubelet panic & crash if `--config-dir` is used
body:
### What happened?

I created a v1.30.0 k8s cluster with kubeadm and created a  drop-in directory for kubelet configuration under `/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.d`. The normal conf file created by kubeadm is in ` /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`

According to the [docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-config-file/#kubelet-conf-d) the kubelet should merge all configs in specified order and start. But the kubelet crashes under two setups:

**Setup 1**:

The `/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.d/20-kubelet.conf` is completely empty the kubelet crashes with:
```
>kubelet --config-dir /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.d --config /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
E0510 13:47:28.749138    9050 run.go:74] "command failed" err="failed to merge kubelet configs: failed to walk through kubelet dropin directory \"/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.d\": failed to load kubelet dropin file, path: /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.d/20-kubelet.conf, error: kubelet config file \"/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.d/20-kubelet.conf\" was empty"
```
If there is just one space or an newline in that file it crashes with:
```
>kubelet --config-dir /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.d --config /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
E0510 13:49:26.243517    9062 run.go:74] "command failed" err=<
        failed to merge kubelet configs: failed to walk through kubelet dropin directory "/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.d": failed to load kubelet dropin file, path: /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.d/20-kubelet.conf, error: Object 'Kind' is missing in '
        '
```
Even when the docs say:

> These files may contain partial configurations and might not be valid config files by themselves. Validation is only performed on the final resulting configuration structure stored internally in the kubelet. 

If there is nothing or only whitspaces in  `/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.d` the merged config should not be invalid and not every file in `/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf.d` must contain a `kind` property.

**

title: Linux 6.6 EEVDF scheduler on Kubernetes: openat2 /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/cpu.weight: no such file or directory
body:
### What happened?

Linux 6.6 comes with a new job scheduler called EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First), replacing the old CFS.

title: Consume zero-sized chunked body before hijacking the connection on SPDY upgrade
body:
### What happened?

We recently faced some [some problems](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cluster-integration/gitlab-agent/-/issues/393) when using our Kube API proxy with various Kubernetes distributions. 

Long story short, the error turned out to be that in our proxy we've sent an attach request like the following to the Kube API server (simplified):

```
POST /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/tmp/attach? HTTP 1.1
Connection: Upgrade
Upgrade: SPDY/3.1
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

```

The reason for this is that the go standard library writes requests with a body where it cannot determine the size as "chunked" and automatically adds the `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` header - so that's why the request was proxied like illustrated above.

And this is actually a problem because on the server side the handler [upgrades the connection](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f51dad586ddc1a02b4fcc4e3974092ad78b630a7/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/httpstream/spdy/upgrade.go#LL86C9-L86C9) by sending the proper `101` response and "correctly" hijacking it - however it never consumed that empty chunk (`0 CR LF CR LF`) which is still readable.
This leads to those bytes being interpreted as malformed SPDY frames.

This is clearly solvable on the client side (our proxy) - which we did.

However, it would be nice if that empty chunked data would be consumed correctly before hijacking the connection for SPDY communication.

The question here is also if the HTTP body on an upgrade request could already contain data for the upgraded protocol - the RFC is pretty vague about this, but [hints](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-upgrade:~:text=The%20capabilities%20and,to%20be%20repeated) that it's okay.

Weirdly enough this error was sporadic for us for different Kubernetes versions with different CRIs etc - so I kind of assume that some parts of the chain (maybe even only sometimes) consume that body and all works. It could also be

title: The Version Skew Policy does not mention aggregated apiservers
body:
### What happened?

Someone opened #124533 saying

> I expected 1.29 libraries to still be compatible with Kubernetes 1.28 based on the kube-apiserver version skew.

I think that is not what the version skew policy (https://kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/) is trying to say. I think that the guiding principle is that you must first upgrade the servers that store objects of a given API group and resource/kind, then upgrade the clients of those servers.

In particular, the existing version skew policy document explicitly discusses several kinds of components, but does not mention aggregated apiservers. I think that these should be explicitly mentioned.

title: Add global rate limit to endpoints/endpointslices controller
body:
<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->

**What would you like to be added**:
@lavalamp suggested in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/88579#issuecomment-592102136 adding a global rate limit.

In that PR we decided to use different approach (adding a constant delay) as our main goal there was to reduce load on kube-apiserver during regular endpoints controller work, but I think it's a good idea to have a mechanism like that to avoid generating more endpoint updates that we can handle in kube-apiserver in extreme cases.

Possible implementations:
* implement simple qps based rate limit for updating endpoint/endpointslice objects
* weighting updates by the number of entries in the updates (i.e. we have a budget of e.g. 1000 entries being updated)
* weighting updates by the size of endpoint objects (i.e. we have budget of e.g. 2MB of endpoints being updated)

Option 2 and 3 allows a lot of small endpoints being updated, but will start throttling when large endpoints are being updated.

The third options is the closest to our actual limits we have (the work we do in kube-apiserver is proportional to O(nodes) * O(endpoint update size)), while the first is the easiest to understand.

**Why is this needed**:
In large clusters (e.g. in our performance test) most of the work (meaning cpu, network traffic, memory allocations) is spent on sending endpoints to kube-proxy processes. Updating a lot of large endpoints in the same time can overload the master. Global rate limit is a way to prevent this from happening.

/cc @lavalamp 
/cc @wojtek-t

title: PVC recreation needed when Stateful set Pod stuck in pending
body:
### What happened?

- User cordons a node with a pvc bound to a local persistent volume
- User deletes a stateful set pod from that node
- The pod is in pending because the pvc is still bound to a local pv on the cordoned node (expected)
- The node dies and the pvc is deleted
- The pod is still stuck in pending because the pvc is missing (bug)

The pod now needs to be manually deleted so that the pod+pvc can be recreated

### What did you expect to happen?

After the pvc was deleted, the statefulset controller should have recreated it and bound it to a new node's local pv so that the pending pod could be scheduled. Currently the only way to get the pod out of pending is to manually delete it so that it recreates itself and its pvc

We used https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/sig-storage-local-static-provisioner for the local PVs, but the problem is not limited to this particular provisioner

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- create a stateful set with a pvc that is bound to a local PV
- use `kubectl cordon` to cordon a node with a local pv
- delete a statefulset pod from that node
- delete the pvc from that node

the pod is now stuck in pending due to a missing pvc

### Anything else we need to know?

There was a related issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/74374 but this only fixed the issue when the order of operations was delete pvc -> delete pod. but in this case, it is delete pod -> delete pvc

title: kubelet's calculation of whether a container has changed can cause cluster-wide outages
body:
Updated 2020-11-09 by @liggitt:

In 1.16+, the kubelet hashes the serialized container spec:

1. API server sends data
    * Defaults for added fields will modify this data
    * If an alpha field that is not defaulted graduates to adding a default in beta, an API server upgrade from alpha->beta will modify this data
    * https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5f1e5cafd33a8863c5dfe9f36c9cba836f0e981b/pkg/apis/core/v1/defaults_test.go#L165-L167
2. Kubelet decodes that data into its v1.Container struct
    * If the kubelet is older than the API server, this means it will drop fields added in newer API server versions
3. Kubelet encodes that v1.Container struct to JSON and hashes that data
    * https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5f1e5cafd33a8863c5dfe9f36c9cba836f0e981b/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L98-L108

This mechanism is used by the kubelet in `containerChanged` and `getStableKey`, which means an API server upgrade that starts defaulting a container field graduating from alpha will instantly modify the computed hash and trigger a container restart. This results in simultaneous restart of all containers across all pods of a replicaset and can cause outages.

The kubelet should limit the fields it considers in the container hash to the ones it expects to be able to change in ways that would affect the running container (currently just `image`, I think). The pod uid is already included in `getStableKey` so a delete/recreate of the entire pod would already compute a different key.

Changing this mechanism on a minor version boundary (to improve the interactions with the API server changes in 1) is acceptable, because pods are expected to be drained as part of that upgrade (xref https://github.com/kubernetes/website/issues/12326#issuecomment-704469840)


-----------

The race between DRA UnprepareResource call and the pod status update was fixed by this PR: https://github.com/pohly/kubernetes/pull/46

The solution needs to be cleaned up and tested:
- new method should be added to the PodDeletionSafetyProvider interface and implemented by the Kubelet.
- kl.containerManager.PodMightNeedToUnprepareResources(pod.UID)  call should be removed from the PodCouldHaveRunningContainers.
- New code and termination conditions should be covered with unit tests.

More details can be found in [in the Dynamic Resource Allocation PR discussion](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/111023#discussion_r1019624463)
and in the [correspondent Slack discussion.](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1668065189545059)

title: [KEP-2400] Address swap impact on memory-backed volumes
body:
Some volumes (notably secret volumes) are memory-backed in order to ensure they do not hit disk.

When swap is enabled, we need to ensure the content of memory-backed volumes continue to not touch disk.

* On cgroupsv2, the kubelet should set cgroupv2 controls to prevent memory-backed volumes from swapping out
* On cgroupsv1, where these controls are not available
  * document (in PRR / KEP / docs) the impact of running with swap on memory-backed volumes
  * consider not supporting swap on cgroupsv1 because of this impact?

/kind feature
/sig node storage
/assign @ehashman

title: Pods that have UnexpectedAdmissionError are not automatically removed.
body:
### Background

I'm using the Smarter Device Manager to allow Kubernetes (K8s) containers access to devices available on nodes (for example, /dev/kvm). However, when the node restarts, it takes a while for the Smarter Device Manager to initialize, as a result, pods scheduled on such nodes requiring access to /dev/kvm error out with a status of `UnexpectedAdmissionError` and with the following error:

```
...
Annotations:  <none>
Status:  Failed
Reason:  UnexpectedAdmissionError
Message:  Pod was rejected: Allocate failed due to no healthy devices present; cannot allocate unhealthy devices smarter-devices/kvm, which is unexpected
```

Although, after a while, I see new pod pertaining to the job scheduled, the older pod still remains errored out and not removed.

### Kubernetes version
Client Version: v1.26.9
Kustomize Version: v4.5.7
Server Version: v1.26.11

### What did I expect to happen?
I expect that pods with status `UnexpectedAdmissionError` are removed automatically by Kubernetes.

### Steps to reproduce
- Create a job that deploys a pod needing access to device drivers (say /dev/kvm through smarter-device-manager).
- Restart the node on which this job is deployed.
- You will see that the pod pertaining to the aforementioned job doesn't get scheduled.

title: We might benefit from a "network should continue working in cases that resemble syn_cookie or syn_flood" test...
body:
### What happened?

There are kernel bugs such as https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/linux-hwe-5.4/+bug/1981658, which we've found on ubuntu versions, which only are visible if a node is pushed to the point that it "Switches" the way it processes packets, to the syn_cookie kernel path...

Now, Looking at https://access.redhat.com/solutions/30453, it doesnt look like we really want this to be a normal scenario...... 
```
        Note, that syncookies is fallback facility.
        It MUST NOT be used to help highly loaded servers to stand
        against legal connection rate. If you see SYN flood warnings
        in your logs, but investigation shows that they occur
        because of overload with legal connections, you should tune 
        another parameters until this warning disappear.
        See: tcp_max_syn_backlog, tcp_synack_retries, tcp_abort_on_overflow.
```

**Status**
I ran our existing e2es (iperf, networkpolicies, and sig-network tests) at high concurrency, and wasnt able to force a synflood/syncookie fallback at any point, but i know of clusters where kubelets have failed due to that path in the kernel.

**Goal**
Would be nice if we had a sig-network e2e that simulated this ?  Feel free to close if one of the existing tests already does this. 

This may or may not be possible.  I THINK that the way to do this would be to fire off lots of TCP connections.... and somehow keep them open for a long time (i.e. maybe serve very large packets?) 



### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes sig-net or similar e2e's would be able to simulate overloaded service/endpoints where non-normal TCP connection handling start happening. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Not sure, thats the purpose of this test :). But... I suppose we might be able to reproduce syn-floods if theres too many TCP asks coming in at agiven time, in parallel (see above linked RH article).

While we tried to scale in/out pods, reconciler failure was reported . Reconciler job scheduled for every 5 minutes but failed to execute with the given error:

title: Faster ResourceQutoa Replenishment
body:
### What would you like to be added?

An enhancement to make the resource quota replenishment faster when resources are updated or deleted. 

### Why is this needed?

The resource quota controller does full sync of resource quotas periodically. And the resource update/delete events are put into the same queue which handles the full sync objects. In a cluster with large amount of namespaces and resource quota objects, the queue becomes too long and makes the quota replenishment slow.

title: Kubectl auth can-i doesn't know about the `approve` verb

If you use `kubectl auth can-i` to test whether a user can approve certificate signing requests, you get a response indicating that `approve` is not a valid verb

Warning: resource 'certificatesigningrequests' is not namespace scoped in group 'certificates.k8s.io'

An example of the `approve` verb being used can be seen [here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/certificate-signing-requests/#approval-rejection-kubectl)

`approve` should be recognized as a valid verb on `certificatesigningrequest` objects.

```bash
kubectl auth can-i approve certificatesigningrequests.certificates.k8s.io

title: "kubectl delete pod" doesn't kill pod's process immediately when specifying --grace-period=0
body:
### What happened?

As far as we read the help of "kubectl delete", it looks like that --grace-period=0 immediately kills Pod's processes.
```
    --force=false:
        If true, immediately remove resources from API and bypass graceful deletion. Note that immediate deletion of
        some resources may result in inconsistency or data loss and requires confirmation.

    --grace-period=-1:
        Period of time in seconds given to the resource to terminate gracefully. Ignored if negative. Set to 1 for
        immediate shutdown. Can only be set to 0 when --force is true (force deletion).
```

In fact, processes gets killed if we set --grace-period=0 in ver1.18.
But it seems that the behehavior got changed between ver1.18 and ver1.27.

- ver1.18 ... grace-period=0 killes Pod's processes immediately
- ver1.27 ... grace-period=0 sends SIGTERM to Pod's processes first, then wait for Pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds before sending SIGKILL. As a result, when I execute `kubectl delete pod grace-period=0 --force` , message "pod pod-name force deleted" is shown, but pod's process is not killed immediately. It lives during `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` .

when execute "kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0" , process will have been deleted immediately unless wating during `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`

title: Split /healthz into /livez & /readyz for kube-scheduler
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Quoted from @wojtek-t 's [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115754#discussion_r1192068894)

Splitting healthz/ into livez/ and readyz/ 



### Why is this needed?

```
I agree that splitting into livez/ and readyz/ is what we need here:

* livez/ inherits the existing behavior of healthz/ [it just becomes true once the component starts]
* readyz/ is failing when the component isn't initialized (i.e. it's only true after informers are already synced)

Now what we get is:

* non-leader with delayed caching will always be non-ready
* non-leader without delayed caching will be ready as soon as its cache initializes
* leader currently initializing can be distinguished from non-leader using the leader-election metrics

```

title: GracefulNodeShutdown does not trigger on nodes shutdown with `shutdown -h now`
body:
### What happened?

Shutting down a node with `shutdown -h now` does not trigger the graceful node drain. 

Despite being indicated in the original proposal
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/2000-graceful-node-shutdown

> In the context of this KEP, shutdown is referred to as shutdown of the underlying machine. On most linux distros shutdown can be initiated via a variety of methods for example:
>
> 1. shutdown -h now
> 2. shutdown -h +30 #schedule a delayed shutdown in 30mins

and explained in the blog:
https://kubernetes.io/blog/2021/04/21/graceful-node-shutdown-beta/

> How does it work?
> On Linux, your system can shut down in many different situations. For example:
>
> - A user or script running shutdown -h now or systemctl poweroff or systemctl reboot.

the command seems to not behave the same way as sending a PrepareForShutdown signal on the dbus.

The node does not drain itself from its pods and pods will stay Running until timeout and it becomes stuck at Terminating 

On the other hand, `shutdown -h now` acts similarly as a forced shutdown and as I understand, a forced shutdown on a node doesn't allow a grace period as it is forced; so one can argue that there is nothing wrong with the behavior. However, the need to clarify the documentation on what counts as a shutdown that can trigger GracefulNodeShutdown may be helpful.

title: Check if CRI runtime supports CDI
body:
As [Dynamic Resource Allocation](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/3063-dynamic-resource-allocation) and [Device Plugins](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/4009-add-cdi-devices-to-device-plugin-api) depend on [CDI](https://github.com/cncf-tags/container-device-interface), Kubelet should check if CRI runtime supports CDI.

Not all CRI runtimes support CDI. It's is supported and enabled by default in `CRI-O >= 1.23.2` and supported, but not enabled by default in `Containerd >= 1.7.0`

Kubelet should issue a warning if runtime doesn't support CDI.

title: asw cache has different outerVolumeSpecName if populated by Reconstruction than by the mountAttachedVolumes in volumemanager reconciler
body:
### What happened?

Some of the pods on EKS Fargate gets stuck in ContainerCreating state with following error which auto resolves eventually.

```
  Warning  FailedMount      86s    kubelet            Unable to attach or mount volumes: unmounted volumes=[persistent-storage], unattached volumes=[persistent-storage kube-api-access-xbk2s]: timed out waiting for the condition
```

This issue might not be specific to EKS on Fargate.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pods should not get stuck in ContainerCreating state with FailedMount errors when other pods in the same replicas go into Running state. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create an EKS cluster with Fargate - https://eksctl.io/usage/fargate-support/#

Create an EFS fs - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/getting-started.html

Apply PV, PVC and deployment with atleast 50 replicas - https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-efs-csi-driver/blob/master/examples/kubernetes/multiple_pods/README.md#multiple-pods-read-write-many

Out of 50 atleast 1 or 2 replicas will get stuck in ContainerCreating state due to FailedMounts.

### Anything else we need to know?

ActualStateOfWorld (ASW) cache is populated with volumes and its mounted pods by two ways.
* Through reconstruction in volume reconciler which marks the volumes as Uncertain and sets the OuterVolumeSpecName to the one read from PVC
* If volumes go though mounts in the reconciler even before the reconstruction and when mounts are successful, volumes are marked as Mounted and name is set to one read from podSpec

### Kubernetes version

<details>

title: Statefulset scales out wrong pods with partition
body:
### What happened?

I have a statefulset with `replicas=4` and `partition=2`. After updating podTemplate to change the image fields, two old version pods and two new version pods are presented. 
Then scale down the statefulset to 0, and scale it up to 2, the 2 newly created pods are of the new version, which is not the expected behavior.

Possible solution: check whether the replicas is zero before changing `currentRevision`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d0084356b3cabdafcfc140d19ad8d544b2fc9b5d/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_utils.go#L583 They should be processed correctly then.

### What did you expect to happen?

After updating the statefulset, scale it down to 0, then scale up to 2, two old version pods should be created, because the partition is 2.

- create a statefulset with replicas=4 and partition=2
- update the image field of the statefulset
- 2 old version pods and 2 new verison pods are presented

- scale up the replicas to 2

title: PersistentVolumeLabel admission plugin provides wrong Azure region
body:
### What happened?

On Kubernetes 1.29 with PersistentVolumeLabel admission plugin enabled and no in-tree cloud provider configured in the kube-apiserver, the admission plugins adds label `topology.kubernetes.io/region: ""` to in-tree Azure Disk PVs.

The label is completely wrong - the Azure cloud provider is not initialized and [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d9d45306df052aa5824fd8b2dab4e61f5ecc481c/staging/src/k8s.io/legacy-cloud-providers/azure/azure_managedDiskController.go#L368) just provides empty string. This makes any pod that uses these PVs unschedulable.

As result, all in-tree PVs dynamically provisioned using CSI migration are not usable, because they have a wrong region.

### What did you expect to happen?

When there is no cloud config provided, PersistentVolumeLabel does not add any labels to PVs. PVs created by the CSI driver + CSI migration already have correct `nodeAffinity`, the labels are useless.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

title: move BoundedFrequencyRunner to another repo or else migrate kube-proxy to workqueue
body:
Right now `async.BoundedFrequencyRunner` is the main thing blocking us from moving `pkg/proxy/` to `staging/src/k8s.io/kube-proxy/` (which is something we had previously agreed we want to do after we fix up some of the code in `pkg/proxy` to be less weird. In particular, this would be a prereq for removing `ipvs` and/or `winkernel` from k/k.)

I had made an effort to move it to `k8s.io/utils` at one point (https://github.com/kubernetes/utils/pull/165) but that ran into weird problems that would require a manual merge and I never got around to bugging the right people to do that and the PR eventually auto-closed and I never picked it up again, and then other repos like component-helpers and component-base were created and maybe it would go better there anyway?

However, while thinking about this again more recently, it occurred to me that maybe BoundedFrequencyRunner is kind of dead/deprecated? The more normal way to do that sort of thing pretty much everywhere else is to use stuff from `k8s.io/client-go/util/workqueue`. If we changed kube-proxy to do that, then we wouldn't have to worry about BFR.

So, this is a call for someone to figure out which of those we should do, and then eventually do it.

/assign @aojea @thockin 
/sig network
/priority important-longterm

title: Codify inter-FeatureGate dependencies
body:
It's becoming increasingly common to add new feature gates for extensions on features that still have a feature gate. Today we handle this in an ad-hoc way, where we sometimes check both feature gates (the one directly controlling the new extension, and the one for the original feature), but in lots of cases we just check the direct feature gate.

Rather than checking multiple feature gates wherever the extension feature is used, I propose:
1. Codify inter-FeatureGate dependencies, so if feature B depends on feature A, we make this explicit in the feature gate spec, and validate it on startup
    - Only allow a feature to be enabled if all it's dependent features are also enabled. Enforced in [`featureGate.Validate`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9da4b7ecfb60ea484f8e6c89c42e63506571bc68/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/feature_gate.go#L304).
    - Only allow a feature to graduate, if all it's dependent features are at least the same level of maturity. In other words, if feature A is beta, feature B can graduate to beta, but it cannot graduate to GA. (What does this mean for deprecation?). Enforced in unit test.
3. Wherever we need to check if feature B is enabled, we only check feature B, and rely on the validation to ensure that feature A is also enabled.

For an example, the new `InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScaling` (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132919) depends on _both_ `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` and `PodLevelResources`.

/kind feature
/sig architecture
/cc @JoelSpeed @liggitt @jpbetz @siyuanfoundation

title: Support an image pull credential flow built on bound service account tokens
body:
ImagePullSecret is a mechanism to provide kubelet with credentials to pull images for pods running as a specific service account. This provides segmentation of image access between tenants of a cluster. Now that Kubernetes has a more featureful service acccount token issuer, we can leverage bound service account tokens rather than static secrets to authenticate kubelet to docker registries.

Strawman flow:
1. Pod running as service account `foo` with image `bar.io/baz` is bound to a node
1. Kubelet on node requests a service account token for service account `foo` with audience `bar.io`
1. (Optional) Kubelet does an [OAuth token exchange](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-ietf-oauth-token-exchange-15) which is a general approach to what we [already do in CRI](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/76518f154b717c977b1bfb506aeb7cd4b176fde0/pkg/kubelet/apis/cri/runtime/v1alpha2/api.proto#L1045)
1. Kubelet passes resulting token to as a `registry_token` (which is just an access token of type Bearer) to the CRI.

@smarterclayton talked about this in the pod-identity-wg meeting a while ago.

@kubernetes/sig-auth-feature-requests @kubernetes/sig-node-feature-requests 

/kind feature
/sig auth

title: StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates validation allows controller to create PVCs, dueling with out-of-band recreation of PVCs
body:
### What happened?

I have a kubernetes operator, which "relied" on the pre 1.34 behavior of STS that accepted an invalid VolumeClaimTemplate. This way, I could create the PVCs myself, for example with different storageClasses, while still utilizing StatefulSet operation, update strategy, etc. Now, with an STS with a fixed volumeClaimTemplate, I still can pre-create the PVCs, howewer, changing a PVC's storageclass (by deleting and recreating with another) wont work anymore, as STS controller will immediately create one with correct specs in volumeClaimTemplate.

### What did you expect to happen?

It would be nice that [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132212) change had been gated with a FeatureGate.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

With, pre 1.34 this statefulset could be created:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  serviceName: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: test
        name: test
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /test
          name: data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
    metadata:
      name: data
```

With 1.34, this is not accepted anymore.



### Anything else we need to know?

Right now, before StatefulSet creation, I already can pre-create the PVCs, so at the end we may observe incosistencies, as actual PVCs might differ from what the volumeClaimTemplate holds. Following this, either we should deny pre-created PVCs at all, or relax restrictions a bit, and perhaps allow the user to create the PVCs himself. Perhaps, with a totally empty `spec` field in volumeClaimTemplate.

title: Job: Consider to limit the number of goroutine workers in parallel executions
body:
### What would you like to be added?

We would like to consider the possibility of limiting the goroutine workers in the following logics:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2caf4eddd8fc1ab7236ed608c1b548404dbc6bcf/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1076-L1079

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2caf4eddd8fc1ab7236ed608c1b548404dbc6bcf/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1127-L1130

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2caf4eddd8fc1ab7236ed608c1b548404dbc6bcf/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1426-L1429

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2caf4eddd8fc1ab7236ed608c1b548404dbc6bcf/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1727-L1736

### Why is this needed?

As we discussed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128513#discussion_r1829829553, the current JobController launches the number of Pods goroutine workers to deletion or creation operation against owned Pods.
This allows us to increase JobController operation throughput as long as the APIServer performance.

OTOH, the APIServer seats have limited resources, and it is not unlimited. 
So, when the Job has 1k and 10k parallelisms (`.spec.parallelism`) and completions (`.spec.completions`), the JobController potentially faces the API Priority and Fairness issues, then the kube-controller-manager might be locked out, finally WRITE operation request by the kube-controller-manager never succeeded.

To mitigate these issues, the cluster administrator might be able to prepare the kube-controller-manager specific seat by APF setting by themselves.

But, by default, we might want to prepare minimum safeguards like limiting the number of workers to 100 at the JobController level.

/sig apps

In 1.12, the kubelet exposes a number of sources for metrics directly from [cAdvisor](https://github.com/google/cadvisor#cadvisor).  This includes:
 * [cAdvisor prometheus metrics](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/docs/storage/prometheus.md#prometheus-metrics) at [`/metrics/cadvisor`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/server/server.go#L277)
 * [cAdvisor v1 Json API](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/info/v1/container.go#L126) at [`/stats/`, `/stats/container`, `/stats/{podName}/{containerName}`, and `/stats/{namespace}/{podName}/{uid}/{containerName}`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/server/stats/handler.go#L111)
 * [cAdvisor machine info](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/info/v1/machine.go#L159) at [`/spec`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/server/server.go#L291)

The kubelet also exposes the [summary API](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/apis/stats/v1alpha1/types.go#L24), which is not exposed directly by cAdvisor, but queries cAdvisor as one of its sources for metrics.

The [Monitoring Architecture](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/design-proposals/instrumentation/monitoring_architecture.md) documentation describes the path for "core" metrics, and for "monitoring" metrics.  The [Core Metrics](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/design-proposals/instrumentation/core-metrics-pipeline.md#core-metrics-in-kubelet) proposal describes the set of metrics that we consider core, and their uses.  The motivation for the split architecture is:
 * To minimize the performance impact of stats collection for core metrics, allowing these to be collected more frequently
 * To make the monitoring pipeline replaceable, and extensible.

### Current kubelet metrics that are not included in core metrics
 * Pod and Node-level Network M

title: Add Fallback to Static Version File in Shallow Clones.
body:
Add Fallback to Static Version File in Shallow Clones.

**Background:**
In environments where the Kubernetes source repository is cloned with the `--depth=1` option 
(e.g., in CI/CD pipelines or containerized builds), the full Git history and tags are not available. 
As a result, the git describe command used in `kube::version::get_version_vars()` fails to produce a valid semantic version. 
This leads to the version being set to a default like `Kubernetes v0.0.0-master+$Format:%H$`, which is not informative or consistent with release expectations.

**Problem Statement:**
When git describe cannot determine the version due to a shallow clone or lack of tags, the current versioning logic does not provide a meaningful fallback. This can cause downstream tooling and image tagging logic to behave incorrectly or inconsistently.

**Proposed Enhancement:**
Introduce support for a static version fallback file [build/build-image/cross/VERSION](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/build/build-image/cross/VERSION) within the kube::version::get_version_vars() function. 
If git describe fails to determine the version, and if [build/build-image/cross/VERSION](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/build/build-image/cross/VERSION) exists, the script will read and use its contents as the 
KUBE_GIT_VERSION and we get version like `Kubernetes v1.33.0+5596991555fa21 `

**Benefits**
	•	Ensures consistent and predictable versioning in restricted Git environments.
	•	Supports reproducible builds by decoupling versioning from Git state when needed.
	•	Minimal impact on existing logic; activated only when git describe fails.

title: APF significantly under-reporting seats for watches without RV
body: From a recent study, we observed API server’s CPU usage (on a 96 vCPU instance) vs "current_executing_seats" was extremely skewed: Computing the CPU usage/seat during that time, it swings quite a bit (0.4-2.0): For that period in the middle where CPU usage/seat is relatively high, majority of the seat usage comes from "workload-low" priority level: Dissecting it further, we can correlate the usage to watch calls from a particular client: These were all watches with RV unset (could've also been RV set to 0): Such calls are expensive upfront due to initial "Add" events being generated for the entire collection, as required by our [API semantics](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/#semantics-for-watch). **So why do they have such low seat usage?** The API server's seat calculation logic intends to count watch calls that don't need to send init events at the lowest cost. It does this by checking SendInitialEvents parameter isn't set to true ([xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f8471a6f5b00e93409422f1a39e4655651c105a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/request/list_work_estimator.go#L91-L95)). But that misses the RV unset/0 cases (i.e. legacy watches), under reporting their penalty too. We need to exclude those from incorrectly being assigned minimum seat

title: Codify inter-FeatureGate dependencies
body:
It's becoming increasingly common to add new feature gates for extensions on features that still have a feature gate. Today we handle this in an ad-hoc way, where we sometimes check both feature gates (the one directly controlling the new extension, and the one for the original feature), but in lots of cases we just check the direct feature gate.

Rather than checking multiple feature gates wherever the extension feature is used, I propose:
1. Codify inter-FeatureGate dependencies, so if feature B depends on feature A, we make this explicit in the feature gate spec, and validate it on startup
    - Only allow a feature to be enabled if all it's dependent features are also enabled. Enforced in [`featureGate.Validate`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9da4b7ecfb60ea484f8e6c89c42e63506571bc68/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/feature_gate.go#L304).
    - Only allow a feature to graduate, if all it's dependent features are at least the same level of maturity. In other words, if feature A is beta, feature B can graduate to beta, but it cannot graduate to GA. (What does this mean for deprecation?). Enforced in unit test.
3. Wherever we need to check if feature B is enabled, we only check feature B, and rely on the validation to ensure that feature A is also enabled.

For an example, the new `InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScaling` (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132919) depends on _both_ `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` and `PodLevelResources`.

/kind feature
/sig architecture
/cc @JoelSpeed @liggitt @jpbetz @siyuanfoundation

title: main container never starts with restartPolicy: Never and sidecar container has a startupProbe and fails the first attempt
body:
### What happened? There is a bug in `kubelet` `startupProbe` if sidecar container is configured. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L249 The worker's decision to continue (return true) or stop (return false) is based only on the pod's restart policy, not the containers (sidecar have restartPolicy:Always) This can lead to a racing condition if the sidecar container fails at the first time and prober incorrectly exits: If sidecar container restarted with no problem at second attempt, startupProbe will never run again. This leads kubelet to think the initContainer never successfully initialized. There is another bug in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober_manager.go#L194 the probe can possibly get recreated here. However if there are more than one containers has startup probes, and the first container has a running probe, it will skip other containers (because of an early`return`). As a result, reproduction requires at least 2 startup probes. With the example in the "How to reproduce", the `main-container` is stuck in Initializing state. kubectl desribe pod

title: DRA: plugin can not pass a mount for a pod with hostUsers: false
body:
### What happened?

When a pod has  `hostUsers: false` in spec, then all mounts should have `UidMappings` and `GidMappings`. In Kubelet this is done in [applyPlatformSpecificContainerConfig](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container_linux.go#L72) function. However, in DRA plugin we do not know about a user namespace generated for a pod in [UserNSManager](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/userns/userns_manager.go#L393). Also, in [CDI](https://github.com/cncf-tags/container-device-interface/blob/main/specs-go/config.go#L49) we can not specify the `UidMappings` and `GidMappings`.  So, in container we will have a permission denied error (if mount won't have a 0666 permissions).

```bash
vboxuser@vboxuser:~/dra-plugin-health-example$ kubectl  exec -ti example-pod -- /bin/bash
Defaulted container "container1" out of: container1, container2, container3
root@example-pod:/# ls -la /opt/exampmle-dir/  
ls: cannot open directory '/opt/exampmle-dir/': Permission denied
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Do not have a Permission Denied error.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The example DRA [plugin](https://github.com/everzakov/dra-plugin-health-example/tree/userns-with-mounts) with passing a mount as CDI device.

Pod manifest:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: example-pod
spec:
  hostUsers: false
  resourceClaims:
  - name: example-claim
    resourceClaimName: example-claim
  - name: another-claim
    resourceClaimName: example-claim-1
  - name: claim-templtate
    resourceClaimTemplateName: example-template
  containers:
  - name: container1
    image: docker.io/library/ubuntu:22.04
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    command: ["sleep", "2000"]
    resources:
      claims:
      - name: example-claim
  - name: container2

title: match the kubelet and CRI implementer cgroup drivers
body:
#### What would you like to be added:

 make it possible for CRI implementers and kubelet to match their cgroup drivers via auto-detection.

https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1614888729200700

the above discussion on slack indicated a couple of options:
1) make the kubelet adapt to the CRI implementer
2) make the CRI implementer adapt to the kubelet

2 seems preferred.

#### Why is this needed:

ideally the two sides should auto-match cgroup drivers, so that we can attempt to hide this detail from user space.

currently, users that install container runtimes and the kubelet need to explicitly configure both to have a matching driver or otherwise the mismatch can cause failures. a lot of users don't know what "cgroup drivers/managers" are and they end up ignoring this important (but low level) detail.

title: Separate log and container lifecycle management
body:
This is a follow-up to issue #123279, as the scope of the discussion has expanded beyond the original issue. Therefore, I am opening a new issue to focus on this topic.

In issue #123279, the goal was to disable kubelet from removing container logs when the container is deleted. However, disabling kubelet from cleaning up logs of removed containers could introduce potential risks, such as log files consuming excessive disk space, eventually leading to the host running out of storage and becoming unresponsive.

With that in mind, I would like to further discuss a topic we had previously considered: **separating the lifecycle management of containers and their logs in kubelet**, with the retention of logs for deleted containers being a subset of this broader topic.
ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/af2bf2d8f1b3437fe67e1686266a176320422465/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go#L1308-L1314

Below are some features that I think:

1. **Rotation and Compression of Logs from Deleted Pods**: Logs for containers are stored by default under /var/log/pods/, with a unique directory structure based on the pod's namespace-podName-podUUID. Perhaps we should consider compressing the entire pod log directory when the pod is deleted?

2. **Kubelet Management of Deleted Pod Logs**: Kubelet should have a clear configuration to manage the cleanup and retention policy for logs from deleted pods. We could introduce new settings, such as **podLogMaxFiles** and **podLogMaxSize**, similar to the existing containerLogMaxFiles and containerLogMaxSize.

3. **Capacity Limits for Pod Log Directories**: Should we enforce a maximum storage limit for pod log directories? If no limit is set, they could potentially fill up the entire host storage.

I'm not entirely sure if these ideas are on the right track, or if simply disabling kubelet's log cleanup for containers is sufficient. I would greatly appreciate any feedback or suggestions.

/sig node

title: uneven Pods spreading across domains
body:
## What 

Implement an uneven Pod spreading constraints between domains. Like domainA:domainB = x:y.

This requires us to introduce a new field to `topologySpreadConstraints` (name it `domains` for now). 
When `domains` field is non-empty, `maxSkew` should be nil. (vise-versa)

```yaml
- topologySpreadConstraints:
    # ...
    domains:
      - topologyLabel: "domainA"
        weight: 7
      - topologyLabel: "domainB"
        weight: 3
```

## Usecases

### Usecase1: spread Pods between zones

```yaml
- topologySpreadConstraints:
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector:
       matchLabels:
         app: foo
    topologyKey: "zone"
    domains:
      - topologyLabel: "zonea"
        weight: 7
      - topologyLabel: "zoneb"
        weight: 3
```

We have a DB in zoneA, so we want to schedule the Pods mostly to zoneA for better latency.
But, want to schedule smaller part of them to zone-b in case of zone failure.

### Usecases2: spread Pods for on-demand/spot

```yaml
- topologySpreadConstraints:
    labelSelector:
       matchLabels:
         app: foo
    topologyKey: "node-availability"
    domains:
      - topologyLabel: "on-demand"
        weight: 7
      - topologyLabel: "spot"
        weight: 3
```

So, we want to keep a large part of Pods running in on-demand Nodes because the spot instance might be deleted suddenly.
But, we're greedy, we want to keep some Pods in the spot Nodes for sure for the cost saving.

### Usecase3: gradual infrastructure migration

```yaml
- topologySpreadConstraints:
    labelSelector:
       matchLabels:
         app: foo
    topologyKey: "nodepool"
    domains:
      - topologyLabel: "old-nodepool"
        weight: 9 # will be reduced gradually
      - topologyLabel: "new-nodepool"
        weight: 1 # will be increased gradually
```

When we migrate workloads from one domain to another, we want to do it gradually.

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] When resize container, before CanAdmitPod, need to check if the node avaliable resources are sufficient
body:
In current code, canResizePod()  only checks node allocatable resource and then execute canAdmitPod(),  but it doesn't check node available resource.
 
For container resize, if node available resources are sufficient, container should enter to Deferred status and stop following process, but with current logic, it still enter to canAdmitPod to allocate cpu and memory for container.

On the other side, in cpu‑manager‑policy=static mode, CanAdmitPod can allocate a cpuset for a Guaranteed pod and then verify the node’s available resources. 
there is an potential error for guaranteed pod resize when node available resources are sufficient.

Consider the following scenario:
Test configuration
  - Node total CPUs: 20
  - Reserved CPUs: 0, 11
  - Allocatable CPUs: 18
  - Total CPU requests on the node: 1100 m
  - Available CPUs on the node: 18000 m − 1100 m = 16900 m
  
Step 1: Create container #0 with a CPU request of 16 cores. The assigned cpuset is `1‑8,11‑18`.
Step 2: Resize container #0, increasing the request from 16 cores to 17 cores. 
           - `CanAdmitPod` allocates a new cpuset `1‑9,11‑18` and writes it to the container’s cgroup (`cpuset.cpus: 1‑9,11‑18`).
          - Afterwards, the node‑resource check fails because the required 17000 m exceeds the available 16900 m, causing the resize to enter Deferred status.

The problem is that, although the resize is deferred due to insufficient node resources, the new cpuset has already been applied to the container’s cgroup. This leaves the container with a resource allocation that the node cannot actually provide, which is undesirable.

Suggested improvements: 
Perform the node available resource check before canAdmitPod, so that container enter deferred status and reduce unnecessary operations in canAdmitPod, and solve the potential error in guaranteed pod resize

title: Kubelet should not add IPv6 entries to /etc/hosts on systems where IPv6 is disabled
body:
### What happened?

Kubelet unconditionally adds IPv6 entries to `/etc/hosts` even when system has IPv6 totally disabled. This results in strange errors due to "happy eyeballs" fallback behavior: when clients see both an IPv4 and an IPv6 address for a host, they first try IPv4 and then fall back to IPv6, but if IPv6 is disabled in the kernel, they then get an "Address family not supported by protocol" exception instead of "Connection refused".

This happens with standard HTTP clients, etc, but here's an example with netcat:
```
# nc -v 127.0.0.1 1111
Ncat: Version 7.92 ( https://nmap.org/ncat )
Ncat: Connection refused.
```
vs
```
Ncat: Version 7.92 ( https://nmap.org/ncat )
Ncat: Connection to 127.0.0.1 failed: Connection refused.
Ncat: Trying next address...
libnsock nsock_make_socket(): Socket trouble: Address family not supported by protocol
Ncat: Address family not supported by protocol.
```

That results in clients needing to handle a different exception. However, even if IPv6 were enabled on the system, it would still be invalid to put loopback addresses in `/etc/hosts` for localhost when they are not actually configured on the loopback interface.

Code here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.29.4/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L373-L377

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should not add localhost entries to `/etc/hosts` for addresses that do not actually exist on the pod's loopback interface.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I don't think you need a reproducer for this one since the code is just unconditionally doing this. However, if you're looking to test this on a system with ipv6 disabled such that you get the "Address family not supported by protocol" error, or guarantee that CNI does not add an IPv6 loopback address, you can boot your kernel with `ipv6.disable=1` on the kernel command line.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

N/A all v

title: kubelet use --register-with-taints=node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable=true:NoSchedule wiil be remove by node-lifecycle-controller if  node.spec.Unscheduleable=false
body:
### What happened?

When `node.spec.Unschedulable = false`, the `node-lifecycle-controller` will automatically remove the `node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable=true:NoSchedule` taint from the node.

Most of the time, this mechanism works well. However, sometimes I want the node to be registered with this taint by default, and only remove it manually when I decide to, instead of having it removed automatically by the `node-lifecycle-controller`.

In this case, maybe I need to add `--register-schedulable=false --register-with-taints=node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable=true:NoSchedule` to the kubelet startup configuration. Unfortunately, this flag(--register-schedulable) has been marked as deprecated, and I am not sure whether I should use it.

```go
        // registerSchedulable tells the kubelet to register the node as
	// schedulable. Won't have any effect if register-node is false.
	// DEPRECATED: use registerWithTaints instead
	RegisterSchedulable bool
```


### What did you expect to happen?

I expect that the `node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable=true:NoSchedule` taint added when registering the node will not be automatically removed by the `node-lifecycle-controller`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a node and configure kubelet with `--register-with-taints=node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable=true:NoSchedule`.
2. Check the node's taints; it does **not** include this taint.

### Anything else we need to know?

I set the log level of` kube-controller-manager` to 4, and I was able to observe that the taint was indeed removed by the `node-lifecycle-controller`.

```shell
I0521 11:21:46.172081       7 controller_utils.go:223] "Made sure that node has no taint" node="192.168.0.200" taint=[{"key":"node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable","value":"true","effect":"NoSchedule"}]
```

title: Asynchronous preemption can be initiated even before the previous one is finished for the same pod
body:
### What happened?

In the asynchronous preemption, the preemptor is blocked in PreEnqueue until API calls are made to delete the victims. However, it doesn't wait for the last victim to be deleted not to cause a race condition (in which we could ignore the Pod/Delete event).

This means that when API calls take longer (e.g., due to throttling), the pod may start the preemption process for that last pod again, even if the previous one hasn't finished. Each preemption process would create a Pod/Delete API call to delete the last victim. As a result, kube-scheduler can create dozens of API calls to preempt a single pod.

Normally, we should have multiple safeguards to avoid such tight loops, but currently, all of them can be bypassed:
- The pod waits in unschedulablePods and must be woken up by some event. However, when there are many preemptions going on in the cluster, some unrelated Pod/Delete events can wake up such a pod.
- Even after being woken up, the pod should go to backoffQ and wait for the backoff penalty. However, we have a Pop from backoffQ feature that, if activeQ is empty, pop these pods from backoffQ directly, ignoring the backoff penalty.
- Synchronous API calls to update the status of a pod when it cannot be scheduled also worked like a kind of barrier, limiting the performance of the scheduler (the number of cycles per second) and making it dependent on the processing performance of the kube-apiserver. In this scenario, such behavior was beneficial, because kube-scheduler wasn't able to retry one pod that quickly. This call has been replaced by an asynchronous version by Asynchronous API calls feature.

/sig scheduling
/kind regression

### What did you expect to happen?

Kube-scheduler shouldn't start the preemption process for a pod until the previous one is finished. At least, such behavior should be minimized.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use scheduler_perf `PreemptionBasic` benchmark, with smaller # o

title: Overaggressive Routes Controller
body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:
/kind bug

**What happened**:
`Route controller` is unnecessary too aggressive. The [current control loop](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/route/route_controller.go#L115) loops through the node list every `10s`. Each node will generate a `GET` call to cloud resource manager (ARM in case of `azure`) to assert the route existence, This quickly burns through the quota afforded to each subscription (the umbrella concept used by `azure` to manage multiple clusters/ resource groups) by the underlaying cloud. Nodes does not change their own ip that frequent on `azure` or any cloud/om-prem deployment for that matter. Once the cluster burns through the quota its control plane will become practically unusable until quota refill, refresh or manual shutdown/start of controller to slow down the calls.

Setting it to higher period is not the best solution, since we need the route controller to kick in in case of scale up/down or the unlikely case of node changing IPs. 

**What you expected to happen**:
`Route Controller` must generate the smallest possible of cloud calls. Ideally, only when needed. And must be reasonably fast in reaction to changing state such as `new nodes`, `deleted nodes`, or changing `node ip`  

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Either run many small clusters (10 X 20 nodes) in the same `azure` subscription (or the equivalent concept on different environments), Or run one large cluster (400++ node). The controller will quickly log `HTTP 429` (in `azure` case) throttling errors 

**Proposed Solution**
change `Route Controller` implementation to `Service Controller` [like](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/service/service_controller.go#L136) implementation using `shared informer`. Because `node` object gets frequently updated (example node status updates) the controller should maintain an in memory c

title: No share ID in DRA kubelet plugin's API
body:
### What happened?

kubelet plugin API does not support ShareID information. The ShareID is an additional identifier to the device name which may be generated by DRAConsumableCapacity feature ( that is introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5104). 

The DRA driver which refers to this API for preparing resource needs to pass ShareID to CDI spec's device ID. Otherwise, the same node will fail to create a container according to the duplicate ID. 



### What did you expect to happen?

Pods can be successfully created when sharing the same device with DRAConsumableCapacity.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable DRAConsumableCapacity feature, Enable DRA driver with allowMultipleAllocations device, Create two pods allocating the same device.

### Anything else we need to know?

Without the change to k/k, a driver can have a workaround which wrap the plugin API appending with shareID and use it as a PreparedDevice.

From 
```go
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
to
```go
type DRADevice struct {
	drapbv1.Device
	shareID *types.UID
}
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
implemented code: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/commit/939b1fdd3e3efec3a3c7ea758c394c5aabdfa422

However, it looks cleaner when we do that in the provided API.
The change needs at driver is only extending the CDI id with share id if not nil: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/commit/4a625314cb46ed38018d05e17a397420335277eb.

title: Add startup resource requirements
body:
<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->

**What would you like to be added**:

I would like startup resources requirements to be added. Now we have `request` and `limits` and I want something like `startup-request` for CPU and RAM.

**Why is this needed**:

Some applications use a lot of RAM and CPU during the startup and use not much while running. Now, such applications need to require high `requests` to be able to started. And when app is running and uses few resources it blocks unused resources so that other applications cannot use it. 

For example, there is an app which requires 1 GB RAM and 1 CPU during the startup. And when it finished all preparations and started to work in normal mode it requires only 200 MB RAM and 200m CPU. Now, to make it deployable to k8s we need to set resource requests as 1 GB for RAM and 1 core for CPU which is honest. But when app is running it uses only fifth part of requested resources and other applications can not claim to use these resources. 

What I am suggesting for this cases is to introduce `startup-request`  which will be actual until `startupProbe` (introduced in 1.16) returns `OK`. So, when app finished startup,  k8s frees unnecessary resources (making them available for other apps) and application left only with resources specified in `request` section

title: Question: Should Kubelet Use a More Restrictive Taint During Graceful Shutdown to Prevent Pod Scheduling?
body:
I've been investigating the behavior of Kubelet during [graceful node shutdown](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/node-shutdown/#graceful-node-shutdown). Currently, Kubelet marks the node as NotReady and applies the node.kubernetes.io/not-ready:NoSchedule taint. This works well for most scenarios, as pods without the corresponding toleration are not scheduled on the node.

However, I've noticed that pods with a matching toleration (e.g., DaemonSets, critical pods) can still be scheduled on a node that is in the process of shutting down. The Kubelet, being in shutdown mode, rejects these pods. In my environment, this results in thousands of pod scheduling retries and many pods stuck in ContainerStatusUnknown, which increases memory usage unnecessarily.

## Questions

Is there a reason Kubelet does not use a more restrictive taint or mechanism during graceful shutdown, such as applying a specific taint that is effectively "untolerable" for all pods (perhaps a new, shutdown-specific taint)?

* Is this the intended design, or is it a trade-off for specific use-cases?
* Would it make sense to use a different taint during graceful shutdown to prevent all scheduling, including pods with tolerations? Would introducing a new taint (e.g., node.kubernetes.io/shutting-down:NoSchedule) that is not tolerated by any system pod by default be a viable approach?

I would appreciate any insights into the design decision here, and whether there is openness to making this behavior more configurable or restrictive to prevent unnecessary pod scheduling during node shutdown.

## Environment

* OpenShift 4.17.33
* Kubernetes 1.30.12

title: volume-binding scheduler prefilter assumes that a node's metadata.name == metadata.labels["kubernetes.io/hostname"]
body:
### What happened?

Running on a system which has node names that look like FQDNs, but hostname labels which are unqualified.

The local path PV provisioner has (correctly) added nodeAffinity constraints to the PV that reference a node's `hostname` label.

A replacement pod for a statefulset that has a bound PVC cannot be re-scheduled, because the scheduler interprets  `PreFilterResult.NodeNames` as node *names*, but the code in volume_binding.go that runs the prefilter collects a set of *kubeternetes.io/hostname label values*.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod rescheduling should not wedge. The volume-binding scheduler plugin should resolve match constraints to a set of nodes and return their node names in its PreFilterResult.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a node with distinct name and hostname label [k8s documentation reiterates that this situation is possible]. Schedule a pod onto it with a local path PV bound. Observe the PV has a nodeAffinity constraint that contains the node's hostname label. Attempt to reschedule a pod to use this PV.

Precise behaviour may vary from 1.27 (which introduced this prefilter notion) forwards. On 1.27, the scheduler failes with a "nodeinfo not found". A workaround was backported into the prefilter loop of `schedulePod` but AFAICT the root cause was never identified. Later versions look to end up filtering out all nodes in `schedulePod` - but the root cause is the same in both cases.

### Anything else we need to know?

The `RelaxedServiceNameValidation` feature gate implementation in `allowRelaxedServiceNameValidation()` might be incomplete. It checks service names in `spec.rules` but does not check `spec.defaultBackend.service.name`.

title: Improper Permissions on ConfigMap and Secret Mounts
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Hey, I am opening this issue publicly as it was approved by a member of the Kubernetes staff on HackerOne (#2867563) to be discussed with the larger community. Since addressing it would break existing users, it may require a Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal (KEP). The staff member also agreed that it is a poor default.

# Description
Kubernetes mounts ConfigMaps and Secrets to containers with default permissions -rw-r--r-- (644) also the permission on the ConfigMaps and Secrets directories mounted to the container is set to -rwxrwxrwx (777),
This configuration allows any user in the container, not just the root user, to read these files, exposing sensitive data and violating the principle of least privilege.
In multi-user containers, any non-root user can access these ConfigMaps and Secrets, further increasing the risk of unauthorized data exposure.
To prevent this, users can use the defaultMode parameter to set stricter permissions, such as 600/750, ensuring only the root user has access.
The current default behavior conflicts with the principle of least privilege, making manual adjustment necessary to protect sensitive data.

# Steps To Reproduce:
1. Create a Kubernetes ConfigMap or Secret.
2. Mount the ConfigMap or Secret into a container.
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secret-mounted-pod
spec:
  containers:

      securityContext:

      volumeMounts:
        - name: secret-volume
          mountPath: "/etc/secret"
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: secret-volume
      secret:
        secretName: my-secret
```
3. Run the container with multiple users, including a non-root user (e.g., user ID 1000).
4. Observe that the default permissions are -rw-r--r-- and that any non-root user can read the mounted data.

title: Enable event watch cache by default
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently, Apiserver disable event watchcache by default. We did this to make test faster. See https://github.com/kubernetes/perf-tests/issues/561. We could disable it in tests, but keep it enabled in the default settings.

### Why is this needed?

Watchcache is critical in reducing etcd pressure. We have ran into some serious issue due to lack of event watchcache. 

We used to have a failure rate over 80% in a proction cluster with 14k nodes and 560k pods. With watchcahe enabled, the failure rate droped to near zero. 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cb9f9472-ce15-4b05-ae32-a440e0154cfa)

The same thing happended to request lantency. 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/aa836747-9365-44c5-b7d3-620f1f58d1fe)

The etcd is really not good at handling large range requests. Without watchcache, the list/watch goes directly to etcd, which cause a serious lock contension. We saw some large range requests took over 1m and kept hodling the lock, while others starved. 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/570ca431-3710-499f-8087-60ff7f0d1966)

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6abb31cd-83b5-48d5-986d-ee51ba02c16a)

This results in watch events pending and raft pending rising. After we enabled watchcache, these issues also dispeared.

title: behavior of PVC::status.capacity when expanding a PVC changed
body:
### What happened?

I noticed that the behavior of `PVC::status.capacity` when expanding a PVC changed before and after RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure feature. Before RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure feature, `PVC::status.capacity` stored the actual capacity returned by the CSI driver, similar to `PV::spec.capacity`. However, when RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure is enabled and a PVC is expanded, copies the value of `PVC::spec.resources` to `PVC::status.capacity`.
This behavior differs from the existing one and is not described in KEP either.

### What did you expect to happen?

In RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure, if there is no intention to change the original meaning of PVC::status.capacity, I think it is reasonable for the actual value returned by the CSI driver after expansion to be stored. If this behavior is intentional, I think it should be explicitly stated in the KEP documentation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a PVC. Use a CSI driver that returns the actual allocated capacity for the request size. In this case, if you set an awkward value for `PVC::resources.requests`, `PVC::status.capacity` should store a value different from the request size.
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: topo
  namespace: default
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 301Mi # 👈Values that are not multiples of the sector size, etc.
  storageClassName: topolvm-provisioner-thin
  volumeMode: Filesystem
  volumeName: pvc-4d9a440d-d5e9-4e74-92f9-a842d67c4ce1
status:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  capacity:
    storage: 304Mi # 👈The capacity actually allocated by the CSI driver is set.
  phase: Bound
```
2. Extend PVC to an awkward size by editing the `PVC::spec.resources.requests`.
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: topo
  namespace: default
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 305Mi

title: support ephemeral rw image volume mounts
body:
### What would you like to be added?

With the continued advancement of image volumes https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/04/29/kubernetes-v1-33-image-volume-beta/ I would like to see an ability to mount the volume as rw.

I do *NOT* want the actual changes to be written to the registry (local or remote) but rather simply want the mount point to be ephemeral in much the same way a rootfs is of a running container.

### Why is this needed?

My specific use-case it to use the volume essentially as a rw cache. For example let's say I have a large git repository I wish to share across CI builds running in a cluster. I would like each build to use the image as a 'starting place' and each build will then simply (ephemerally) do a `git pull` and `git checkout` etc on the mount point and be able to generally function as a rw volume. Once the build is done the modified data is simply discarded and the source image is left untouched.

A side-benefit is that each relevant node will only store the data of the repo once (ie: copy-on-write-like semantics) reducing storage requirements. The source image can periodically be updated to the latest upstream content and inherit the goodness of image deltas for that process as well.

Thanks for the consideration!

title: Analysis of Kubelet Init Container Restart Count Issue
body:
### What happened?

The user created a pod with an init container. After the init container was created but before it started, the system rebooted.

After the system rebooted, clock synchronization was performed, causing the time to jump forward by several tens of seconds. At this point, the kubelet recreated the sandbox and init container and started it. The start time of the newly launched init container was earlier than that of the init container in the "created" state that existed before the reboot.

During subsequent operations, the status of the init container was retrieved, but it corresponded to the container created before the reboot. When attempting to create a new one, the restart count of the container was actually undercounted by 1. This caused the newly created container to have the same sequence number as the one after the reboot, preventing it from starting at all.

I am not sure whether this qualifies as an issue.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/runtime.go#L424-L433
```golang
