remove old conntrack setup workaround once we stop supporting containerd 1.7
body:
Kube-proxy has a very old workaround for the inability to set one of the conntrack parameters at startup, #28697. (If we detect the bug happening, we just fail to set the conntrack parameter, and log an Event.)

It seems that the underlying problem is in the kernel, and is that if you try to start a hostNetwork container with sysfs mounted read-write while there is already a hostNetwork container with sysfs mounted read-only, then the kernel will silently ignore the "read-write" and just give you a read-only sysfs. (eg, https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/24000#issuecomment-906367168)

It was originally believed that the bug only happens at scale, because it was only seen in 1000-node tests, but it might just be that those are the only jobs that are trying to override the relevant conntrack parameter. (At least on Fedora, the default value of `/sys/module/nf_conntrack/parameters/hashsize` is larger than it needs to be to support the default value of `--conntrack-max-per-core`, so kube-proxy wouldn't even try to set it unless you were overriding `--conntrack-max-per-core`.)

Anyway, the problem is believed to be fixed in containerd 2.0.3+ and 2.1+ (https://github.com/containerd/containerd/pull/11271), and in cri-o since forever ago (https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/pull/2627).

I think we don't require containerd 2.x, so we can't remove the workaround yet. Assuming that the problem even still exists, which I don't think we have any information about... it was allegedly fixed in dockershim in 1.21 (#96877) but it's not clear if any corresponding fix was made/needed/possible in the CRI codepaths.

So:
1. If someone could figure out if the bug ever still exists anywhere (5000Node job logs?) that would be cool.
2. If it doesn't still exist anywhere, we should remove the workaround now.
3. If it does still exist, we should update the [comments in the code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0-alpha.0/cmd/kube-proxy/app/conntrack.go#L76-L82) to reference thi

title: E2e test "should preempt lower priority pods using ReadWriteOncePod volumes" flakes
body:
### What happened?

We observed the e2e test `External Storage [Driver: disk.csi.azure.com] [Testpattern: Dynamic PV (default fs)] read-write-once-pod [MinimumKubeletVersion:1.27] should preempt lower priority pods using ReadWriteOncePod volumes` causes flakes in other e2e tests in a downstream CI job with Azure Disk CSI driver.

[The test](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4e94e70dcad423e9f59f12ac5a048d2137d20e86/test/e2e/storage/testsuites/readwriteoncepod.go#L133) runs a default (low-prio) pod1 with a `ReadWriteOncePod` volume and then starts a high prio pod2 that tries to use the same volume. To run pod2, the scheduler has to evict pod1 to make the RWOP volume "free" for pod2. That works great, however, it may evict also pods of other e2e tests that run with the default priority.

What happened on a busy clusters, with all nodes at their attachment limit.

1. pod1 runs, pod2 is created.
2. The scheduler evicts pod1. That frees the RWOP volume and it also frees the last attachment slot on the node.
3. Some other e2e tests creates a Pod and scheduler puts it on the node, taking the last attachment slot.
4. The scheduler schedules pod2 agaian and it sees there is no node with a free attachment slot -> new round of eviction, now evicting a pod of unrelated e2e tests. The unrelated test will fail.  

We observed it with Azure, which can attach only 8 disks on the cheaper nodes, so it's more reproducible there.

### What did you expect to happen?

The preemption test should not affect other e2e tests

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See above

title: Codegen tools creates wrong conversion for struct if member order is not matching
body:
The `conversion-gen` tool produces wrong conversion code for a pointer to a struct, if source and destination struct have multiple members of the same type, but the member ordering is different.

Here is an example to show the issue for an extended struct from k8s.io/code-generator/examples/apiserver/apis/example:

Type `example/v1`:
```go
package v1 // "k8s.io/code-generator/examples/apiserver/apis/example/v1"

type TestTypeStatus struct {
	Blah  string `json:"blah"`
	Times *Times `json:"times,omitempty"`
}

type Times struct {
	Start *metav1.Time `json:"start,omitempty"`
	End   *metav1.Time `json:"end,omitempty"`
}
```

and the internal type:

```go
package example // "k8s.io/code-generator/examples/apiserver/apis/example"

type TestTypeStatus struct {
	Blah  string
	Times *Times
}

type Times struct {
	End   *metav1.Time
	Start *metav1.Time
}
```

Note, that the ordering of the members `Start` and `End` have been changed.

Converting `example/v1` to `v1` shows that the values have been swapped:

```
$ go run ./main.go
examplev1.TestTypeStatus:
blah: blah
times:
  end: "2023-12-31T23:00:00Z"
  start: "1993-12-31T23:00:00Z"

---
example.TestTypeStatus:
Blah: blah
Times:
  End: "1993-12-31T23:00:00Z"
  Start: "2023-12-31T23:00:00Z"

---conversion ok: false%
```

The complete example code can be found [here](https://github.com/MartinWeindel/code-generator/compare/master...MartinWeindel:code-generator:example/wrong-conversion?expand=1)

title: Default memory eviction-hard threshold in kubernetes should be set more than `vm.min_free_kbytes`
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Current default eviction threshold is hardcoded as 100MiB, this works for default linux default (66MiB). But this can be adjusted, and with swap use-cases, kubernetes environments will likely see this sysctl parameter adjusted to a higher value than default.

This proposal suggests to set the sysctl parameter based on the observed value instead:

`max( DefaultHardEvictionThresholdValue , NodeMinFreeKbytes + SafetyMargin )`

Where:
- `DefaultHardEvictionThresholdValue` is the current default (100MiB).
- `NodeMinFreeKbytes` is the value read from /proc/sys/vm/min_free_kbytes, converted to MiB.
- `SafetyMargin` is a buffer (e.g., 50MiB or a percentage of min_free_kbytes) to ensure eviction triggers comfortably before the kernel's absolute minimum is reached. 

Proposal discussed at SIG-Node: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1qBkCuB7hPbCfCkTc7ilYwwDzyG_ykpP7losidyuOiTU/edit?usp=sharing
 

### Why is this needed?

This is required to ensure Kubernetes handles eviction before the OOM killer starts handling for memory pressure. This is particularly important for swap use-cases as the swap watermarks are directly influenced by this sysctl parameter.

title: Lack of Graceful Rolling Eviction When Using PriorityClass Can Cause Downtime
body:
I'm trying to understand the eviction behavior in Kubernetes when using `PriorityClass` for preemption, and I believe there's a gap in how gracefully the system handles eviction of lower-priority pods.

Let's say I have the following setup:

- A critical DaemonSet using a high PriorityClass
- That DaemonSet needs to schedule a pod on a specific node
- The node already hosts a lower-priority Deployment with two pods running
- The Deployment is configured with a rolling update strategy, e.g.:

```yaml
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxUnavailable: 0
    maxSurge: 1
```

My expectation was that Kubernetes would attempt to evict one pod at a time from the lower-priority Deployment in a rolling fashion, honoring the update strategy and avoiding disruption.

However, from what I understand, Kubernetes may evict both pods immediately to make room for the higher-priority DaemonSet pod — potentially causing application downtime, even though the Deployment's maxUnavailable is 0.

What I’d Expect:

Some sort of graceful eviction mechanism that:

- Evicts pods one at a time if possible
- Honors maxUnavailable or respects PodDisruptionBudget
- Provides better coordination between PriorityClass-based preemption and Deployment rolling update behavior

Questions / Discussion Points:
- Is this the intended behavior, or is it a known limitation?
- re there any plans or proposals to make preemption more graceful - for example, by allowing a custom `.sh` script to handle restarts as a plugin for more complex resources like StatefulSets?
- Would this be a fit for future enhancement (e.g., opt-in rolling eviction mode)?
- Should the scheduler consider Deployment strategies or disruption budgets during preemption?

This behavior can lead to unintended outages when using `PriorityClass` to protect critical workloads (e.g., system agents, DaemonSets, StatefulSets), especially when the cluster is under pressure. Graceful degradation is often essential in production-

title: pod name and host name differ in indexed completion mode
body:
In case[ .spec.completionMode = Indexed](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/#completion-mode) in our Kubernetes job yaml,
The host name will look like (in /etc/hostname in a pod container) looks like:
'xxxxxxxxx-0'
'xxxxxxxxx-1'
'xxxxxxxxx-2'
etc.

However,
The pod name will be:
'xxxxxxxxx-0-{randomid}'
'xxxxxxxxx-1-{randomid}'
'xxxxxxxxx-2-{randomid}'
etc.

Why is the pod name not set identical to the host name? 
In case of  .spec.completionMode=NonIndexed mode pod name and hostname are identical.  
So this is an unexpected inconsistency.
The random id can be left out:  xxxxxxxxx-{IndexNr}  is already an unique id.


It is important, because we let our containers write their hostname in our log messages.
However, we cannot directly derive the pod name from the host name, which is needed to find back the pod logs written to persistent storage later on.
Of course we can work around this, by adding the pod name to the env variables of the container and log that additionally, but that should not be necessary in my opinion. It is very confusing that pod name and host name differ in indexed mode.

title: Missing documentation on FilteringResourceEventHandler behavior with dynamic filters
body:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/73bd83cfa74730ecab263a886698b7ea8a2e02ad/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/controller.go#L291-L299 defines a convenient filtering handler.

However, it doesn't define what the behavior is with a FilterFunc that is not static. For example, we may have 

```go
AllowedNamespaces := sets.New("namespace1")
handler.FilterFunc = func(obj any) bool {
  return AllowedNamespaces.Has(obj.GetNamespace)
}

// Later...
AllowedNamespaces.Insert("new-namespace")
```

The current behavior is:
* New adds and deletes will not be handled
* there is races in OnUpdate, as we check the filter against `newer` and `older` seqentually. We could have the filter change in between these, leading to weird behavior like calling OnUpdate when OnAdd had never previously been called.

It would be helpful to document and test what is intended or not intended to be supported here.

We are also actually trying to use dynamic filters, so if there are any examples that already solve these problems it would be very helpful

/sig apimachinery

title: Allow scaling up to meet PDB constraints
body:
**What would you like to be added**:

Currently if you have a PDB spec like `minAvailable: 1`, and a HPA defining minReplicas=1 and maxReplicas=N, you may end up in a scenario where disruptions get "stuck" if the HPA has scaled to 1. At any point an increase in load could cause the HPA to scale up to 2+, allowing the PDB to be satisfied, which leads to a weird scenario where a disruption can only occur if there is high load.

Ideally, the PDB would be able to trigger the HPA to scale up to meet constraints. For example, if I have 1 replica and a disruption is triggered, scale up a new replica first, then terminate the old one. Given an HPA is in place, I have already clearly specified I am OK with my pod being scaled up, so this shouldn't have negative impact on stateful workloads.

Some more context: https://github.com/istio/istio/issues/12602

title: EndpointSlice API returns `endpoints: null` even though OpenAPI schema defines `endpoints` as required array
body:
### What happened?

When a Service has zero backing Pods (e.g., Deployment scaled to 0 or no Pods ever matched the selector), the EndpointSlice object returned by the API server contains:
```
{
  "kind": "EndpointSliceList",
  "apiVersion": "discovery.k8s.io/v1",
  "metadata": {
    "resourceVersion": "828044619"
  },
  "items": [
    {
      "metadata": { ... },
      "addressType": "IPv4",
      "endpoints": null,  // null here
      "ports": null
    }
  ]
}
```
This breaks clients / validators that rely on the published OpenAPI schema where `endpoints` is treated as a required field and modeled as an array (not nullable).

### What did you expect to happen?

According to the API Spec, `endpoints` should be a JSON array. For the “no endpoints” case, it should be an empty array.
```
"endpoints": []
```
Ref.: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/api/openapi-spec/v3/apis__discovery.k8s.io__v1_openapi.json#L228-L231



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
kubectl scale rs/replicaset.apps/demo-5f6c9cb999 --replicas=0
```

### Anything else we need to know?

- The API type defines `Endpoints []Endpoint` without `omitempty`, so it’s expected to be present and modeled as a list in generated schema/docs: https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/discovery/v1#EndpointSlice
- A related client breakage report (Java client) describing the same behavior: https://github.com/kubernetes-client/java/issues/3226

title: Kubelet restart causes NotReady pod to be briefly marked Ready before probe workers exist
body:
### What happened?

When kubelet restarts, there is a race condition in `prober_manager.go` that causes pods that were NOT Ready before the restart to be briefly marked as Ready. This happens because:

1. During `SyncPod`, `UpdatePodStatus` is called before prober workers are created
2. The code assumes "no worker exists = no readiness probe configured" and marks the container Ready
3. The pod is updated to Ready in the API server
4. Prober workers are then created and the first probe runs
5. The probe fails and the pod is marked NotReady again

This brief Ready window (we observed ~4 seconds) is enough for PodDisruptionBudget checks to succeed, allowing evictions that should have been blocked.

### Code Location

In `pkg/kubelet/prober/prober_manager.go`, the `UpdatePodStatus` function (around line 350):

```go
} else {
    // The check whether there is a probe which hasn't run yet.
    w, exists := m.getWorker(pod.UID, c.Name, readiness)
    ready = !exists // no readinessProbe -> always ready
```

The comment says "no readinessProbe -> always ready" but `exists` is false in TWO cases:
1. No readiness probe configured (intended)
2. Prober worker hasn't been created yet after kubelet restart (potential bug)

### Timeline from Production Incident

| Time (UTC) | Event | Source |
|------------|-------|--------|
| 05:13:53 | Pod marked NOT Ready | Kubelet logs |
| 05:14:25 | Kubelet stops and restarts | systemd logs |
| 05:14:26 | Pod marked **Ready** | API server audit logs |
| 05:14:29 | Another pod eviction **succeeds** | API server audit logs |
| 05:14:30 | Pod marked NOT Ready | API server audit logs |

The pod was Ready for only 4 seconds, but this was enough for Karpenter (retrying evictions) to successfully evict another pod, causing two pods to be down simultaneously despite PDB `maxUnavailable: 1`.

### Why KEP-4781 Doesn't Fix This

title: NodeLifeCycleController: all pods are marked as not ready making workload services unavailable during network partition b/w master & worker nodes
body:
### What happened?

We've encountered a failure scenario in production where if master nodes hosting etcd, apiserver, controller-manager etc gets network partitioned with worker nodes (say due to apiserver lb outage or a widespread network infra outage), all the pods hosted in that k8s cluster gets [marked as not ready](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5935da7151c5f171c2263976042b254b5f57f2b8/pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/node_lifecycle_controller.go#L846) making endpoint controller remove the pods IP addresses from all services matching them. It causes a widespread outage for all the service workloads hosted on that kubernetes cluster as pods are marked as not ready even though all the containers comprising them are ready.

### What did you expect to happen?

We expected only pods that are marked for [eviction](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/nodes/#rate-limits-on-eviction) during the above circumstances to be marked as not ready. It'll help us in delaying or eventually stopping a widespread workloads service unavailability.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Host a few load balancer/clusterIP services in k8s cluster.
- Create a network partition between master & worker nodes (using iptable rules or something similar). Each master node is able to connect each other and deployed with components [stacked together](https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/production-environment/tools/kubeadm/high-availability/#stacked-control-plane-and-etcd-nodes) hosting etcd, apiserver, controller-manager, cloud-controller, scheduler, cni etc.
- You can see that the load balancer external IP address is not able to route traffic to pods since addresses are removed from the endpoint resource after the node lifecycle controller marking pods as not ready.

title: Informers: cache Indexer interface to support generics
[workqueue] Monitor the full latency of items added to the rate-limit queue
body:
When an item is added to a rate-limiting queue, users may want visibility into how long a key has been waiting before it's actually added to the queue (i.e., the delay duration). This can be helpful to understand the extent of rate limiting in a controller’s traffic patterns.

I believe it would be useful to expose one more metric in [waitForPriorityQueue](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/util/workqueue/delaying_queue.go#L199), similar to how the [latency](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/util/workqueue/metrics.go#L112) of the queue is measured. 

Another option is to have users wrap the queue and track timestamps in the application code. Given that we already track the [retry](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/master/util/workqueue/delaying_queue.go#L154) count, it seems cleaner to me to add a new metric to the library directly. 

Happy to contribute a patch if the team agrees this would be a worthwhile addition.

Thanks!

title: Leader election acquire loop should fail if the cluster is not reachable.
body:
### Problem:
The leader election acquisition loops currently attempts indefinitely to acquire a leader, even if the cluster is unreachable. 

### Proposed Solution:
We should introduce a configurable timeout to bail out and fail the leader election process if the cluster is not reachable within a specified time. By default, we can retain the current behavior of indefinite retries, but we should allow users to configure this timeout, either to enable the timeout or to adjust its duration.

title: Missing request total apiserver latency and components break down in the audit log annotation
body:
### What happened?

Missing request total apiserver latency and components break down in the audit log annotation causes trouble when we want to narrow down which component took longer for a specific slow request. 

In the audit http filter, `writeLatencyToAnnotation` will track latency in annotation only when the total latency of the given request exceeds 500ms. The total latency is calculated by subtracting request start time `ac.GetEventRequestReceivedTimestamp().Time` from end time `ac.GetEventStageTimestamp()`. 

However, the end time is not assigned until the audit log event is persisted to the audit backend [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/612122f1d79eb148b06bb63fbf392c03f9b73d60/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters/audit.go#L107)

The issue was probably introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/129472

### What did you expect to happen?

audit log with latency annotation when the request latency exceeds 500ms

title: `kubectl describe service` does not display `appProtocol` field
body:
## Problem

The `appProtocol` field (GA since v1.20) is not displayed in `kubectl describe service` output, even when set. Users must use `kubectl get svc -o yaml` to verify this field.

This can be problematic when debugging Service Mesh or Gateway API configurations where `appProtocol` affects traffic routing. Given that `appProtocol` has been GA for several years and is actively used in Service Mesh environments, displaying it in `kubectl describe` output would be beneficial for users.

## Proposed Solution

Display `appProtocol` in the port section of `kubectl describe service` output:
```
Port:              http  80/TCP
TargetPort:        8080/TCP
AppProtocol:       http          # <-- Add this
NodePort:          http  30080/TCP
```

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/describe/describe.go#L3015

## Benefits

- Consistency with other port fields (`name`, `protocol`, `port`, `targetPort`, `nodePort`)
- Easier debugging for Service Mesh and Gateway API users

title: Memory EmptyDir tmpfs size capped at 100% of node RAM size, not SizeLimit as specified
body:
### What happened?

I have a bit of an odd use case -- running a Kubernetes 1.29 cluster with NodeSwap enabled on AWS. The EC2 nodes have swap memory enabled on attached SSDs, and have successfully been able to utilize the swap (allocate/use more memory than RAM) when running pods in production. 

On Linux, tmpfs I believe is typically able to be allocated to sizes larger than RAM, and in the cases where swap is present the files in tmpfs will be swapped out. 

When configuring an EmptyDir backed by memory, I set a limit equal to the node's RAM + swap for a pod (say, 150GB). Upon exec'ing into the pod, I noticed that the size of the tmpfs corresponding to the EmptyDir was capped at the node's RAM size (say, 50GB). There does not seem to be a way to enable EmptyDir sizes greater than node RAM sizes, which is limiting for some of our applications which choose to use RAM via writing to tmpfs. It would be preferable to have no limit on EmptyDir memory size, and allow the pod to be evicted/killed if RAM + swap (or just RAM) is exhausted. 



### What did you expect to happen?

The size of the EmptyDir would be equal to the specified size in the configuration file, as opposed to being capped to the amount of physical RAM on the node. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Spin up a cluster with NodeSwap Enabled
2. Enable some amount of swap on a node (say, 10GB)
3. Create a pod with a memory-backed EmptyDir with SizeLimit == Node's RAM + 10GB (swap size). Configure no RAM limit on the pod. 
4. Verify that EmptyDir presents in pod as tmpfs capped at Node's RAM size, not RAM + Swap size. 

### Anything else we need to know?

Thank you for taking a look!

title: In-Place Updates for StatefulSet
body:
**What happened:**

When modifying only metadata (labels or annotations) in a StatefulSet's pod template spec, the StatefulSet controller unnecessarily recreates all pods, causing service disruption for workloads that are otherwise healthy and functioning correctly.

**What you expected to happen:**

Changes to pod metadata (labels/annotations) in the StatefulSet template should be applied directly to existing pods without recreation, similar to how kubectl can directly modify pod labels/annotations without restart.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):**

1. Create a StatefulSet with 3 replicas:
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: test-sts
spec:
  replicas: 3
  serviceName: test-svc
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.20
```

2. Wait for all pods to be Running
3. Update only the metadata in the template:
```bash
kubectl patch statefulset test-sts -p '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"labels":{"version":"v2"}}}}}'
```

4. This triggers the StatefulSet controller to recreate pods one by one due to template hash change

**Anything else we need to know?:**

This is the documented behavior of StatefulSets where any template change triggers a rolling update based on template hash comparison. However, this creates operational challenges:
- Production workloads suffer unnecessary downtime when adding operational labels (monitoring, alerting, compliance tags)
- The same metadata changes can be applied directly to pods using `kubectl label` or `kubectl annotate` without restart
- This creates inconsistent behavior where direct pod updates work fine but template updates cause recreation
- Forces operators to choose between:
  - Accept downtime for metadata changes
  - Use direct pod modification (which gets overwritten on future updates)
  - Use external operators/co

title: [KubeProxy-Windows] RequireDualStack Service intermittently misprogrammed in Windows kube-proxy
body:
### What happened?

When creating a Service with ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack or PreferredDualstack on Windows nodes, kube-proxy sometimes programs incorrect load balancers.

The issue manifests in two main ways:

1. Incorrect backend selection
    - IPv6 endpoints are sometimes programmed as backends for IPv4 VIPs
    - IPv4 endpoints are sometimes programmed as backends for IPv6 VIPs
    - This results in traffic blackholing or connection failures

2. Incorrect load balancer flags
   - IPv6-specific HNS flags are sometimes applied to IPv4 load balancers
   - IPv4 flags are sometimes applied to IPv6 load balancers
   - This causes inconsistent behavior and unexpected failures in datapath programming

These issues appear intermittent and are more frequently observed under:

- Endpoint updates
- Service updates
- Rapid pod churn 

### What did you expect to happen?

For a RequireDualStack Service:

- IPv4 VIPs should:
    - Use only IPv4 endpoints
    - Be programmed with IPv4-specific HNS flags

- IPv6 VIPs should:
    - Use only IPv6 endpoints
    - Be programmed with IPv6-specific HNS flags

The programming behavior should be deterministic and consistent, matching the dual-stack service semantics defined in the Kubernetes dual-stack KEP.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Windows cluster with:
    - Dual-stack networking enabled
    - Windows nodes using winkernel kube-proxy
2. Create a Service:
 
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: test-dualstack-lb
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4
    - IPv6
  selector:
    app: test
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
```
 
3. Deploy dual-stack pods with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses
4. Trigger updates:
    - Scale pods up/down
    - Restart kube-proxy
    - Update endpoints or service annotations
5. Observe HNS load balancers and backend programming

### Anything else we need to know?

- This issue

title: ci-kubernetes-unit-dependencies failing due to otelgrpc v0.64.0 nil pointer panic
body:
### What happened?

The `ci-kubernetes-unit-dependencies` CI job is failing after updating `go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/instrumentation/google.golang.org/grpc/otelgrpc` from v0.60.0 to v0.64.0.

**Failed job**: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-unit-dependencies/2002001097211777024

### Root Cause

Commit [07504e453](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go-contrib/commit/07504e45307f41b8b4e609324a3b62374ad6008f) in otelgrpc removed nil checks from `WithTracerProvider` and `WithMeterProvider` options. When Kubernetes passes a nil `TracerProvider` in `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/storagebackend/factory/etcd3.go:326`:

```go
otelgrpc.WithTracerProvider(c.TracerProvider),  // c.TracerProvider can be nil
```

The nil now overwrites the default global provider, causing a panic in `NewClientHandler()` when it calls `c.TracerProvider.Tracer(...)`.

/kind bug
/priority important-soon

title: Using Dial function with client-go kubernetes.NewForConfig triggers a memory leak
body:
### What happened?

After we upgraded k8s.io/client-go package to v0.26.0, we noticed memory leaks in our components that access the Kubernetes API.  For some components we managed to remove the leak by rolling back client-go to 0.25.4, but for other components it creates a dependency hell.

After some profiling and debugging I managed to write a mockup code that is roughly based on our production code and reliably triggers the leak in client-go 0.26.0 to 0.27.3.  The code is uploaded to https://github.com/kublr/memory_leak_demo .  It includes the pprof endpoint so you can verify the leak.  The memory allocations happen in transport.(*tlsTransportCache)get method.

The leak is triggered by the presence of a custom Dial function in rest.Config object.  As I infer from the commits like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/117311 , this usage is now considered incorrect, but we need some guidance or advice how to adapt our production code.


### What did you expect to happen?

We expected to use public interfaces without triggering memory leaks in the package. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Compile and run the sample code in https://github.com/kublr/memory_leak_demo .  Using pprof you can observe growing amount of memory allocated in transport(*tlsTransportCache)get(), and using the debugger you can observe that every call of kubernetes.NewForConfig() creates a new entry in TLS cache.

### Anything else we need to know?

As I understand, the real culprit is line https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fa78f28f0a011e9922cf12145dd602c5a63981e8/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/transport.go#L115 , where client-go creates a DialHolder structure for configs that do not have one, but have a Dial hook.

title: DRA: DRA Driver and ResourceSlices in Composable System
body:
### What would you like to be added?

In composable system, it is necessary to consider the optimal design of the composable DRA driver for managing fabric devices and the vendor DRA driver for managing node-local devices.
According to KEP-5007 (https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5012), especially (https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5012#discussion_r1941473468), there are three ideas:
(If I've missed something, please let me know.)

**1. Moving the device and update ResourceSlice**
- Basic concept:
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5012#discussion_r1942323646
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5012#discussion_r1942712677
- Advantages: It is possible to minimize the addition of features to the vendor DRA
- Problems: It is necessary to consider conflicts due to moves and updates
- Vendor DRA driver needs to be newly implemented: Only periodic rescan

**2. Implement a device autoscaler in ClusterAutoscaler**
- Basic concept:
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/5007-device-attach-before-pod-scheduled#alternative-approach
- Advantages: The scheduler does not need to reschedule pods.
- Problems: Requires major addition of functionality in CA. May not fit with CA concept (CA scales nodes horizontally)
- New implementation required in vendor DRA driver: Periodic rescan only

**3. Make vendor DRA driver aware of fabric devices**
- Basic concept: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5012#discussion_r1947411169
- Advantages: The scheduler does not need to reschedule pods. Can use happy path (can proceed directly to binding after device attachment). It is possible to avoid moving devices between ResourceSlices.
- Problem: A large feature needs to be added to the vendor DRA.
- New implementations required for the vendor DRA driver: 
  - Fabric device recognition
  - Composable-related IFs such as attach,
  - Updating ResourceSlices after attach
  - Updating BindingCondi

title: Watches are not drained during graceful termination when feature gate APIServingWithRoutine is on
body:
### What happened?

I tried to observe the graceful termination of kube-apiserver, in particular, how watches are drained.
1) I created a cluster in 1.30 with kube-apiserver flags
```
--shutdown-delay-duration=10s --shutdown-send-retry-after=true --shutdown-watch-termination-grace-period=60s 
```
and with feature gate `APIServingWithRoutine` on.
Also, I added to kube-apiserver's manifest the following line
```
"terminationGracePeriodSeconds"=60,
```
2) I killed the kube-apiserver, and found the following log during graceful termination:
```
"[graceful-termination] active watch request(s) have drained" duration="1m0s" activeWatchesBefore=0 activeWatchesAfter=0 error=null
```
`activeWatchesBefore=0` is not the expected behavior.
Also, I do not observe any logs of watches being closed.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected a non-zero number of watches to be drained during graceful termination.

### What happened?

While auditing stale TODO comments in the GCE configuration scripts (following my recent merged cleanup PR #136379), I identified a 9-year-old TODO at line 525 of cluster/gce/config-test.sh. The environment variable KUBE_PROXY_DAEMONSET still defaults to false, causing kube-proxy to be deployed as static pods in certain GCE test configurations.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect GCE cluster configurations to align with modern Kubernetes standards (like kubeadm), where kube-proxy is managed as a DaemonSet by default. This change will allow for the future removal of legacy static-pod logic in cluster/gce/gci/configure-helper.sh, significantly reducing technical debt.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Inspect cluster/gce/config-test.sh at line 527.
2. Observe KUBE_PROXY_DAEMONSET=${KUBE_PROXY_DAEMONSET:-false}.
3. This stems from Commit 1102656 (PR #50705) from 2017, where the variable was introduced as an experimental option but never flipped to the default.

### Anything else we need to know?

I am a DevOps Engineer and am happy to take ownership of this transition. My plan is to:

title: Duplicate ports with different protocols in pod spec get merged after pod spec update
body:
### What happened?

When I add a port with a duplicate port number but different protocol (UDP instead of TCP) to an existing Deployment, one of these two ports get removed.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect both to be present.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply this:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: test-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: test
        image: busybox
        command:
        - sleep
        - infinity
        ports:
        - containerPort: 1000
          protocol: TCP
```

Then `kubectl edit` the `Deployment`, duplicating the containerport, but with UDP, like this:

```
        ports:
        - containerPort: 1000
          protocol: TCP
        - containerPort: 1000
          protocol: UDP
```

And you'll observe that one of the two ports is gone in the `Deployment`.

### Anything else we need to know?

There are no mutating webhooks involved. Even with all hooks removed, I still observ this.

When you `get deploy -o yaml`, edit the yaml, `apply --server-side -f /the/yaml`, it does seem to get applied.

My guess is it is due to (only) `containerPort` being the merge key in types.go.

This is very similar to #105610, but that issue is about `Services`.

title: Make healthCheckNodePort Optional for On-Premises LoadBalancer Services with externalTrafficPolicy: Local
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Introduce a way to disable automatic allocation of healthCheckNodePort for LoadBalancer services when externalTrafficPolicy: Local is set, particularly for on-premises environments where external load balancers do not rely on this port.

### Why is this needed?

In on-premises Kubernetes/OpenShift clusters using MetalLB with BGP and external load balancers (e.g., F5), the healthCheckNodePort is not used. However, Kubernetes still allocates and exposes this port when externalTrafficPolicy: Local is set.

**This leads to:**

Unnecessary open ports on nodes.
Potential security concerns.
Port exhaustion risks in large-scale clusters.
Operational confusion for administrators.
There is currently no native way to disable this behavior while preserving externalTrafficPolicy: Local, which is often required for source IP preservation.

**Proposed Solution**
Introduce an opt-out mechanism for healthCheckNodePort allocation, such as:

**Option 1: Annotation-based opt-out**

metadata:
  annotations:
    service.kubernetes.io/disable-healthcheck-nodeport: "true"

**Option 2: API field**

spec:
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  disableHealthCheckNodePort: true

**Risks and Mitigations**
Misconfiguration could lead to traffic being sent to unhealthy nodes if the external load balancer is not properly configured.
Clear documentation and validation should accompany the feature to ensure safe usage.
**Additional Context**
This enhancement would benefit on-premises setups where:

MetalLB is used with BGP.
External load balancers perform their own health checks.
healthCheckNodePort is not required and adds unnecessary complexity.

title: Auto-approved but unissued kubelet client CSRs persist indefinitely
body:
### What happened?

An incident was triggered by unexpectedly high etcd storage usage on production Kubernetes clusters. Initial analysis revealed that the majority of the space was consumed by a large number of Certificate Signing Requests (CSRs).

Using `etcdctl`, the top resource consumers in etcd were identified:

| Resource Type | Count |
|---------------|-------|
| **CertificateSigningRequests** | **520,858** |
| Events | 1,395 |
| CRDs (Calico) | 1,005 |
| ReplicaSets | 864 |
| RoleBindings | 473 |
| Services | 428 |
| Pods | 416 |

This overwhelming number of CSRs was far beyond what could be explained by normal node provisioning or rotation activity. A sample of 1,000 CSRs showed an average size of **1,192 bytes**, meaning the CSRs alone were consuming **~592 MiB** of etcd space—nearly a third of the 2 GiB etcd limit.

This dates on the resources showed the build up had been happening for years, with one being generated for each node every 15 minutes.

On examination they were all of the type:

```
apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1
kind: CertificateSigningRequest
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2025-07-09T06:51:01Z"
  generateName: csr-
  name: csr-jllx7
  resourceVersion: "296695671"
  uid: 0f6d31fd-c8ed-465e-ac45-e283f453f56c
spec:
  groups:
  - system:nodes
  - system:authenticated
  request: 
  signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet
  usages:
  - digital signature
  - client auth
  username: system:node:

title: HNS loadbalancers for services are not recreated
body:
### What happened?

HNS loadbalancers appear to persist in cache, if removed these are never created throughout the lifecycle of kube-proxy. This out-of-band cleanup of loadbalancers could occur during service restarts of kubelet a CNI or race condition with another service.

Similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133928 however this issue applies to all service types. Reproduction has occurred using the default `internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster`



### What did you expect to happen?

kube-proxy invalidates cache and recreates missing HNS loadbalancers to avoid service disruption

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This has been known to occur during rke2 service restarts, the simplest reproduction is a manual removal of a loadbalancer:

On a Windows worker node:
- List the load balancers: `hnsdiag list loadbalancers`
  - Example:
  ```
  Load Balancer    : 3599612c-54b4-4b9d-9258-4fc5e2100549
    Virtual IPs      : 172.30.0.1
    Direct IP IDs    : 78c19c4d-7edf-43bd-ab2a-5ccf97f214fe
  ```

- Select an LB to remove: `hnsdiag delete loadbalancers <ID>`
  - Example:
  ```
  > hnsdiag delete loadbalancers 3599612c-54b4-4b9d-9258-4fc5e2100549
  ```
- Monitor the LB list, and kube-proxy logs:
  - `hnsdiag list loadbalancers`
  - In kube-proxy logs the LB is persisted in a cache:
  ```
  I1217 23:36:36.438104    7712 proxier.go:1225] "Policy already applied" serviceInfo="172.30.0.1:443/TCP"
  ```

The kube-proxy sync interval continues to log that the policy is applied, yet the loadbalancers list has no matching LB. Restarting kube-proxy will rebuild the loadbalancers.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

RKE2 v1.31.14 (however other versions have been tested, v1.33.6 and v1.34.2)

title: Batch update node status in cloud node controller
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Cloud node controller reconciles on all nodes periodically by quering and updating nodes address. It processes each node one by one. Supporting batch update on nodes can improve the throuput.

https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider/blob/f5511889f9d28a97c8244a8c59bc37856e55715b/controllers/node/node_controller.go#L270-L294

### Why is this needed?

Current behavior is to parallelize the node update across workers, and each request processes single node. Supporting batch node update can improve the throughput of the cloud node controller and reduce the volume of API requests issued to cloud provider.

A security issue was discovered in ingress-nginx where the nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-proxy-set-headers Ingress annotation can be used to inject configuration into nginx. #### Affected Versions

- ingress-nginx: v1.12.5
- ingress-nginx: v1.13.1

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

ACTION REQUIRED: The following steps must be taken to mitigate this vulnerability: Upgrade ingress-nginx to v1.12.5, v1.13.1, or any later version.

#### How to upgrade?

To upgrade, refer to the documentation: [Upgrading Ingress-nginx](https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx/deploy/upgrade/)

### Detection

Suspicious data within a configmap passed to the `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-proxy-set-headers` annotation of an Ingress resource could indicate an attempt to exploit this vulnerability.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact **security@kubernetes.io**

body:

A security issue was discovered in [ingress-nginx](https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx) where the protection afforded by the `auth-url` Ingress annotation may not be effective in the presence of a specific misconfiguration.

If the ingress-nginx controller is configured with a default custom-errors configuration that includes HTTP errors 401 or 403, and if the configured default custom-errors backend is defective and fails to respect the X-Code HTTP header, then an Ingress with the `auth-url` annotation may be accessed even when authentication fails.

Note that the built-in custom-errors backend works correctly. To trigger this issue requires an administrator to specifically configure ingress-nginx with a broken external component.

### Am I vulnerable?

* This issue affects ingress-nginx. If you do not have ingress-nginx installed on your cluster, you are not affected. You can check this by running \`kubectl get pods \--all-namespaces \--selector [app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx](http://app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx)\`.
* This issue only affects Ingresses using the `auth-url` annotation. If you are not adding authentication to your Ingresses using the `auth-url` annotation, then you are not at risk.
* This issue only affects ingress-nginx controllers that have been configured with default custom-errors settings via editing the controller command-line arguments and configuration map. If you are using per-Ingress custom-errors set via Ingress annotations, then you are not at risk.

title: client-go: Replace deprecated BackoffManager with DelayFunc in Reflector
body:
## Why is this needed?

The `Reflector` in `client-go/tools/cache` uses `wait.NewExponentialBackoffManager()` which is deprecated. The deprecation notice recommends using `wait.Backoff{}.DelayWithReset()` instead.

Related issues #117829 and #118638 noted that the deprecation documentation is incomplete - it suggests using `delayFn.Timer()` with `BackoffUntil`, but this doesn't compile because `Timer` doesn't implement `BackoffManager`. 

This issue proposes:
1. Replace `NewExponentialBackoffManager` with `Backoff{}.DelayWithReset()` in the Reflector
2. Use `DelayFunc.Until()` as the loop mechanism (which does work, unlike the documented suggestion)
3. Optionally expose `Backoff` configuration in `ReflectorOptions` for customization

## Benefits
- Removes usage of deprecated API
- Enables context-aware cancellation (BackoffManager doesn't respect context)
- Allows optional customization of backoff strategy when constructing Reflectors

/sig api-machinery
/kind cleanup
/priority backlog

title: NCC-E003660-JAV: Redirection of API Server Traffic to Kubelet
body:
### NCC-E003660-JAV: Redirection of API Server Traffic to Kubelet
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Impact**
A user with GET permissions on the `nodes/proxy` subresource and either PATCH on `nodes/status` or `CREATE` on nodes can manipulate the API Server into authenticating to itself, resulting in cluster-administrator permissions.

**Description**
The Kubernetes API server proxy is a feature which allows users to proxy requests through
the API server to workloads or nodes. The user’s own credentials are not proxied to the
destination, but if the API server recognizes the proxy target as a kubelet, it will
authenticate the request using its own client certificate. It is possible to abuse this
behavior to cause the API server to connect to itself using its own credentials (which
typically will have cluster administrator permissions), by temporarily modifying the cluster
state so that the API server directs proxied traffic to the wrong destination.
While this represents a potential privilege escalation to cluster administrator, the attack
does require significant existing permissions against nodes as a starting point.

For an example, please see the original finding on page 24 of the [Kubernetes 1.24 Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-security/blob/main/sig-security-external-audit/security-audit-2021-2022/findings/Kubernetes%20v1.24%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Recommendation**
Consider whether it is possible to implement additional defensive measures to prevent
proxied requests being sent to the API server’s web port.

**Component**
kube-apiserver

**Anything else we need to know?**
See umbrella issue [#118980](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118980) for current status of all issues created from these findings

title: Consider providing separate etcd destination for CRDs
body:
### What would you like to be added?

As of now, Kubernetes api server provides a mechanism to push events to a separate etcd cluster using the --etcd-servers-overrides="/events#" flag. This issue is to request similar mechanism for sending CRDs to separate etcd cluster.


### Why is this needed?

Primary motivation is to keep the main etcd cluster performant.

* CRD listing - Some workloads use their CRDs for events (example argo). These events cause issues similar to the Kubernetes native events - they have spiky writes and they keep getting LIST calls typically from monitoring tools. The motivation for moving these out of main etcd cluster is similar to the reasoning for moving Kubernetes events out of main etcd cluster.

* CRD count - Some CRDs produce millions of objects and affect the performance of main etcd cluster.

title: Implement watch limit in APF
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Implement a limit mechanism in APF to limit how many ongoing watches can be accepted. 

### Why is this needed?

Current APF only limits the rate of accepting watch requests. As a result, the total number of watches can creep up with long watch duration regardless how low the rate is limited, which puts a risk on kube-apiserver's memory usage. A crude estimate of memory overhead for a watch is around 50KiB-100KiB.

This feature can be incorporated in most APF concepts and limit watch number per priority. But it might need to have a new tunable similar to `--max-requests-inflight` as in `--max-watches-inflights` and then each priority has a share of this total number.

title: failing device-plugin health checks causing kubelet SIGABRT by systemd watchdog during initialization.
body:
### What happened?

We have Kubelet, version 1.34, running in a systemd service, configured to expect watchdog updates atleast every 20 seconds. 

If the updateRuntimeUp function does not run to completion within this deadline, it causes the `device-plugin` health check to fail, causing watchdog updates to not be sent to systemd, which causes kubelet to crash-loop. 

In our case, the updateRuntimeUp function was blocked on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3ec72e2e973664a0690bc7122c9cd291702b5f36/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L3020

The device-plugin health check is failing because device manager service is initialized, but the device-plugin start is blocked by the delayed updateRuntimeUp. 




### What did you expect to happen?

device-plugin health check should not be expected to pass until kubelet is fully initialized?

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

run kubelet with the recommended watchdog timeout of ~15 seconds, and cause updateRuntimeUp to be blocked on first start.

title: kubelet: static pod manifest changes to command/args/volumes silently ignored — containerChanged() hash limited to name+image since PR #124220
body:
### What happened

When modifying static pod manifests on disk (e.g., adding `--encryption-provider-config` to kube-apiserver), the kubelet:
1. Detects the file change via inotify ✅
2. Reads the new spec from disk ✅
3. `podsDifferSemantically()` detects the spec changed ✅
4. Pod workers receive the update and call `SyncPod()` ✅
5. `computePodActions()` calls `containerChanged()` → returns **false** ❌
6. **No container restart occurs — old configuration persists** ❌

**Impact:** This prevents any post-deployment static pod configuration changes that don't involve an image change. Specifically tested and confirmed broken:
- Adding `--encryption-provider-config` flag (encryption at rest)
- Adding `volumeMounts` and `volumes`
- Any command-line flag additions/changes

Tested on **6 control plane nodes** across **2 independent clusters** (SIT and UAT), all running Kubernetes v1.33.3 with kubeadm.

### What you expected to happen

When a static pod manifest file is modified, the kubelet should detect spec changes and restart the affected container with the new configuration, as documented in the [Kubernetes static pod documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/static-pod/).

### Root Cause Analysis

The bug involves two code-level issues that compound for static pods:

#### Primary: `pickFieldsToHash()` only hashes `name` and `image`

**File:** `pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go`

```go
// pickFieldsToHash pick fields that will affect the running status of the
// container for hash, currently this field range only contains `image` and `name`.
// Note: this list must be updated if ever kubelet wants to allow mutations to other fields.
func pickFieldsToHash(container *v1.Container) map[string]string {
    retval := map[string]string{
        "name":  container.Name,
        "image": container.Image,
    }
    return retval
}
```

This function was intentionally limited by **PR #124220** (merged May 2024) to prevent cluster-wide co

title: watchlist request will be closed abnormally when cacheInterval contains a large amount of watchEvents
body:
### What happened?

I'm conducting an investigation into watchList benchmark in 1.30 Kubernetes cluster. I found that using `watchList` request to make the reflector become synced takes longer than using `list` request. 

Then, I found that the apiserver always prints `Forcing %s watcher close due to unresponsiveness: key.... ` log.  I realized that if `cacheInterval ` containes lots of watchEvents, then cacheWatcher.Process will not be invoked until all watchEvents in `cacheInterval` have been sent. As a result, the `input` channel in `cacheWatcher` may become full, leading to the abnormal closure of the watchlist request.

Therefore, are there any solutions to address this issue? Perhaps we need a new watchList request handler to process watchList requests instead of reusing the original watch request handler's logic. 

If there isn't a similar issue in this problem, we can use the current issue to track it. :)

### What did you expect to happen?

Using watchList request to make the reflector become synced takes approximately the same amount of time as using list request.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create 5K Pods
2. use watchlist request to make reflector become synced. At the same time, start many client to update pods
3. watchlist request will be close and apiserver prints `Forcing %s watcher close due to unresponsiveness: key.... ` log

title: Ephemeral-storage data on node status does not reflect actual available storage after disk expansion
body:
### What happened?

When expanding available node disk space (e.g. expanding root disk size on EKS node), the kubelet does not take into account the available filesystem size change and still advertises initial `ephemeral-storage`  `capacity` and `allocatable` values on node status, obtained by the kubelet on startup. **Because of that, both scheduler and kubelet reject pods with ephemeral storage requests, that actually are satisfiable by the current node root disk size.**

The root cause I believe lies in fact, for node status kubelet only ever fetches actual data on startup and then never refreshes it again: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/243d8c000e451da6f0e8f80704db5d5f672d3d18/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L939
 
It is already done properly for node metrics (`/api/v1/nodes/worker-1/proxy/stats/summary`) and for eviction logic, meaning by not setting an ephemeral storage requests or limits I can run a pod on such node, that will effectively use more `ephemeral-storage` than what kubelet advertises (but within the bounds of expanded node disk of course) and it will not get evicted.

### What did you expect to happen?

`ephemeral-storage` capacity (and allocatable) for node status should be dynamically calculated (taken from cadvisor) on each update, without the need to restart kubelet.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create for example an EKS cluster, increase size of an EBS Volume used as root disk on any node, and grow the partition, where `/var/lib/kubelet` is. Now compare `ephemeral-storage` values in node status with actual available storage on the disk (e.g. on `/var/lib/kubelet`, to be precise).

### Anything else we need to know?

Based on the code I assume the issue is vendor-agnostic.

title: Scheduling queue cleanup ideas
body:
While adding PopFromBackoffQ feature I found some areas of improvements in the scheduling queue code:

- [ ] Add comments to `activeQueuer` and `SchedulingQueue` interfaces.
- [ ] Move `unschedulablePods` struct and its methods to a separate file. We have already moved activeQ and backoffQ. (@onasser1)
- [ ] Make the interfaces of  `activeQueue`, `backoffQueue` and `unschedulablePods` consistent to improve readability. Especially, add `has` method to the `unschedulablePods`, split its `addOrUpdate` to `add` and `update`, make `get` returning `ok` parameter.
- [ ] Unify logging "Pod moved to an internal scheduling queue". Sometimes it's logged two times. Probably, it would be the best to log it in queues' add methods where we already increment `scheduler_queue_incoming_pods_total` metric.

/sig scheduling
/kind cleanup

title: Allow go k8s client to accept KUBECONFIG env readily
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The kubeconfig environment variable typically uses a colon-separated format for specifying multiple paths. However, the Kubernetes Go client library currently only supports a single path. This inconsistency can be confusing for developers. To simplify things, let's make the Go client accept the colon-separated format for kubeconfig paths, making it consistent with the standard environment variable format.

KUBECONFIG env doc: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/access-application-cluster/configure-access-multiple-clusters/#set-the-kubeconfig-environment-variable

Following is the simple example to explain the issue:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0d439b43-0220-4501-bd25-eb72a56e425b)


### Why is this needed?

Currently, users have to do extra work to get the config-path value from `KUBECONFIG` env. The Go client library expects a single value, but the system environment variables for `KUBECONFIG` are separated by colons. Let's make the Go client accept the `KUBECONFIG` env value readily. This would make it consistent with how the system handles these variables and make things easier for developers

title: Copy files after a job completed
body:
### What would you like to be added?

GIVEN a job that has been executed like:

`kubectl run job1 --image=busybox --restart=Never -- /bin/sh -c "echo test > /output.txt"`

WHEN copying the output after the job has been completed:

`kubectl cp job1:/output.txt output.txt`

THEN the file should be copied but the following error message is displayed instead:

`error: cannot exec into a container in a completed pod; current phase is Succeeded`

### Why is this needed?

The reason why you don't want to define a volume is that you just want to get the result of your job this one time, it is not something that is needed long-term.

This issue is almost 4 years old: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubectl/issues/454

Also in combination with the existing feature TTL-after-finished (see Link[1]: Automatic Clean-up for Finished Jobs) this issue makes really sense in my opinion.

Link[1]: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/ttlafterfinished/

title: Support TLS Server Name overrides in EgressSelectorConfiguration
body:
## What would you like to be added?

Add a `tlsServerName` field to the `TLSConfig` structure in `EgressSelectorConfiguration` to allow overriding the hostname used for TLS certificate verification, similar to the existing `tls-server-name` field in kubeconfig (added in[ #88769](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/88769)).

## Precedent

This functionality already exists in:
- **kubeconfig files**: The `tls-server-name` field was added in #88769 for similar use cases
- **kubectl**: The `--tls-server-name` flag provides command-line access
- **Go's `tls.Config`**: The underlying `ServerName` field supports this

The egress selector `TLSConfig` would benefit from the same capability for consistency.

## Why is this needed?

### Use Case

This addresses scenarios where components using EgressSelectorConfiguration connect through Kubernetes Service DNS names (e.g., proxy.svc.cluster.local) but that hostname is not included in the server certificate's Subject Alternative Names (SANs), which define which hostnames a certificate is valid for.

**Example scenario:**
- Egress selector is configured to connect to: `https://konnectivity-service.example.svc.cluster.local:8443`
- The proxy's TLS certificate contains SANs for: `proxy.example.com`
- Connection fails because `konnectivity-service.example.svc.cluster.local` is not in the certificate SANs

### Current Workaround Limitations

The current workaround of updating certificates to include all possible service DNS names has significant drawbacks:
- Requires certificate regeneration and rotation across many clusters
- Service names may vary across environments (dev, staging, prod)
- Certificate management becomes complex in multi-tenant environments
- May require coordination with external PKI infrastructure

Add an optional `tlsServerName` field to override the hostname used for certificate verification:

title: CEL cost budget exceeded when using messageExpression
body:
### What happened?

I have a CRD with the following property within the top level spec schema:
```
config:
  type: object
  x-kubernetes-validations:
    - messageExpression: '''invalid attempts: '' + string(self.attempts)'
      rule: self.attempts >= 0
  properties:
    attempts:
      type: integer
      maximum: 2147483647
      minimum: -2147483648
```

The API server rejects the CRD with the following error:
```
* spec.validation.openAPIV3Schema.properties[spec].properties[config].x-kubernetes-validations[0].messageExpression: Forbidden: estimated messageExpression cost exceeds budget by factor of more than 100x (try simplifying the rule, or adding maxItems, maxProperties, and maxLength where arrays, maps, and strings are declared)
* spec.validation.openAPIV3Schema.properties[spec].properties[config].x-kubernetes-validations[0].messageExpression: Forbidden: contributed to estimated rule cost total exceeding cost limit for entire OpenAPIv3 schema
* spec.validation.openAPIV3Schema: Forbidden: x-kubernetes-validations estimated rule cost total for entire OpenAPIv3 schema exceeds budget by factor of more than 100x (try simplifying the rule, or adding maxItems, maxProperties, and maxLength where arrays, maps, and strings are declared)
```

This entire CRD contains a single CEL rule, and this is only a problem when using `messageExpression` in the validation rule. 

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect `string(intValue)` to not cause the cost budget of the validation rule to be exceeded.

title: client-go v1.32/v1.33 WatchList is incompatible with kube-apiserver v1.34
body:
### What happened?

When using `client-go` `v1.32.x` against a Kubernetes `v1.34.x` API server, informers/reflectors may log:
> The watchlist request for nodes ended with an error, falling back to the standard LIST semantics, err = "kubernetes.io/initial-events-list-blueprint" annotation is missing content

The client then falls back to standard `LIST/WATCH`, so this is not always a fatal failure, but the WatchList path itself is not compatible.

### What did you expect to happen?
`client-go v1.32.x` should either:
1. remain compatible with a `v1.34.x` API server for WatchList, or
2. cleanly avoid using the incompatible WatchList path.


### How can we reproduce it?

Use:

- `client-go`: `v1.32.x` (same applies to `v1.33.x`)
- `kube-apiserver`: `v1.34.x`



Enable the client WatchList path (`WatchListClient`) and start an informer/reflector against a `v1.34` apiserver.

The reflector will attempt WatchList and then log:

> The watchlist request ended with an error, falling back to the standard LIST/WATCH semantics ...

with the specific error:

> `"kubernetes.io/initial-events-list-blueprint" annotation is missing content`

### What do you see in the code?

In `client-go v1.32.x`, the WatchList client logic still expects the bookmark event to contain:

`kubernetes.io/initial-events-list-blueprint`

The old code path is in `staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request.go`:

- `WatchListResult`
- `WatchListResult.Into()`
- `Request.handleWatchList()`

That code explicitly reads `metav1.InitialEventsListBlueprintAnnotationKey` from the bookmark and returns an error if the annotation is empty/missing.

In Kubernetes `v1.34`, the API server removed that annotation from the synthetic bookmark event. The 1.34 changelog explicitly says:

> Removes the `kubernetes.io/initial-events-list-blueprint` annotation from the synthetic "Bookmark" event for the watch stream requests.

Also, newer reflector code no longer reconstructs a typed `List` from the watch stream. Instead it uses:

title: Pod affinity implementation with multiple rules does not match documentation
body:
### What happened?

When using multiple rules in `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution`, they must currently both match the same pod, or else the pod will not be able to be scheduled.

This makes it impossible to use pod affinity to require that a pod be placed on the same node as multiple other separate pods.

### What did you expect to happen?

The [API documentation](https://kubespec.dev/kubernetes/v1/Pod) says this:

> When there are multiple elements, the lists of nodes corresponding to each
> podAffinityTerm are intersected, i.e. all terms must be satisfied.

So I expected that since both rules can be satisfied for the node, the pod should be scheduled on that node.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Assuming a single node cluster:

```yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: required-a
  labels:
    name: required-a
spec:
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: required-b
  labels:
    name: required-b
spec:
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: affinity-test-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: pause
    image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9
  affinity:
    podAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      - labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            name: required-a
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      - labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            name: required-b

```

PVC should get mounted on the pods without any failedMount messages.

The issue can be easily reproduced on a 10 node cluster with Kubernetes deployment having 800 pod replicas asking to mount the same PVC.

### Anything else we need to know?

This issue is related to an old bug [84169](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/84169) that was closed saying the issue got fixed with k8s 1.17+ but it seems the issue still persists.

title: Cloud Controller Manger doesn't query cloud provider for node name, causing the node to be removed
body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!-->


**What happened**:

- Launch a node with container linux `CoreOS-stable-1911.3.0` on aws, with customized ignition configs.
- The hostname turns to be `ip-10-3-18-1`, instead of the full private dns `ip-10-3-18-1.us-west-1.compute.internal` because `/etc/hostname` is not set.
- kubelet starts with `--cloud-provider=external` and skips [this code path](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.14.0-alpha.0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L382-L395). So it's not able to set the private dns as the node name.
- When CCM starts, it tries to read the node name from the node spec.
- CCM calls [`GetInstanceProviderID()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.14.0-alpha.0/pkg/controller/cloud/node_controller.go#L361) and fails.
- CCM calls [`getNodeAddressesByProviderIDOrName()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.14.0-alpha.0/pkg/controller/cloud/node_controller.go#L372) and fails too.
- CCM then removes the node.


**What you expected to happen**:

Since now the kubelet runs with `--cloud-provider=external`, no one is executing that code path to query the cloud provider to get the node name anymore.
However this code path still needs to be executed by someone to get the correct node name from the cloud provider for the node.
I think the CCM might need to query the cloud provider for the full node hostname in case the hostname given by the kubelet is not the full hostname (in AWS case).

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Launch a container linux with non-empty ignition config in the user data, then the hostname won't be the full `private-dns`.
Then launch kubelet with `--cloud-provider=external` and CCM will reproduce the issue described above.

title: CVE-2026-3865: CSI Driver for SMB path traversal via subDir may delete unintended directories on the NFS server
body:
**CVSS Rating:**  
[CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3-1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H) — **Medium (6.5)**

A vulnerability was discovered in the Kubernetes CSI Driver for SMB where the subDir parameter in volume identifiers was insufficiently validated. Attackers with the ability to create PersistentVolumes referencing the SMB CSI driver could craft volume identifiers containing path traversal sequences (../). During volume deletion or cleanup operations, the driver could operate on unintended directories outside the intended managed path within the SMB export.

This may lead to deletion or modification of directories on the SMB server.

### Am I vulnerable?

You may be vulnerable if:
You run the CSI Driver for SMB (smb.csi.k8s.io)
Your cluster allows users to create PersistentVolumes referencing the SMB CSI driver
Your CSI driver version does not validate traversal sequences in the subDir field


#### Affected Versions
All versions of the CSI Driver for SMB prior to the v1.20.1 release containing the fix for traversal validation are affected.

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

This issue can be mitigated by:
Upgrading the CSI Driver for SMB to a patched version
Restricting PersistentVolume creation privileges to trusted administrators
Reviewing SMB exports to ensure only intended directories are writable by the driver

As a best practice, untrusted users should not be granted permission to create arbitrary PersistentVolumes referencing external storage drivers.


#### Fixed Versions

CSI Driver for SMB versions >= v1.20.1

To determine if your cluster may be affected:
Inspect PersistentVolumes using the SMB CSI driver and review the volumeHandle field.
Look for traversal sequences such as: `../`
Review CSI controller logs for unexpected directory operations. e.g. “Removing subPath: /tmp/mount-uuid/legitimate/../../../exports/subdir”

title: Race window between scheduler and device plugin restart in kubelet
body:
### What happened?

We restart a device plugin frequently as part of our design.

When a device plugin goes down, kubelet [marks the devices it was managing as unhealthy](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L240), removing it from allocatable, and preventing Pods from scheduling. However, it [keeps the resource in capacity for a grace period](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L415) in hopes that the device plugin will come back up and scheduled pods can keep running with no disruption.

Kube-scheduler reads node state and chooses nodes to schedule pods on based on allocatable resources.

If the device plugin restarts between the kube-scheduler decision and when kubelet tries to start allocating resources for the new Pod, then the pod is rejected and enters a Failed state.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod to either successfully schedule, or to stay in pending until the device plugin restarts

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I have not found a reliable reproducer. I think adding a large sleep before the lock acquisition [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L548) would widen the timing window significantly, but I could not figure out how to deploy a changed kubelet

title: kubectl get storageclass should indicate the effective default StorageClass when multiple defaults exist
body:
### What would you like to be added?

When multiple StorageClasses are annotated as default (`storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"`), Kubernetes uses the most recently created one as the actual default applied to PVCs without an explicit storageClassName.
https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/storage-classes/#default-storageclass

However, kubectl get storageclass currently shows all of them simply as (default), which makes it unclear which StorageClass will actually be used.

I propose enhancing the kubectl get storageclass output to indicate which default StorageClass is effective.

For example:
```
NAME                       PROVISIONER                   RECLAIMPOLICY   AGE
nfs-client (default, effective)   k8s-sigs.io/nfs-...  Delete          3s
standard   (default, inactive)    rancher.io/local-path Delete         48m
```

or by adding a new column:
```
NAME         PROVISIONER                   DEFAULT   EFFECTIVE   AGE
nfs-client   k8s-sigs.io/nfs-...           true      true        3s
standard     rancher.io/local-path         true      false       48m
```

now display
```
NAME                    PROVISIONER                RECLAIMPOLICY   AGE
nfs-client (default)    k8s-sigs.io/nfs-...        Delete          3s
standard   (default)    rancher.io/local-path      Delete          48m
```

### Why is this needed?

This improves user experience and reduces operational mistakes.

title: [declarative validation] `+k8s:minimum` / `+k8s:maximum` do not correctly handle signedness and associated type bounds/boundary-values (ex: int32 vs int64)
body:
Declarative validation's `validation-gen`'s `ParseInt` returns Go `int` (64-bit) but does not validate that the parsed value fits in the target field's type. Values outside the target type's range are silently accepted at codegen time. For unsigned types, large values cannot be parsed at all. No boundary condition tests exist.

### Impact

**int32 vs int64:** All Kubernetes API integers are `int32` or `int64`. Writing `+k8s:minimum=-2147483649` on an `int32` field passes codegen without error but emits a literal that overflows `int32`.

**Unsigned types:** `strconv.Atoi` cannot parse values above `math.MaxInt64`, so `+k8s:maximum=18446744073709551615` on a `uint64` field fails. No kubernets native API types use unsigned integers today (from looking through `*/types.go` files), so this would be for library correctness currently.

**Untyped literal emission:** `toGolangSourceDataLiteral` uses `fmt.Sprintf("%v")` which emits untyped literals that may overflow or truncate near type boundaries.

### How to reproduce

1. Add `+k8s:minimum=-2147483649` to an `int32` field on a type with validation-gen enabled.
2. Run `hack/update-codegen.sh`.
3. Codegen succeeds, but the generated literal overflows `int32`.

Or:

1. Add `+k8s:maximum=18446744073709551615` to a `uint64` field.
2. Run `hack/update-codegen.sh`.
3. Codegen fails: `strconv.Atoi` cannot parse the value.

### What should happen

Codegen should reject values outside the target type's range with a clear error (e.g., "value -2147483649 does not fit in int32"). Values at the boundary (e.g., `-2147483648` for int32) should work correctly and emit properly typed Go literals.

### Fix outline

1. Split `ParseInt` into `ParseSignedInt` (returns `int64`) and `ParseUnsignedInt` (returns `uint64`).
2. In `minimumTagValidator`/`maximumTagValidator`, check the field's signedness, call the right parser, and validate the value fits the target type's range.
3. Emit typed literals (`int64(...)`, `uint64(...)`) in `toGolangSourceD

title: kubelet does not start when kubelet folder is on ZFS filesystem because of missing cadvisor plugin in 1.36.0
body:
### What happened?

After upgrading to Kubernetes 1.36.0, the kubelet crashes directly after startup on systems that have the `/var/lib/kubelet` folder configured on a ZFS filesystem. The direct error shown in the logs is:

```
E0423 21:45:14.682963  326484 kubelet.go:1821] "Failed to start ContainerManager" err="failed to get rootfs info: failed to get device for dir \"/var/lib/kubelet\": with major: 0, minor: 60: could not find device in cached partitions map"
```

This error is caused by the kubelet not being able to determine the available space for empheral storage, which it normally gets using cadvisor.

After increasing the log level, it seems that this is caused by cadvisor not having access to its ZFS plugin:
```
Apr 23 21:45:14 strike01 kubelet[326484]: I0423 21:45:14.680361  326484 fs.go:406] no plugin found for filesystem type: zfs
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Like Kubernetes 1.35.3 (or 1.35.4 for that matter): I expect the kubelet to startup and work.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

As described above: Ensure `/var/lib/kubelet` is on a ZFS filesystem and start the kubelet with any configuration.

### Anything else we need to know?

I am aware that Kubernetes does not maintain cadvisor and that cadvisor bugs should not be posted here. However, I believe that cadvisor is working correctly, it is just missing its ZFS plugin.

FS plug-ins in cadvisor are introduced in version v0.55.0, before the introduction everything was built-in. Kubernetes 1.36.0 brings cadvisor from version [v0.53.0 → v0.56.0](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/compare/v0.53.0...v0.56.0). It was specifically introduced in https://github.com/google/cadvisor/commit/28ecaa9d9b4aa2ea878f7692a315797c2a9d7a7c

In the PR merging 0.55.1, #135829, I see that some file system extensions are specifically being imported (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135829/changes#diff-ca41d4fa89358cfbf866e71de1c54ab978a448e805495bf8bca923d85da
